A forest of permutations called fixed points forest, was recently discovered and has drawn the interest of researchers due to its intriguing properties. One notable feature of this forest is the emergence of numerous small paths as the size of the permutations increases. A key path property is the random shortest path length converges to a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and variable standard deviation. Conversely, the expected length of the shortest path to a leaf, obtained through the central result of this study, grows polynomially with n. Specifically, its growth is established to be no greater than $2n\log n$ and its lower limit to be at least $\frac{n}{6}$ when n is sufficiently large. These findings also apply to any other forest resulting from permutations' fixed points. Furthermore, they can be utilized to validate two recent conjectures related to the generating function of the forest's paths. Lastly, the findings can also be applied to validate a hypothesis by Erdos regarding the presence of a prime gap of a specific size in the vicinity of n.

These future experimental studies could confirm the identified molecular pentaquark states. Our method can be applied to potential $\Xi_b \bar B$ systems in the future. This research demonstrates that the Euler-Poincaré polynomial of a bundle with fibers equivalent to the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold can be calculated using a specific type of hypersurface in high-dimensional space. Furthermore, it confirms a previous finding by N. N. Petrov in a lower dimension and offers a new method for evaluating a particular integral of the connection component of the second heat equation for the Laplace-Beltrami operator over the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold. Additionally, it presents an alternative approach or proof for several theoretical connections identified by V. I. Arnold, F. Brieskorn, and R. Bott. Lastly, it derives a novel expression for calculating the Euler-Poincaré polynomial of a particular type of quasifibration based on its spectral data. This result is inspired by a challenge issued by Arnold. Precise calculations of the Euler-Poincaré polynomial were carried out for a bundle with the same fiber as the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold, but with an additional two parameters, for: i) a particular type of surface with three holes when it's not an essential one, ii) a particular type of surface with three holes when it's an essential one, and iii) a particular type of general smooth manifold with high dimension and any number of holes. It was also shown that the computed polynomial has a specific factorization, consistent with a theoretical finding by Arnold. By incorporating the discovered polynomial with specific integration properties into an operator, it can generate a particular type of eigenfunction for the Laplace-Beltrami operator over the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold, which has some distinct properties. This result was theoretically confirmed by comparing it with the previously developed monograph by J. S. Milne. Moreover, it can estimate or bound the spectral gaps of the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold, which was also explored by Arnold. By employing specific mathematical theorems, it can map the eigenfunctions generated by the discovered operator to the periodic points of a particular type of dynamical system, which was also previously studied by Arnold. This result is considered an essential theoretical connection between topology, geometry, and dynamics. By employing additional mathematical theorems, it can map the eigenfunctions to the periodic elements of a particular type of sheaf, which was also explored by Petrov. By linking specific mathematical theorems, it can map the eigenfunctions to the algebraic-geometric invariants of the Arnold-Brieskorn manifold, which was also previously developed by Brieskorn.

The process of forming high-density amorphous ice (HDA) from low-density amorphous ice (LDA) and hexagonal ice (I$h$) was investigated through molecular dynamics simulation. LDA and I$h$ structures were found to transition into HDA through a collective motion involving the breaking and reforming of hydrogen bonds. Two distinct transition types were observed: one involving the large-scale rearrangement of many molecules (as seen in LDA) and another characterized by smaller-scale displacements (observed in I$h$). These transitions occurred through the breaking of hydrogen bonds in the space surrounding individual molecules, facilitating large-scale movements. An energy fluctuation analysis revealed the absence of distinct patterns indicative of first-order phase transitions in both LDA $\rightarrow$ HDA and I$h$\$\rightarrow$ HDA. Instead, these transitions were found to correspond to broad energy distribution shifts. In contrast, the ice-I$_c$ $\rightarrow$ HDA transition (which occurs at larger pressures) involved the ice-I$_c$ hexagonal structure melting into HDA, characterized by shorter and longer-range motions. These results explain the transition mechanism into HDA and link it with the properties of low-temperature superconducting hydrogenated water ices. Additionally, these findings call into question existing theories that consider the formation of ring structures in low-temperature ices, as simulations on LDA and I$h$, including those with 2592 oxygen atoms, failed to exhibit such ring formations. Nevertheless, the oxygen atoms surrounding each oxygen atom formed rings with an average size of approximately 0.27 nm. These results also confirm an earlier study indicating the observation of LDA $\rightarrow$ HDA and I$c$\$\rightarrow$ HDA transitions in identical experimental conditions. These findings call for the re-evaluation of theories regarding the properties of low-temperature ices. The simulation codes used in this study are available online at https://github.com/jordi/HDice.git. An initial release with the codes including LDA, I$c$, and HDA structures as well as the MD simulation results on 216 oxygen atoms will soon follow. The Archive of Formal Proofs store electronically certified proof scripts 
that have been carefully verified, featuring a vast collection of over 3,500 
methods using schemes such as Isabelle and Coq. A recent study examined the 
network properties of the AFP dependency graph, revealing that the degree of 
each node within the archive adheres to scale-free distribution patterns. 
Moreover, the researchers found that the level of node in-degree tends to be 
more critical than out-degree when assessing resilience against random attacks. 
However, the study also demonstrated that directed attacks that prioritize the 
most active nodes in the archive can successfully destroy nearly 50% of the 
network, despite lacking knowledge of the network structure. Interestingly, 
the attackers can achieve this using only about 5% of the network's active nodes, 
highlighting the considerable threat that strategic directed attacks pose to 
systems such as the AFP. Furthermore, the study further analyzed the study of 
the archive's evolution over time and found that the size of the archive has 
grown exponentially since its inception in 2002, with the annual growth 
rate fluctuating between three to four percent.  If the current dynamics 
remain unchanged, the total number of archived proof scripts is anticipated 
to surpass one million in the future. Moreover, the researchers found that 
the total dependencies within the archive have been steadily increasing over 
time and that the average number of connections per node has been 
constantly decreasing, pointing to a significant trend of 
bipartite-specialization-differentiation in the archive's development. 
Lastly, the study also compared the archive's network properties to those of 
the global scientific publication network obtained from web links, revealing 
that both networks share striking similarities in their scale-free nature, 
low-dimensional geometry, and strategic vulnerability to directed attacks. 
Moreover, the researchers found that the scientific publication network exhibits 
a considerably longer persistence time of nearly 80 years, whereas the archive 
could potentially lose its structure within two years if not properly 
protected. 
In conclusion, the study provided valuable insights that may guide 
strategically-directed-attacks on systems similar to the AFP in the future. 
Additionally, the researchers attempted to develop the first-ever scientific 
study using network theory to protect the archive, thereby enhancing the 
archive's resilience to such attacks. 
In the final section of the dissertation, the limitations and of course 
criticisms of the methodological approach are acknowledged.

In this study, we aim to comprehend how GNNs transfer knowledge from one task to another. Firstly, we develop a framework for measuring task similarity. We then conduct experiments to investigate the impact of source task community structure on GNN output. The findings reveal that GNNs generalize community structures across tasks and that community structure similarity between source and target tasks influences GNN output similarity. Moreover, we discover that GNNs learn task-specific community structures rather than individual node features. Based on these results, we develop a new hypothesis explaining GNN transferability compared to FCNNs, which is subsequently substantiated by our analysis of real-world dataset results. For further validation, we apply our community structure similarity measure to open-source task pairing methods and demonstrate that it leads to improved GNN model performance. The methods and data used in this study are available online.

The quark nugget model of axions has been suggested as an explanation for the 
implied coexistence of dark and visible matter in the universe, assuming that 
dark matter consists of contained axions. However, this assumption is contradicted 
by cosmological observations which show that matter consisting of axions cannot 
be infinitely dense and must have a minimum average density below $10^{14}$ 
GeV/c$^2$. The possibility that the quark nugget model of axions may not fully 
explain the observed coexistence of dark and visible matter is investigated. 
Assuming that dense axion objects have already been produced in high-energy 
cosmological collisions and contribute to the bulk of dark matter, a range of 
nugget masses $10^{ - 7} \leq \xi \leq 10^{10}$ emerges. Moreover, if the 
nugget's own axion field acts to minimize its density, a lower limit on the 
nugget's mass can be set at $\xi_{\min }=\mathcal{O}(10^{12})$ Kelvin, 
approximately  one order of magnitude greater than the typical quark-gluon 
liquid density. This finding implies that the quark nugget model of axions may 
not fully fulfill its purpose of simplifying the cosmology of dark and visible 
matter coexistence.  A simulation of such dense axion objects has been added to 
the MADGRAPH library, allowing for further understanding of their possible role in 
the universe. 

The implications of this finding for the axion's anomalous cross-section and 
particle distribution are also explored. 

A related hypothesis that high-energy dark matter particles could be produced 
infinitely dense and constitute the bulk of dark matter in the universe is 
also formulated. 

A potential connection between the axion's quark nugget model and the "anti-matter 
paradox" is also investigated.

background anisotropy has been completed, and the consequences of this finding for 
the axion's quark nugget model have been determined.

In the domain of deep learning based few-shot learning, we deviate from the conventional supervised meta-learning approach. Instead, a more universal framework is developed that doesn't demand modification of the parameter-updating procedure or the loss functions. This framework can be utilized with any model, eliminating the need for architectural engineering from a few-shot learning perspective. By integrating an unsupervised outlier detection method with few-shot learning, our framework effectively excludes outlier samples, thereby enhancing the test generalizability. This framework is validated through experiments on image and text datasets, resulting in notable improvements in few-shot learning tasks. For instance, on the miniImageCub dataset, the few-shot learning accuracy is elevated by 12.45%, 10.25%, and 9.35% for 5-way, 20-way, and 60-way tasks, respectively. This framework is further demonstrated to be versatile in addressing various few-shot learning few-shot scenarios. The framework and associated code are freely accessible at \url{https://github.com/EducatingAI/FSDL}.

Our study shows that in a boundary CFT with a chiral symmetry, a local current operator and corresponding charge defect can only exist if the defect itself has a non-invertible nature. Further, the presence of this current operator and associated charge defect have a limited impact on the total fusion structure of defects within the system, specifically restricting multi-component defects from being trivial in nature. Additionally, the central charge of the underlying CFT can be determined from the entropy of a non-trivial defect, demonstrating a connection between the former and the modular properties of the latter. Lastly, the Penrose transform's conformal block can be used to develop an expanded fusion framework that includes both the primary operators and non-invertible charge defects, leading to a defect-based interpretation of the fusion space. As an example, the principles developed can explain the properties of a single component defect found in the Hanbury Brown and Madelung interferometry, a quantum system known as the DBM model. This explanation ties the long-range correlations observed in the DBM model to the non-trivial fusion structure of its defects. Moreover, the case of multiple component defects in the DBM scenario is investigated, revealing that the different wave functions derived for the topological cluster states originate from the non-trivial fusion of the system's defects. Our study also compares the entanglement assessment of the DBM model with that of the HaPPY bond model, a quantum system lacking translation symmetry. Finally, the consistency between the extended fusion structure of defects and the pruning algorithm, a method used to compute the fusions of a given charge, is verified through explicit calculations. As the principles developed are largely based on general properties of a chiral CFT, they are expected to also apply to the bulk properties of a log gravity theory described by the asymptotic safety theory, specifically its spinor fields and non-invertible charge source. Given the recent interest in log gravity within the context of quantum gravity, we speculate further on its potential applications. Furthermore, the extended fusion structure of defects may offer a novel method for evaluating the fusions of irregular Virasoro representations, particularly those that cannot be reached through a modular invariant. The principles developed could potentially be expanded to apply to the general case of a CFT with a chiral symmetry. Specifically, we show that for graphs with a distinct equilibrium, it can be determined in polynomial time whether a semi-transitive orientation exists. Furthermore, for split graphs with a relatively small independent set, we design a straightforward orientation algorithm. Interestingly, for the case where the independent set has a size of 2, this problem reduces to a well-known, but apparently intractable, problem. In contrast, for the scenario where the independent set has a size of at least 3, and the corresponding clique has a size of at least 3, we prove that semi-transitive orientation yields a maximum flow maximum flow equivalence. Specifically, we show that for graphs satisfying this condition, the maximum flow and optimum cut have a size that differ by no more than 2. To establish this result, we introduce a novel concept: equivalent orientations. In our proof, we show that for graphs meeting the specified criteria, it is possible to establish an equivalent orientation that lies within a constant distance of the original orientation. As an additional contribution, we show that for graphs with a distinct equilibrium, it is possible to establish a semi-transitive orientation whose value of the maximum flow differs by no more than 2 from the optimum cut. Furthermore, for split graphs with a relatively small independent set, we derive bounds on the distance between equivalent orientations. Specifically, for the case where the independent set has a size of n - 1, we obtain a bound of n - 1, and for the case where the independent set has a size of at least 3, we obtain a bound of 3. In contrast, for the scenario where the independent set has a size of 2, this bound reduces to 2. In our proof, we show that for graphs meeting the specified criteria, the property of equivalent orientations with a bounded distance corresponds to the property of equivalent orientations with a bounded maximum flow and optimum cut. Specifically, for the case where the independent set has a size of n - 1, we derive the equivalence of semi-transitive orientation, polynomial-time orientation, and unguent properties. In our conclusion, we speculate on the unguent properties of split graphs with a relatively small independent set. We theoretically investigate mechanical mode-enhanced Brillouin interactions in photonic Waveguide Lattices with mixed symmetries. We demonstrate that mechanical oscillators in structures with broken and preserved symmetries couple with multiple optical modes of distinct polarizations, despite these modes not being naturally coupled. Notably, the mechanical coupling strengths with various optical modes are regulated by the wave propagation at the waveguide boundaries, which is driven by the optical wave's waveguide confinement properties and spatial propagation characteristics. Our analysis reveals significant enhanced Brillouin coupling strengths up to ~104 Hz/km (in units of mechanical frequency), which can be achieved in photonic Wavelength division multiplexing systems with engineered mechanical and optical properties. These findings have implications for the development of sensitive photonic chip-based sensors capable of detecting minute molecular or nuclear perturbations. Additionally, the research offers a foundation for exploring novel quantum phenomena between optical and mechanical components on a chip. Due to their versatility, these systems can be designed using various waveguide geometries, such as drawbridges, or modulator structures like ring resonators, cross-absorption or anti-resonant systems. Furthermore, the study explores the feasibility of integrating mechanical components with existing fiber-based optical systems, and mixed symmetry photonic crystal structures, which exhibit unique properties in comparison with other systems. Our research lays the groundwork for developing advanced quantum-optomechanical systems in integrated photonics, leading to promising applications in sensitive sensing and quantum information science. Yet, the coupling can be reinstated when the system is subjected to optical pumping, which introduces anti-resonant frequency tuning in the system. We investigate the impact of various irrelevant operators on the effective magnetization boundary condition in Ising Field Theory, specifically obtained via holography from the PGQMS model. By introducing specific fluctuations of a secondary field across a boundary in the target space, we derive a system integrability criterion. Conformally coupled fields at the boundary are then applied to examine boundary condition changing operators, with our analysis indicating that a particular operator disrupts the boundary condition and potentially makes the effective magnetization model non-integrable. This finding is further backed up by a corresponding change in the operator's Casimir energy, which is calculated using a boundary state approach. Additionally, we explore the role of irrelevant operators on the target space's boundary, discovering that one of them gives rise to a non-integrable mirror description of the effective magnetization model. This non-integrability is also reflected in the operator's influence on holographic duality in the context of the PGQMS model. Lastly, with the irrelevant operators' impact assessed, we establish a system of constraints on the two-point functions in the effective magnetization model by applying boundary state techniques. These constraints are then connected to a system of constraints in the bulk space, with our analysis showing consistency across both contexts. This consistency checks our previous findings on the impact of irrelevant operators. Lastly, with the impact of irrelevant operators assessed, our analysis moves on to explore the physics of three-point functions in the effective magnetization model by applying boundary state techniques. This leads to new insights into the physics of three-point functions, along with a demonstration of how the impact of irrelevant operators influences these interactions. Our analysis reveals that only specific fluctuations of a secondary field across a boundary in the target space are needed to calculate these interactions. This insight is then used to establish relationships between conformally coupled fields at the boundary and the components of the Ricci tensor in the target space, further advancing our understanding of the physics of three-point functions. Our analysis provides a system of constraints on the central charge of the effective magnetization model by applying boundary state techniques. This relationship is then used to establish connections between conformally coupled fields at the central charge's codegree and the components of the central charge's curvature in the target space. Our final conclusion reaffirms the non-integrable nature of the effective magnetization model when affected by the irrelevant operator. This realization leads to new insights into the physics of the Ising Field Theory's magnetization boundary condition, along with the identities of specific fluctuations of secondary fields across a boundary in the target space

This study investigates the path planning issue for non-convex obstacles in a 2D environment for robotic systems that exhibit uncertain behavior. A novel approach based on the mixed-integer semi-definite programming method is introduced to determine an optimal navigation route, taking into account the system's model uncertainties as expressed through chance constraints. This approach aims to find a trajectory of minimal length while limiting the probability of obstacle avoidance. However, the presence of chance constraints and model uncertainties means that the optimality condition cannot always be met due to stochastic effects, and thus robust navigation paths must be designed to accommodate a range of possible system behaviors. Furthermore, this research examines several approximation techniques, such as probabilistic inference and Monte Carlo simulation, to approximate the probabilistic distance to obstacles. Our approach is demonstrated through a series of numerical examples that highlight its capabilities. This research is significant because it provides a mathematically robust framework for designing navigation systems that can adapt to changing environments. A comparison with existing adaptive path planning methods, such as genetic algorithm-based approaches, is also conducted to showcase the proposed method's advantages. Moreover, the influence of the relaxation tolerance on the computation time and navigation robustness is thoroughly investigated. This research offers a promising solution for tackling the path planning problem in environments with uncertainties. Moreover, its versatility allows it to be applied across various robotic systems with uncertain behavior. This study has an added benefit of providing insights to designers on how to engineer resilient robotic systems that can withstand uncertainties. Furthermore, the robust path planning method can easily be extended to handle multi-robot scenarios where interactions among robotic systems pose a complex obstacle. This research has significant practical implications, suggesting the use of robust navigation paths to counteract uncertainties of various nature and scale. A step-by-step guide to extending the robust path planning method to multi-robot systems is also outlined in this study. To further illustrate the proposed approximation techniques' efficacy, a real-world implementation of the path planning method on a robotic arm is described. This research reports the successes and challenges of porting the path planning code to CPU and GPU platforms, with GPU-based implementations yielding remarkable speedup in performance. A comprehensive list of open-source path planning tools is provided in this study. These tools include implementations of the proposed path planning method using MATLAB, C++, and C++ programming languages. Recent research on adversarial examples has revealed that neural networks with a relatively low error rate can still be vulnerable to carefully crafted manipulations. Prior studies demonstrated ResNets are particularly susceptible [1], [2], but a more recent findings [3] suggest that a type of neural network with a simpler architecture is equally vulnerable. A key factor contributing to a network's vulnerability is its constraint on error, which must be proportional to the layer's width [4]. To address this, we introduce a method that significantly diminishes a network's capacity for adversarial exploitation: for every layer, we modify the neural network architecture so that the error constraint is minimized. Polar codes, the standard in 5G, are extensively used for efficient data transmission. Despite achieving the information-theoretic optimal limit, they fall short in providing meaningful error patterns for NewDirect decoding methods. To bridge this gap, our research focuses on pre-transformed polar codes, such as CRC-aided codes, and develops a novel decoding approach. By integrating the pre-transformed transformation with the classic Arctic algorithm, the proposed method significantly enhances performance, especially for shorter codes, while maintaining low computational complexity. When applied to CRC-aided polar codes of up to 128 bytes, the output error patterns are more diverse and scattered over the error pattern space, outperforming the Arctic algorithm in polar codes. Furthermore, the proposed method yields superior error rates compared to state-of-the-art polar code decoders, such as LDPC and LDPC-augmented polar codes, under finite block lengths. While the advantage over the Arctic algorithm diminishes with increasing block sizes, the diverse error patterns facilitated by the proposed method enhance the NewDirect decoder's resilience. Moreover, the proposed method's scalability is compatible with the recently proposed CRC-aided polar code transforms, such as SplitTransform and GeneralTransform. In conclusion, our results indicate that the proposed decoding approach is a practical solution for the NewDirect decoder. We developed computational models to study how an initially smooth crack surface begins to fracture, using contact-correcting Kirchhoff-Love plate strips to simulate elastic energy. By demonstrating that a specific type of crack tip instability leads to a new length scale in fracture, our research identified the pivotal factor behind how cracks initiate to be the relationship between the notch's angle and the ratio of crack tip height to tip opening distance. Moreover, our models revealed that smaller notch angles and greater tip heights relative to opening distances lower the energy required to fracture and thus make it easier for cracks to initiate. Furthermore, these models explained why linear-branching fractures often fail to occur in isotropic materials by demonstrating that their predicted length scale lies above a certain threshold, beyond which notches in these materials cannot exploit this fracture mechanism. Finally, our models were validated by comparing their predictions to the outcomes of experiments on notched specimens, which shared the same structural characteristic of having a curved crack tip with respect to the material behind it. These comparisons, which involved both two-dimensional and three-dimensional geometries, showed that our research' results accurately captured the fracture patterns of these experiments, thus underscoring the relevance of our variable tip stripping framework to the study of fracture mechanics, a field where its implications were previously unexplored. This study demonstrates that if the initial data's high-frequency components are negligible, its solution also exhibits a slow rate of growth. Specifically, it has been proven that the solution's derivatives cannot grow faster than the solution itself, given a certain level of data smoothness. This finding agrees with the theory of energy methods but also extends to non-integral parts of the energy equation. Meanwhile, the solution's behavior can be described using the Anderson-Mizinin estimates, which impose a gradual growth on the solution's high-frequency components. This outcome represents a significant extension of previously established results, as it shows that the solution remains smooth for all time, even when its initial data is nearly white noise. This research further explores the solution's behavior when its initial data is characterized by different spatial patterns, such as a step function or a highly oscillatory pattern. In these cases, the solution's behavior can be described using the slowness of its front propagation speed. In the case of a step function initial data, it has been shown that the solution's high-frequency components exhibit a propagating behavior, with the solution's ability to propagate depending on its normal velocity towards the singularity. Finally, the solution's behavior when its initial data is oscillatory has been studied. Our CV Quantum Key Distribution (CVQKD) protocol is an improved variant of the theoretical Fincke-Politzsch position paper algorithm. This innovation yields a faster verification process, with a time complexity of O($\log p$), when compared to current CVQKD protocols. Consequently, the precision threshold for validating random numbers can be lowered even further, such as down to one in ten thousand, without a corresponding increase in the computational burden for checking these numbers. Notably, the CVQKD protocol is an instance of the more general Fast CVQKD family of algorithms. When tested, this protocol demonstrated an approximate two-fold acceleration over the baseline in scenarios where the random number validation precision was high. Moreover, the CVQKD protocol is the first member of this family to have been tested. A detailed analysis of the trade-offs between speed and precision in our protocol is provided through comprehensive numerical simulations. These experiments showed that lowering the precision threshold allows for faster verification, with a precision threshold of one in ten thousand requiring roughly twice the computational time as an unoptimized threshold. Our results suggest the potential for the CVQKD protocol to be used in real-time applications such as hardware design. Additionally, the CVQKD protocol may be a viable solution for quantum-based random number generation in scenarios where direct access to certified randomness is not available. A possible practical implementation of the CVQKD protocol, tailored for use in modern General Purpose GPUs, is also explored in this research. When compared to the best specialized quantum random number generation hardware available today, the CVQQC protocol was found to generate random numbers at a rate of approximately 71.5MB per second, while the hardware generated them at a rate of 59.5MB per second. In summary, the CVQQC protocol is a fast and highly precise method for generating random numbers. When tested against the best specialized quantum random number generation hardware available today, the results show that the CVQQC protocol is able to generate them just eleven percent faster. More importantly, the integration of the CVQQC protocol into modern GPUs comes with no added upfront cost, making it an attractive option. Perhaps more surprisingly, the analysis revealed that the CVQQC protocol is able to achieve the same precision as the hardware with a computational time that is about a hundred thousand times faster. These findings suggest that the CVQQC protocol could potentially be a valuable tool for scenarios where the generation of high-precision random numbers is essential. A cutting-edge consensus of LC4IoT is thoroughly examined and its unique features analyzed. LC4IoT supports a high level of transactions (blocks) that contain a high number of transactions (fourteen), a characterization not previously considered in the consensus literature. Following a descriptive overview of LC4IoT, a systematic evaluation is conducted of its components such as nodes, network, network transmission, packet structure, and operating procedures. This evaluation reveals that LC4IoT is suited for IoT applications, including supply chains, due to its IoT node adaptability and efficient packet structure. However, a critique of LC4IoT reveals several shortcomings, such as a lack of formal proofs for key LC4IoT elements like node voting and network transmission, and the reliance on random processes in its operating procedures, potentially reducing the algorithm's efficiency relative to other consensus types, such as PoW or PBFT. A crucial observation is that LC4IoT's packet structure tends to be overly specialized for a blockchain application. As a final conclusion, the concept of characterizing a consensus is formalized and preliminary work on a classification of consensus algorithms, including LC4IoT, is introduced with a view to further research in this area. LC4IoT is compared to other consensus algorithms, such as PBFT, PoW, and Raft, based on the characteristics formalized in the classification notion. Additionally, potential applications and characteristics of consensus algorithms, such as those for blockchains in supply chains, are explored. Potential future research directions on consensus characterization and classification of algorithms are identified along with an invitation for further community involvement in this area. A practical implementation of LC4IoT is developed using the programming language Python and a package called Flask, as well as the blockchain analysis tool blockly, to enable users to create and launch LC4IoT blocks and analyze these blocks in a graphical environment. Furthermore, a discussion forum for characterization and classification of consensus algorithms, including the option for community membership, has been set up on the platform of stackoverflow at https://blockchaincharacterization.groupchat.stackexchange.com/. A last point is made regarding the need for more research on the classification of consensus algorithms, including potential related work topics. Potential related work topics are listed such as classification problems, consensus algorithm applications, blockchain analysis, and characterization tasks. A final call for community involvement in the proposed research is made with the hope of gathering more information on previously unpublished consensus algorithms, as well as drawing the community's attention to existing research efforts in this area. As high-resolution spectroscopy plays a crucial role in the field of exoplanet science, particularly in the detection of planetary companions to stars, it may be underutilized in the ongoing search for these celestial bodies. By combining the precision of spectroscopy with techniques like radial velocity analysis, it can be challenging to differentiate between spectral signatures resulting from stellar interference versus genuine planetary signals. As a result, there is currently limited information available about exoplanets detectable only through high-resolution spectroscopy. In this study, we aim to improve our understanding of the capabilities of spectroscopy in this field, surveying a sample of known low-mass stars in the Southern Hemisphere to identify any planets that may be present. We accomplished this task with the aid of the Very Large Telescope's UVES instrument and the Harps spectrograph, both of which offer the high resolution necessary to identify the spectral signatures of planets, including M planets with masses less than 100 times that of the sun. We discovered two radial velocity anomalies that resemble planetary signals: one with a mass of approximately 10-20 times that of the sun and an orbital period of two days, and another with a mass of around two times that of the sun and an orbital period of 16-22 days. However, these anomalies require confirmation as they could also be influenced by activity phenomena in the spectra of these stars. We also cross-referenced our findings in this study with high-resolution spectroscopy data from the Harps instrument and UVES, and our analysis yields no distinct signals that could be interpreted as planetary in nature in the spectra of 85 known low-mass stars in our sample, instead indicating that any remaining scatter in the data could be influenced by activity phenomena or statistical noise. As a result, our analysis shows that high-resolution spectroscopy data offer limited possibilities for discovering exoplanets, suggesting that the vast majority of exoplanets detectable only through high-resolution spectroscopy have yet to be identified. Furthermore, our analysis also demonstrates the difficulty in distinguishing the spectral signatures of planets from stellar interference and real planetary signals with the precision of high-resolution spectroscopy data. The increasing availability of large-scale aerial video sequences for surveillance and mapping has led to an increased demand for efficient place recognition systems. Leveraging the capabilities of 3D point clouds to describe environments in these scenarios has considerable potential. A key drawback of conventional 3D point cloud descriptors, however, is their high computational cost, which typically necessitates the use of low-resolution, scaled-down point cloud representations to facilitate real-time descriptions. In this context, places or pathways with complex, geometrically significant points may be difficult to accurately match. Our research introduces the Neural Detail Descriptor (NDT), a 3D point cloud descriptor inspired by the Neural Detail Descriptor, to address this challenge. Combining the scalability and robustness of NDT representation with the descriptive capabilities of local surface features and a similarity measurement based on local surface gradients significantly enhances place description and recognition efficiency. Our experiments using the Change of View dataset demonstrated that an NTD-enabled place recognition system outperformed state-of-the-art methods, with results that included a 96% accuracy rate at a 50% reduction in computational complexity compared to the MobileNet V2 mobile neural network. This paper investigates the impact of inter-regional interactions within functional connectivity networks and their influence on distinguishing individual and group differences within brain network variations. The study generates synthetic data sets with diverse inter-regional effects for multiple subjects and uses the Spatial Autoregressive model to create network maps. Analyzing these inter-regional effects, the research assesses how reliable they are in identifying individual and group differences, as well as predicting subject categories. The findings suggest that when weighing large network data against various prediction criteria, misclassification rates are significantly lower for networks with diverse inter-regional effects compared to those without such effects. However, it's essential to note that post-processing steps are necessary to achieve reliable subject classification. The study's results provide valuable insights for utilizing functional connectivity networks derived from resting-state fMRI data to accurately classify individuals with different mental health conditions, such as ADHD and cognitive disorders. The research also offers opportunities for future investigations into the consequences of varied inter-regional effects on brain network analysis. In the realm of distributed communication, our research focuses on two core challenges: achieving consensus without central authority, and the development of efficient algorithms for the tasks of naming and counting in different distributed settings. The naming problem, for instance, requires generating a common, sequential value sequence, while the counting problem involves reaching a global agreement on the number of ones in a shared binary string. The efficiency of our proposed solutions is measured by their communication cost, specifically their energy efficiency. We introduce novel algorithms designed to minimize energy consumption while still achieving optimal results, specifically counting algorithms constructed from energy-efficient problems. The energy complexity of these algorithms grows linearly with the number of stations in the system, similar to the best known naming algorithms, but our methods outperform existing solutions in terms of counting energy efficiency. Furthermore, our research explores the minimum required sequence lengths for the counting algorithms and compares the communication efficiency of our proposed methods with the current state-of-the-art solutions. The performance of our new algorithms is assessed both theoretically and experimentally, showing their practical benefits, especially in naming, through practical tests. The originality of our work lies in its comprehensive assessment of energy efficiency in the naming and counting fields, as our study is the first to provide exact values for the required sequence lengths of the counting algorithms and compare the results of naming algorithms experimentally. The implementation of our algorithms is done using a programming language called Go and their practical tests were conducted across 16 stations on a local network. The algorithms we developed are shown to be compatible with multiple distributed settings, such as the combinatorial models, as well as various communication models like the binary and the direct access to the stations. The evaluation of their performance reveals their operational effectiveness in different settings. The theoretical foundation of our work is built upon previously established energy-efficient algorithms for the tasks of naming and counting, and their modified versions with reduced energy consumption while still producing optimal results. The study and analysis of these algorithms led to the development of our own solutions, as well as an understanding of their connection to the already existing, but less efficient alternatives. The algorithms we developed are presented in the form of a general, adaptable framework, capable of handling multiple, specific, but less efficient algorithms for the tasks of naming and counting, and their modified versions with reduced energy consumption while still producing optimal results. The study evaluates their performance, the execution time, communication efficiency and energy efficiency in the naming and counting problems, and shows their practical benefits, specifically in naming, through experimental tests. This research explores the ergodic theory of Markov processes under a lifespan constraint. Under a specific, practical assumption that the Markov process is a homogeneous strong Feller continuous-time process with a natural lifetime, we demonstrate the existence of a unique equilibrium distribution that prioritizes survival above all else. Furthermore, we prove that this equilibrium distribution leads to a detailed balance condition, provided the process can be paused and restarted at any point within its lifetime. If the process has a natural exit time and is reversible, we demonstrate the existence of a unique distribution that maintains its mass within a specified subset and leads to a stationary distribution when combined with a killing mechanism at the boundary of that subset. Crucially, we establish the conditions under which these stationary distributions are reached exponentially quickly and that transitions between them occur exponentially quickly as well. Through a comparison theorem, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the detail balance condition, and hence the uniqueness of the most preferred stationary distribution. Additionally, we use irreducibility to show that a specific, key submatrix of a stochastic semigroup must be entry-wise positive. This new finding has potential applications in the analysis of cyberphysical systems and the study of populations that decline over time. It is complemented by two real-world case studies in the fields of both a physical system that declines over time and the analysis of a population that declines over time. The research further provides a novel link between the theory of quasi-stationary distributions and the study of systems that are driven by gradient descent. Our elastoresistance measurements on LiFeAs and NaFeAs have yielded some significant results. Firstly, we've found that the response of the resistance in LiFeAs and NaFeAs to strain exhibits similar temperature-dependent characteristics as previously seen in superconducting and non-superconducting BaFe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ compounds. This suggests the presence of a common underlying property governing the response in all three systems. Furthermore, by comparing the response to strain at different temperatures in NaFeAs and LiFeAs, we've found that the fluctuations in the latter have a greater magnitude. This contrasts with 12% and 26% reductions in the response at their respective critical temperatures in NaFeAs and LiFeAs, and could be attributed to the compound transitioning into an insulating antiferromagnetic state as a result of the fluctuations. Additionally, the compound's critical strain at the Antiferromagnetic critical temperature has been found to be $2\times10^{-4}$. The key to this enhancement lies in the application of both the Generalized Fermat and Rabin (GFR) number and its associated public key. The security and efficiency of the GFR cryptosystem are further improved using a modified version of the Baby-Step Attack, known as the Multiple Baby-Step Attack. This Multiple BSAT attack makes it computationally impossible to achieve a breakthrough in the GFR system if the public key is significantly larger than the private key. Consequently, the GFR cryptosystem's public key size and transmission rates can be minimized. The proposed modifications include a message recovery scheme, which is compatible with multiple baby-step attacks. The system's computational feasibility has been demonstrated using the SHA-3 algorithm, executed on NVIDIA GPU, the V100. The results show that the GFR cryptosystem can perform encryption and decryption in approximately 6.8 million cycles and around 13.6 million cycles, respectively. Additionally, the CPU execution time for the same operations was found to be significantly higher at around 101.7 million cycles. In contrast, the Pawale and Blum security thresholds for the original ElGamal cryptosystem were found to be significantly weaker at 2^16. This research focuses on a specific graph problem denoted as the Minimum Spanning Acycle problem (MSA). Initially, the study establishes that the weights of the extremal edges in the best solution for MSA, after the weights have been normalized, converge to an independent and identically distributed Gumbel distribution for large scenes as per the Percolation-derived result by McDiarmid et al. This Gumbel distribution result is further extended to apply to all edges in the graph. Additionally, the investigation explores the pairwise convergence of extremal edge weights, demonstrating that extremal edges within a small distance from the extremity exhibit a coupled convergence and also showing convergence for extremal weights farther than a small distance from the extremity. These findings are derived using an innovative and general approach that may offer useful insights for future research into the convergence properties of extremal edges in various graph problems, as observed in recent studies. This new methodology may provide an alternative strategy to the major tools currently used to analyze such convergence problems, such as the concentration results from McDiarmid et al. and the ergodic theorem from Hermon and Vigoda. Furthermore, the study establishes that the extremal weights of the best Minimum Spanning Acycle for large scenes converge to a Dirichlet distribution and also explores the pairwise convergence of these extremal weights. As a result, the extremal weight distributions for the best MSA can be calculated for underlying scenes with specific degree sequences. Recently, the feasibility of attacking vertical federated learning with private data was shown, despite assuming participants had no prior data privacy. However, the majority of adult data sets consist of records from individual entities, raising the possibility of a participant's information being compromised. In this study, the vulnerability of two advanced vertical FL protocols that prioritize participant privacy was investigated. A privacy attack utilizing differential privacy was applied to one of the protocols, while the other was attacked using record-linkage techniques. Successful record-linkage attacks were conducted against two popular adult data sets using two distinct approaches, including those that account for differential privacy. The results demonstrate that our method can link approximately 75% of records across two datasets, including M01OS and M02OS, which were previously shown to be resistant to such attacks. Furthermore, the application of our attack method to these datasets prior to training demonstrated similar results to using the trained models alone. The findings indicate that even state-of-the-art vertical FL protocols with differential privacy are not secure against record-linkage attacks. Therefore, the development of more robust privacy protocols that protect against such attacks is necessary. The code and data required to reproduce the results of this study are publicly available. A planned extension of this work includes exploring the potential for participants to detect these types of attacks against vertical FL systems. 

Keywords: vertical federated learning, record-linkage attack, differential privacy, adult data sets, machine learning.

By extending standard model particles with dark antibaryonic and dark baryonic components, researchers have studied the interaction between these particles and heavy mesons. The study shows that the presence of a dark antibaryon and an effective dark coupling significantly affect the decay width of a B+ meson converting into a proton and a psi particle. The mass of the dark antibaryon and the standard model coupling also play important roles. Furthermore, researchers have found that the dark light approach can be applied by introducing a specific dark lagrangian to describe this decay process effectively. The study provides a method to use decay data to determine the mass of a dark antibaryon and the effective coupling between the dark antibaryon and itself. The future use of the LHCb experiment's data for this purpose is also considered. The established theoretical framework holds promising implications for understanding dark matter-related particles that may comprise part of dark matter in the universe. By varying parameters within the dark lagrangian, researchers have obtained a series of predicted decay widths. The study suggests that the decay process of a B+ meson converting into a proton and a psi particle could be potentially observable, and researchers believe that related decay processes could offer valuable insights into this phenomenon. The established theoretical framework and related predictions are expected to be further expanded to include other decay processes. The study initially assumes that the dark antibaryon has a specific property called strangeness, but this assumption can be relaxed. Theoretical models such as QCD sum rules have provided upper bounds for the decay process of a B+ meson converting into a proton and a psi particle in the standard model. The study has discovered that in this decay process, the coherent conversion of a B+ meson and a proton could offer a secondary pathway for a B+ meson to convert into a psi and a meson. The theoretical models suggest that this decay process is unlikely to occur if the dark antibaryon has a specific property called strangeness. This study investigates the solution to a complex cooperative game known as the Generalized Defensive Game. It involves analyzing the Behavioral Defense Game, a modified version of the game that accounts for responses to an adversary's strategic planning. Both players in this game have limited resources, and the outcome is determined by a two-dimensional vector of allocated resources. We focused our investigation on a specific instance of this game, known as the Resource Allocation Game, which occurs when both players also have full control over their resource pools. Through our analysis, we gained insight into the best strategies for both players in this game and developed a mathematical model to describe these strategies. We found that this game follows a specific pattern and our model describes this pattern accurately. Next, we investigated the solution to the Behavioral Defense Game by simulating a Linear City Defender. The simulation results showed that a Linear City Defender's policy can be accurately described using a mathematical formula. Finally, we conducted a case study to compare the performance of different game models, including the Generalized Defensive Game and the Resource Allocation Game. Our case analysis highlighted the advantages of the Resource Allocation Game in certain scenarios and suggested potential research directions to expand our findings. These suggestions include exploring situations with more than two players or examining the coherence of different game models. Additionally, our study reveals that urban defense policy-making is heavily influenced by resource allocation decisions and cities should develop strategies to counter terrorist attacks by allocating their resources effectively. More specifically, our analysis shows that urban defense policy-making benefits from a linear allocation of resources when the attacker's damage linearly scale with the city's perimeter. Ultimately, our study contributes to the understanding of the solution to the Behavioral Defense Game and provides valuable insights into the coexistence of two players with limited and shared resources. Our findings offer valuable recommendations for both city agencies and government leaders to effectively defend against terrorist attacks. This paper describes an innovative sampling approach called bag sampling, capable of efficiently processing lengthy documents by reducing computation in query overlap. Unlike conventional caching techniques, bag sampling guarantees no redundant caching issues and is easily integrated into existing ranking systems. Moreover, the method is modular, allowing its performance to be evaluated in small groups, simplifying deployment. Experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements in long document ranking with significant reductions in computation needed to achieve the best results. Notably, the improvements obtained at lower levels of computation overlap closely mirror those at higher levels, making the method's performance predictable. Not only does this sampling approach enhance long document ranking, but the methodology developed can likely be adapted to improve other ranking tasks as well. Overall, the method is straightforward to implement and offers a reliable solution for large online search engines and content systems facing long document querying challenges. Furthermore, the approach has been successfully applied to other long-form content retrieval tasks, such as video retrieval, and is currently in use in at least one major online platform. In the semi-supervised node classification task for Graph Neural Networks, 
labeling unknown nodes with labeled ones holds significant importance. 
Although early pseudo-labeling methods yielded positive outcomes, their own limitations prevented them from attaining optimal performance. 
This was primarily due to the robustness of these methods against the potential issues in the labeled data they used. 
The application of pseudo-labeling in more advanced scenarios, such as the semi-supervised node classification, demands not only the enhancement of its ability to correct labeling errors but also the mitigation of the influence of the labeled data on the global representation learning. 
This paper presents a semi-supervised GNN node classification framework, named Response-Based pseudo-Labeling (RPL), which uses response-based pseudo-labeling to balance the influence of the labeled data with the ability to correct labeling errors. 
RPL combines information from the multi-layered neighbors of each node to predict the node's label and uses a response-based strategy to derive pseudo-labels that are less impacted by the labeled data. 
Moreover, it adapts a semi-supervised GNN model to confront the influence of the labeled data on the global representation learning by requiring the model to separate node features from the global representation and to identify the source of the information in addition to predicting the node label. 
This separation induces a more robust global representation capable of withstanding the influence of the labeled data. 
Experiments conducted on various GNN models demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in improving the semi-supervised node classification, especially in the cases where labels are scarce and the GNN models are shallow. A Coherent Betatron Radiation (CBR) source is conceived, integrated with a TW-level plasma wakefield accelerator, designed to boost the radiation signal enough to track the beam's behavior in real-time. A simulation study of the CBR source started with investigating how variations in beam edge roughness affect the signal, followed by examining the impact of mismatch on the beam's behavior within the wakefield. As a rapidly evolving field of radiomics, high-throughput quantitative image analysis has shown significant potential in developing easily reproducible biomarkers for various types of cancer care and pharmacology. However, its application is hindered by the labor intensiveness required to process the images, making it a major bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, the development of effective and semi-automated, quantitative image analysis techniques facilitated by advanced computational tools is essential. Unfortunately, the existing domain-specific software is often difficult to use, and its integration into a more comprehensive and user-friendly analytical framework has become a necessity. 

We present the Radiomics Docker Image, a freely available, open-source environment that streamlines image analysis using established techniques such as ADAS, ILD, and CLD. The image specifically utilizes ITK-Space for 3D data management and offers well-documented, automated workflows to streamline the process. To assess its performance, our image was applied to two challenging data sets containing diverse tumors: the NCI-CC data set and the MASTCAR data set. 

Our results demonstrate that our image-based, high-throughput quantitative analysis outperforms existing methods, such as ADAS and ILD, in terms of predictive accuracy. The Radiomics Docker Image provides a user-friendly analytical framework with pre-installed software to streamline image-based quantitative analysis. We include detailed instructions on installing and utilizing the image in the methods section. The Radiomics Docker Image is freely available for download at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jconimsu.2022.02.002.

This study examines the credibility of AI-generated news, focusing on a task where a human request is entered into a language model, and it subsequently creates a headline. Three prominent transformer models were utilized to create content based on input prompts, and then evaluate the generated texts on relevance, coherence, and overall quality. To measure their reliability, these generated headlines were mixed with actual human-written headlines, and participants were asked to determine which were written by humans. Surprisingly, the results showed that three top-performing transformer models were no more accurate than relying on chance in identifying human-written headlines, despite consistently producing texts with lower coherence and quality scores. The findings also highlighted significant variability in the quality of content generated by the same model, suggesting that the credibility of AI-generated texts is highly dependent on the specific application and can be a challenging task to master. In recent years, real-time calibration techniques have become essential for large-scale, redundant antenna arrays to maintain minimal skies surveys, but their impact on the variability of antenna gains remains understudied. To address this, we utilized the Square Kilometer Array's science verification data to investigate the effect of calibration on the gains of its antenna systems for two specific scenarios: narrowband and multiband processing. Our findings revealed significant reductions in the variability of antenna gains after calibration. These gains were then applied to an analytical model of an antenna beam to predict its gain variation. The results demonstrated that multiband processing yields better performance, especially in low frequency channels, while broadband calibration increases the uncertainty of antenna gains. The precision of antenna gains was found to be directly related to the frequency range considered in the multiband approach. Multibeam gains were found to be dependable but ineffective in determining the antenna gains accurately. Consequently, we need to calibrate each individual beam independently, though this demands more computational resources and data storage space. Nonetheless, employing multiband processing with broadband calibration appears to be a reasonable trade-off between these competing factors, given the current hardware capabilities. While our research focused on the SKA's science verification data, the methodologies discussed are also applicable to other large-scale antenna arrays. Furthermore, using external gain models instead of on-site measurements may lead to slightly enhanced calibrations, although with reduced accuracy compared to measurements from test antennas. Moreover, under ideal circumstances, the cross-polarized antenna gains can be estimated and incorporated into the calibration processes, but this demands better hardware capabilities to detect the cross-polarized signals. A detailed discussion of these requirements and limitations, along with the associated computational demands, is also explored. Lastly, an assessment of the effectiveness of time-average techniques, such as mean, median, and Kalman filter algorithms, is also presented and compared in terms of their ability to determine antenna gains accurately. The findings reveal that Kalman filter algorithms yield the most reliable outcomes, especially in multiband processing scenarios. Consequently, implementing a combination of real-time calibration, time-domain processing, and Kalman filter algorithms may be a suitable approach to maintain the reliability of antenna gains within large-N redundant arrays. This research applies the autoencoding CGAN technique, 'ACGAN,' to test whether it can learn a portfolio allocation strategy superior to the traditional Markowitz method, which is the traditional approach to portfolio optimization. Utilizing the 'ACGAN,' our model can forecast the future returns of stocks as pseudo-labels, enabling us to determine the optimal portfolio allocation by evaluating the likelihood of each asset based on its potential returns. The results from our large-scale experimental assessments on two separate datasets reveal that ACGAN's investment recommendations are indeed more stable and secure compared to the traditional Markowitz model. One of the major advantages of our ACGAN-based strategy is its ability to avoid significant losses during periods of market volatility, such as the 2008 financial crisis. In addition, our investigation into the potential sources of ACGAN's success led to the surprising finding that certain blue-chip assets, such as Google, are correlated with assets in unrelated industries, such as Google and Spotify. Finally, our study includes a theoretical discussion of the implicit risk aversion level inherent in ACGAN and ACGAN's portfolio allocations characterized by moderate risk. Bayesian neural networks have gained more attention due to their ability to incorporate uncertainty and make informed predictions with limited information. They are particularly useful when working with small or imbalance-classified data. Thanks to the advancement of computational power and sophisticated sampling algorithms, it's now possible to apply Bayesian neural networks to a wider range of tasks, including classification and regression. However, implementing a well-functioning predictive posterior is a challenging task. In this study, we detail how we created a practical predictive posterior for Bayesian neural networks by combining novel and established techniques. Our proposed approach leverages a novel approximation for the posterior, which is then optimized through data augmentation and regularization. It also employs a practical approximation for the computation of the predictive posterior. Our Bayesian neural network is designed to handle high-dimensional data and can be efficiently used for classification and regression tasks. To demonstrate its capabilities, we achieved state-of-the-art classification accuracy on the CIFAR10 dataset with our proposed Bayesian neural network. Our code is publicly available for anyone to use and replicate our results. Additionally, we performed an analysis of the requirements for the predictive posterior of Bayesian neural networks and investigated their performance with varying training set sizes, data augmentation intensity, and regularization coefficients. Our findings indicate that the predictive posterior approximated using a second-order Taylor series expansion is superior to other methods. Our analysis also reveals that the performance of the predictive posterior is sensitive to the parameters of the MCMC sampling algorithm. Our results even surpass the performance of the latest non-Bayesian deep learning methods on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 datasets. It should be noted that our proposed Bayesian neural network falls short of the latest results on the ImageNet dataset due to the significantly larger size of the dataset. The application of tensor methods to study spectral characteristics of hypergraph networks has been limited by the availability of suitable mathematical tools. We have introduced an operation called tensor join to facilitate the efficient computation of spectral properties in weighted hypergraphs. This approach can be used to derive explicit formulas for the normalized hypergraph Laplacian and the normalized Laplacian tensor based on the underlying graph and hyperedges. As a result, we have developed a computational method for calculating the eigenvalues of the normalized hypergraph Laplacian tensor, which cannot be resolved by standard tensor methods. We have also used this technique to improve the approximation of the hypergraph Laplacian tensor eigenvalues and to solve optimization problems on hypergraph networks. Our methods have been validated by various numerical tests. We have further extended our research to study directed multi-ordered hypergraphs, developing new mathematical tools in the process. We have derived a tensor join operation for directed multi-ordered hypergraphs and used it to develop expressions for the directed multi-ordered hypergraph Laplacian tensor. We have then explored its use in calculating the eigenvalues of the tensor join operation and applied it to optimize directed multi-ordered hypergraph networks. Our study shows that our proposed method is effective in modeling complex relationships between data points and can significantly reduce the dimensionality of the data, thus avoiding the curse of dimensionality, even for multi-ordered hypergraphs with a high order r. This method has been proven to be efficient in practical terms, supporting its use in large-scale applications. We have demonstrated the applicability of our model by using it to fit data from a real-world problem and showed that our model can provide a simple way to understand complex interactions between data points. We have observed that our proposed real-world application is a classic example of the emergence of collaborative filtering, which is a highly rewarding research area. We introduce INSIST, a comprehensive inventory of significant individual objects in the Milky Way's field, which is derived from a 15,000 square degree sky map of distant individual objects in the latest version of the VVV survey. Using a sophisticated approach for statistical analysis of the VVV survey data, we extracted approximately 315 million individual object entries including stars, galaxies, and other objects, which we then visually inspected to identify distinctive entities and subtracted artifacts. Following a series of refinement processes, we obtained a 3150 square degree sky map of remarkably accurate individual objects, which we then validated by comparing it to various benchmark sources, such as the Hubble Space Telescope. Based on these comparisons, we found imaging improvements of up to two times better, and correspondingly, a substantial decrease in errors from 0.5 to less than 0.25 arcseconds, with plans for releasing detailed information on object categories and their properties. Due to its vast coverage of the entire Milky Way's field, we now have a desperately needed database to understand the formation of individual objects in our own galaxy. Therefore, we make available through a web platform the necessary tools to inquire about object categorization and imaging, with plans for expanding this service to include object light curves in the future.

In clinical trials, a particular type of longitudinal data analysis is often

preferred over other methods. When analyzing longitudinal data that changes

gradually, such as growth curves, we find that conventional approaches can be

satisfactory. Nevertheless, these methods have significant biases when the rate of

change varies significantly from one subject to another and if the data is subject to

any form of error. To address these limitations, we have developed and executed

a constrained smoothing method using cubic splines. Utilizing our own simulated

data, as well as a well-known dataset from a multiple sclerosis trial, we have

demonstrated that this new method yields more accurate estimates compared to

other techniques. Furthermore, we have found that this new method allows for

accurate predictions of future data points. Importantly, we have found that

predicting future data points based on this constrained smoothing method provides

insight into the underlying change patterns. Such insights can aid in

determining when to terminate a clinical trial early if the data suggests a

substantial and instantaneous change in outcome for patients. To facilitate the

application of this constrained smoothing method, we have developed a user-friendly

R add-on package named 'SmoothMSCT'. The package includes the 'MSCT' data

format, which allows for the analysis of multiple types of data with varying

numbers of time points and variables. With our package, users can easily fit the

constrained smoothing method using multiple types of data and perform various

types of analyses. Moreover, the package includes functions for generating random

data based on the predicted data from the constrained smoothing method. We have

also integrated users from the multiple sclerosis community into the package's

development and testing process. The 'SmoothMSCT' package is available for download

This study presents a new framework for a family of typed lambda-calculi, 
each of which expands on a base system capable of replicating the expressivity 
of Church encodings in typed lambda-calculus. The resulting family of languages 
includes some that possess undecidable type inference problems, alongside others with 
well-defined and computable inference procedures. The framework also allows us to 
recreate known results concerning typed lambda-calculi and extends this analysis to 
conclude that a specific system, including a regular lambda-calculus with additional 
constructs, is capable of replicating the expressivity of Church encodings. The 
newly developed framework also facilitates a detailed analysis of the relative 
expressiveness of different lambda-calculi, including a comparison with typeless 
systems. Additionally, the framework provides a mechanism for creating and evaluating 
finite trees in an expressive and type-safe manner. The framework has been proven 
to accurately represent finite trees through a process called subject reduction 
and consequently demonstrates that any type system capable of accurately representing 
finite trees in this manner must also replicate the expressivity of Church encodings. 
This methodology differs from traditional methods, where the presence of Church encodings 
is assumed and their validity is then examined in the context of that assumption. 
Instead, the framework first identifies the underlying reason for the expressivity 
of Church encodings and then uses that explanation to develop the corresponding 
lambda-calculus. The approach was chosen in an effort to create a foundational 
model for understanding the relative expressivity of typed lambda-calculi. The 
introduction of Church encodings as the benchmark for expressivity may seem 
non-standard; however, this assessment is supported by past studies on the topic 
and as demonstrated in the paper, the resulting typed lambda-calculi developed 
through this framework possess notable connections to existing work in the field. 
Finally, the framework is further exemplified by detailing how and why a 
particular type system, including a regular lambda-calculus with additional 
constructs, is capable of accurately representing finite trees in an expressive 
and type-safe manner. The subject reduction approach used in this study relies 
on basic type system concepts, including type safety, the correct application of

This presentation outlines a novel approach to solving a broad category of stochastic differential equations characterized by intermittent input functions or switched control signals. Specifically, we establish the concept of Lions-type measure derivatives, demonstrating how they can facilitate the substitution of integrals involving those derivatives with inequalities featuring measure-related terms. This methodology is then applied to the study of stochastic differential equations with similar properties. Furthermore, we explore the potential intersection between these equations and hyperbolic partial differential equations, as well as the development of stochastic control theory frameworks for stochastic hybrid systems that incorporate Lions-type derivative constraints. In addition, we showcase several illustrative examples that showcase the practical utility of our findings. Lastly, we briefly outline ongoing research endeavors aimed at expanding our results to encompass more complex scenarios, such as higher-dimensional systems and fully coupled stochastic and partial differential equations.
