In 1959, the mathematicians Eisenberg and Segal defined a specific topology on the collection of all normal subgroups of a given topological group, by which a group $G$ becomes locally compact if and only if it is locally connected. This topology has a strong relationship with the first separation axiom. Additionally, by equating open sets with their closures, the topology satisfies the zero-dimensional separation axiom. This method of topology extension also leads to a new compactness type, analogous to the hull-kernel-type topology. The paper explores these topological properties within the context of specific topological groups, namely toroids $\mathbb{T}^{n}$ and soliton groups $\mathbb{S}^{n}$, to demonstrate how the previous results can be applied to solve problems related to factorization and unique factorization in number theory and algebra, by factorizing proper ideals of commutative polynomials and algebraic number fields into symmetric products of ideals and field extensions, by factorizing weakly embedded graphs into weakly Hamiltonian graphs and weakly convex graphs into weakly concave graphs. The problem of maximizing projective semilinear functions arises in the specific case of toroids $\mathbb{T}^{n}$. The last chapter explores the hull-kernel-type topology in toroids $\mathbb{T}^{n}$. The main contributions of this work include the demonstration that the hull-kernel-type topology is compact if and only if the original topological group is compact. The final section addresses the Hausdorff-type ordering in toroids $\mathbb{T}^{n}$. The last problem investigated is related to the interaction between this specific topology and the order on projective semilinear functions, as applied to toroids $\mathbb{T}^{n}$. The paper concludes with the formulation of three open problems derived from the exploration of the interconnection between topology and order theory. The problems pertain to the generalization of the Krull-Baer theorem to the context of proper $R$-modules, as well as the application of the hull-kernel-type topology and von Neumann-Bohr compactness order to the simplicial and toroidal compact spaces and their exploration within the context of locally compact group topologies. The last section discusses the applications of the von Neumann-Bohr compactness order to the generalization of the seven combinatorial properties of the Smith normal form for ideals in the context of the hull-kernel-type topology and von Neumann-Bohr compactness order

Recent advancements in semantic-guided machine learning have improved database efficiency, yet successful execution relies on accurate knowledge of available data sources, including types, restrictions, and relationships. However, our research reveals that many queries can successfully execute even without a complete understanding of the underlying database, as long as they have access to sufficient incomplete information. To address this, we have developed an approach that generates plausible database incomplete content for query-optimized optimization, effectively providing the required incomplete data even in the absence of complete database information. The proposed framework combines semantic guidance with learning-based techniques, allowing it to tackle complex databases containing diverse database models. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach is feasible, running on databases containing no content, and can achieve query execution accuracy comparable to traditional methods, with some cases actually outperforming them due to the generated incomplete data being more suitable for query execution. The framework also offers a novel application for generating Plonk zk-SNARKs, a challenging task requiring significant computational resources. Our approach can achieve significant time savings, a 5-fold speedup, accompanied by a comparable increase in the size of the generated proof. To effectively navigate crowded spaces, robots necessitate a sophisticated collision avoidance system, relying on precise estimates of their movements and surroundings. Presently, most collision avoidance strategies depend on internal perceptions and motion planning algorithms. Nonetheless, neglects uncertainties in perception and dynamics often result in inadequate approaches. This paper presents a novel method that integrates an uncertainty model into the collision avoidance protocol. By using sample-based predictive error data, the proposed strategy addresses the limitations of existing methods by considering the actual capabilities and limitations of on-board sensors and computational capabilities. This method not only accounts for the positions of other robots, but also their probable movements, thus making it more suitable for applications involving uncertain environments. To demonstrate its efficacy, the presented approach was simulated in two complex scenarios, with the results showing a considerable reduction in successful engagements from $16.7\%$ to $3.3\%$, and a notable $37\%$ decrease in the average safety margin. Moreover, the proposed protocol resulted in a considerable speedup, of average $61\%$, compared to a traditionally applied collision avoidance strategy. We apply these principles to simulate the adiabatic dynamics of moist air, equivalent to the system studied by Bickes et al. in [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA, 2020]. We develop simplified models based on the instanteous constitutive laws, focusing on the linear and nonlinear approximations for dry and moist adiabatic scenarios. Although the complete moisture transport is represented by a system of seven first-order partial differential equations, these models reduce the complexity to sets of second-order equations. Numerical results demonstrate that the consistent $\kappa$ approximation in the linear and nonlinear cases yield precise results for dry adiabatic dynamics, similar to the original paper. Moreover, the linear and nonlinear models provide an accurate representation of moist adiabatic dynamics, in contrast to the original paper. These new models offer a middle ground between the comprehensive system of seven first-order equations and the simplified seven-order closure model previously derived. Additionally, the seven-order closure model was validated in [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA, 2020] and this study confirms its consistency with the new models through the Derivative Triple Product Rule. By combining the linear and nonlinear models, we are able to reveal the physical basis of the derivative law for air at standard pressure. Specifically, the research shows the potential for the models to be used in the study of polyatomic gases, as well as in the application of generalized hydrodynamic models in both theory and practice. We explore the application of attention mechanisms to the dialogue state tracking task. A new model structure, the attentional confusion network encoder (ACNE), is developed by integrating an attentional encoder with the confusion network, an established direct recognition model. The attentional encoder draws global relationships within the dialogue turns to optimize recognition accuracy. Experiment results on the MultiWOZ dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the ACNE, with word-level attention leading to a 3.38% increase in the joint goal accuracy over the current state-of-the-art model. Furthermore, the benefits of the ACNE are abnormally validated by experiments utilizing a slacking attention strategy that is contrary to its designed purpose. Building upon the ACNE, we also investigate the combination of the attentional confusion network with a graph attention network (ACNE+GAN) to provide a more complete understanding of attentional improvements in dialogue state tracking. Notably, the full attentional model, ACNE+GAN, is found to be fragile and requires slacking to improve its performance. However, this phenomenon is notably distinct from its individual components. Ultimately, the research uncovers both the performance and reliability challenges associated with attentional improvements in dialogue state tracking. The code and pre-trained models for the ACNE and ACNE+GAN can be found at https://github.com/AnnanDong/ACNE.git. The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 61876241). Both datasets and the project source code are open to the public.

Most current continual learning approaches train custom-made neural networks, but in reality, it's more common to see existing models being adapted. This study investigates the effectiveness of continually updating the parameters of pre-trained convolutional neural networks using a series of incremental training tasks, employing a Nearest Mean Classifier for a straightforward identification model. Surprisingly, the results show that the performance of this simple approach rivals that of more sophisticated continual learning methods, especially when the new data follows a similar distribution to the initial task. Moreover, incorporating a minimal interference strategy using a basic memory-based approach nearly matches the performance of established continual learning techniques. Alongside analytical investigations into interference and the impact of task order, this study demonstrates that the key to successful continual learning when updating pre-trained models lies in minimizing the changes to the feature representations. It is proposed that incorporating purposeful distortion of the features could offer an additional safeguard against overfitting to individual tasks. Collective oscillations in coupled network systems are significantly influenced by the strengths and variability of the connections between cells. The purpose of this study was to examine how the characteristics of connection strengths in a neural network affect the emergence of synchronized oscillations. We extended existing Scrone-Lynn-Stewart model to incorporate degree distribution variability and heterogeneous connection strengths and observed the effects of different parameters on the network behavior. The simulations revealed that increasing the coefficient of variation (CV) for connection strengths in a non-oscillatory network can trigger synchronized oscillations. Additionally, we found that broad degree distribution can suppress oscillations, while the distribution shape has a more complex impact on their occurrence. The results of our study contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms underlying synchronized activity in coupled cells. Further investigation of these mechanisms could lead to a better comprehension of physiological processes in cells. Programmers frequently apply well-documenting comments to explain their code's logic, but unfortunately, these comments are often missing.  Automatic comment generation from code comments written in natural language can fill this gap.  Despite recent advancements in this area, there has not been much multi-language support.  Most current approaches rely on a significant amount of professionally written abstractions, which are not always readily available.  To address this, we present a new, groundbreaking framework for comment generation, which builds on standard neural machine translation.  Initial evaluations suggest that our method performed exceptionally well in translating codes across multiple languages - 67% of the generated comments matched the exact wording of human provided comments in a preliminary study.  Further testing on three large-scale datasets revealed that our method significantly outperformed other methods in multiple aspects, including factual accuracy and overall coherence.  Most notably, our multi-language training data consisted of only English codes and non-English natural language comments, which highlights the impressive robustness of our method in cross-lingual settings.  Ultimately, our code is made available for public viewing at https://github.com/ali9090/cross-domain-comment-gen.  A recent re-evaluation of our code generated comments using comprehensive datasets from the industry has confirmed the previous findings.  The study found an impressive 51% of the generated comments matched the exact wording of human provided comments, and our method outperformed other methods in multi-sentence comment generation. We have enhanced the Kalman filter's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) analysis for a general multi-input, multi-output Gaussian channel by incorporating interference into the calculation. Interference structure is utilized to derive more accurate inner channel bounds, thereby refining the channel capacity upper limit. The modified Kalman filter SNR analysis is demonstrated with various channels, including those with multiple inputs and outputs, correlated noise, and interference, achieving an average accuracy of 0.95 and a maximum error of 30 percent in various scenarios. The paper also provides an introduction to calculating channel capacity and interference structure recognition. The newly developed Kalman filter SNR analysis can serve as a practical channel capacity upper bound, especially for complex multi-input, multi-output Gaussian channels. The method may also offer insights for maximizing interference structure recognition, which is beneficial for cognitive radio operations. In healthcare, well-intentioned individuals share patient data with third-party organizations, either for processing or storage. This collaboration poses a significant security risk, as sensitive patient information could be inadvertently exposed. To mitigate this issue, we propose a data utilization policy that aims to protect patient privacy by controlling the interactions between data owners and shared information. We represent this policy as a directed graph, where accessible data are contingent upon specific conditions. Machine learning models can be utilized to predict these conditional accessibility features, effectively minimizing the risk of information leakage. Notably, our privacy-preserving approaches do not rely on complex cryptography. Instead, we focus on educating data owners about sensitive patient data, thereby fostering a culture of responsible data usage. Our approach involves training statistical models to forecast shared data sets, thereby providing an easily interpretable diagnosis of potential security threats. By establishing a systematic representation of security policies, we enable seamless sharing of sensitive patient data among diverse healthcare institutions, thus promoting interoperability and harmony among them. The performance of our model can be further enhanced through incremental training, incorporating an interactive exploration system to display data inputs and model outputs. This approach enhances readability and understanding of our model's predictions. Lastly, our comprehensive evaluation involves simulated interactions between data owners and the shared information to assess our approach's robustness and resilience. The source code for our model is freely available on GitHub. Additionally, our technique has been successfully applied to protect the privacy of Greek volunteers in the ALICE mobile app. In the future, we aim to collaborate with data owners to explore alternative strategies for maintaining patient privacy, as well as integrate our approach with existing privacy plans and compliance frameworks. Furthermore, our future developments will be announced on the project's website. The preliminary findings from our evaluation have been published in an initial paper. Lastly, the research demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in minimizing data exposure and the economic benefits it can provide. The study also revealed some notable limitations that need to be addressed. These limitations will be further elaborated in the forthcoming sections. Notably, our approach has substantial implications for healthcare settings where data usage agreements often fail to prevent unauthorized data sharing. These situations may result in significant security breaches, as illustrated by the Massachusetts General Hospital data breach in 2020. Nesterov acceleration can be achieved in stochastic gradient descent when paired with a specific adaptive formula for its convergence rate, however its effects on formulas such as RMSProp and Adam remain unclear.  We resolve this by showing that these popular adaptive methods actually eliminate the benefits of Nesterov acceleration.  This is confirmed through both theoretical and numerical evidence.  The inclusion of Nesterov acceleration also has an unexpected effect: it allows stochastic gradient descent to remain convergent with certain adaptive methods that would otherwise fail, such as the tensorweed Adam.  We are able to confirm these findings through numerical experiments.  Ultimately, our results suggest a new approach to incorporating Nesterov acceleration into stochastic algorithms, as well as highlight the potential for a new generation of adaptive algorithms.  This paper is an expanded version of an earlier arXiv posting, with significantly more theoretical and numerical content.  The software to reproduce the results in this paper can be found at https://github.com/fergusn/nesterov_acceleration_adaptive. Grasp diversity is a vital consideration in robotic perception systems, yet achieving it is complicated by the need to balance different priorities such as grasp success and object reliability. Most existing methods focus on improving grasp quality, yet their simplicity prevents them from reaching the desired level of object reliability. In an effort to address this challenge, we present DexGraspNet, a cutting-edge approach for synthesizing diverse and effective grasps. Leveraging a large-scale dataset of grasp-skeletons and corresponding labels obtained through experience replay, DexGraspNet employs a neural network to synthesize graps with various characteristics. Moreover, our approach uses a novel loss function to enhance the robustness of the graps, achieving better performance than state-of-the-art methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by successfully integrating it with a perception system, which achieves superior performance compared to current baselines on the Hook3D dataset. Notably, our findings indicate that graps synthesized by DexGraspNet are consistently more stable and diverse than those produced by other methods. Furthermore, over time, our approach continues to refine its performance, ultimately reaching levels of object reliability and grasp success currently unattainable for comparable techniques. The code for our proposed contribution is publicly available at: https://github.com/UTIEE-DAR-GA/DexGraspNet.utter. A demonstration video of our work can be found at: https://utm.io/oeQ.

We investigate spatial non-local effects in ecological systems, applying a mass-conservation framework to model how ecosystem size changes due to resource availability. Our work focuses on grazing ecosystems, exploring how spatial non-locality influences these systems' stability in response to aridification. We introduce a stability metric and perform a number of parameter studies, comparing the behavior of spatially non-local and locally averaged systems. Our results demonstrate that spatial non-locality typically makes ecosystem dynamics more unpredictable and resilient, but in severe cases of aridification, non-locality can actually reduce the system's resistance to collapse. However, non-locality does not necessarily lead to a system transition between stable and unstable states. Additionally, we find that spatial non-locality does not significantly speed up the system's approach to equilibrium. Our work highlights the significance of considering spatial non-local feedbacks in ecological studies, particularly in contexts where ecosystem dynamics are highly unpredictable. Furthermore, non-locality may influence the emergence of patterns such as spotted or striped patterns in ecological systems, making these spatial patterns even more unpredictable. This paper introduces a novel learning approach for finite and infinite dimensional models that offers stronger theoretical guarantees than traditional methods, including the represenational power of neural networks. Unlike standard estimators used in dimension reduction techniques, our approach adapts to changing models, providing robust results even when the model is not known in advance. We initially demonstrate the adaptive capability of neural networks in recovering the underlying structure of a given model, using a Gaussian linear model as a key proof, before extending our findings to other models, including a Gaussian copula model and a generalized linear model. Experimentation has confirmed the efficacy of our approach, reducing the number of required neurons. These findings address concerns surrounding overfitting in neural networks, showing that adaptive estimators can perform better than their non-adaptive counterparts. Moreover, neural networks with fewer neurons may lead to better outcomes, counterintuitively reducing the negative effects of overfitting. This research advances our understanding of neural networks as robust adaptive estimators, providing stronger theorems than previously established. These results have significant practical implications, allowing neural networks to effectively handle complex, unknown models, which may be invaluable for reducing dimensionality in high-dimensional data. Details of the employed neural network architecture, as well as further experimentation on simulated and real-world data, are presented in the accompanying supplement. A substantial number of research projects, notably those related to quantum information and communication, have been conducted with real-world applications in mind despite the limited availability of funding compared to traditional IT projects. Our analysis is centered on a specific use case where quantum-compatible communication technologies can provide seamless integration with high-frequency trading systems, allowing for the generation of profits through the sale of "qbits" and their inherent uncertainty to other traders. Furthermore, our research can be viewed as a case study of the feasibility of processing real-world data using shallow neural networks and observing the emergence of quantum-like communication properties. Our findings are based on trade data and apply to the domain of LOFAR antenna sales where an unusual antenna model, the Berkeley LOFAR, was temporarily sold at an exceptionally low price due to a pricing error. By applying suitable data transformations and a relatively simple neural network with 5-10 units, we have replicated the "qbit"-like communication phenomenon observed in a previous study. Additionally, our research demonstrates that a completely different dataset, one containing information on car sales and prices, does not display the same communication features, and we attribute this phenomenon primarily to the application of a non-linear transformation in our neural network to real financial data. Our study thus represents one of the initial evaluations of the practical feasibility and real-world validity of quasi-quantum communication technologies in real trading systems. Our research further highlights the relevance of high-precision floating point arithmetic in real financial applications, analogous to recent findings on the feasibility of binary arithmetic in quantum-compatible communication. Our analysis also reveals the occurrence of information leakage in a leading quantum-compatible communication system when communicating critical financial information of real stocks and shares. Furthermore, our safety and privacy evaluation is founded on the fundamental principles of data privacy, including the principles of confidential informatics and information therapy, and is informed by the extensive body of literature on data privacy and cryptography. Our real-world applications and findings of the occurrence of information leakage in suitable quantum-compatible communication systems provide concrete evidence of the significant practical relevance and relevance to industry of the fundamental principles of data privacy and information confidentiality. Our study thus represents one of the initial evaluations of the feasible applications of the fundamental principles of data privacy and information confidentiality in the realm of quantum-compatible communication technologies. Our analysis further demonstrates that our findings of the occurrence of information leakage in suitable quantum-compatible communication systems can be avoided through the relevant design of the underlying information sharing system. We've revised the contact condition used for tidal ice flow and explored its impact on a glacial model, specifically in systems where ice sheets interact with their bedrock through friction. By applying a law of friction founded on the theory of variational inequalities, we've reformed the contact condition and examined its implications, including the absence of rigid modes in the ice's velocity and the loss of weak solutions due to a penalization technique's influence on the model's critical points. Further analysis has involved the use of a SLEIPNIR II kernel to assess spatial regularization and the absence of rigid modes in velocity, leading to a fully periodic model with no slip boundary. As a result, we've derived existence and infinite-time compactness results for the model's solutions, as well as a new hybrid version of the model that combines penalization and contact conditions. Furthermore, by assuming that contact occurs everywhere over an idealized sloping terrain, we've demonstrated the model's existence and uniqueness of solutions, even in the slip-free periodic case. These results lay the groundwork for further research on the long-term behavior of these models. Using a discrete approach, we've also tested our theoretical findings on a basic model, even when its boundary has partially melted. However, simply transferring our analytical methods from the full domain to the partially-melted boundary yielded disappointing results, as did imposing a separation of scales on the model, with outcomes that depend on whether we first improved to a weak solution or not. Consequently, we've left the thorough investigation of these complex issues undetermined. On a more practical level, our analytical work suggests that methods currently employed to analyze the stability of climate models may contain flaws, particularly in how they handle boundary conditions in partially-melted ice scenarios. Moreover, our findings imply that general-purpose numerical tools that have not been optimized for problems with moving boundaries may produce results resembling those from slip-free periodic domains, as seen in our own experiments. These outcomes highlight the urgency of developing more effective numerical techniques to tackle problems across a variety of boundary conditions, as exemplified by our own contribution of a new numerical approach that retains consistency when applied to partially-melted boundaries without requiring modification. This new approach has been successfully tested against the latest version of the CISM model, widely employed in scientific community, and has even demonstrated its capability to recover results from the full domain that were previously obtained only through assuming smooth boundary conditions. By achieving this goal, our approach has effectively eliminated reliance on the model's degree of freedom, as exemplified by our own contribution

For robots to effectively navigate, they need to understand their surroundings and especially how they are shaped. Learning scene geometry can be beneficial for robot navigation, but generating enough data to train a network through experience can be impractical. Instead of relying on networks trained for image classification, we suggest teaching robots about geometry by having them learn from incomplete 3D models of their environment. Our solution restructures and simplifies these models to create a manageable amount of data with clear labels, and uses this condensed information to teach a network how to accurately predict the shape of the environment from sparse and imperfect observations. Our method, called Maximal Sub-trees, allows our network to achieve impressive accuracy with very little input data. We show this solution works on simulated scenarios and real-world tests with LiDAR sensor data. Our code is available for others to build upon it. With this breakthrough, we demonstrate our network's ability to accurately predict the shape of the environment from a few noisy sensor data points. Interestingly, our results suggest that teaching a network about scene geometry is more effective than teaching it for image classification. Our work opens the possibility for robots to learn and understand their surroundings better, and could be a valuable tool for solving related challenges in computer vision and machine learning. In the field of ecology, dynamical systems are employed to design and understand prey-predator and competitor-competitor interactions. Often, researchers are concerned with a single system, although in reality, numerous interconnected dynamics can emerge when considering multiple similar systems. While a system may be stable, its duplicates may not be, leading to unstable equilibrium states. To address these complexities, we utilize bifurcation theory, which helps in identifying phase transitions within a system. To facilitate this, we've created bifurcation-visual, a tool that uses Julia to detect various types of bifurcations, such as changes caused by a parameter increasing or decreasing, to help researchers understand and interpret the dynamics of a system and predict potential instabilities. Our tool allows users to specify a system and the parameter to adjust, as well as determine the type of bifurcation to search for. bifurcation-visual then generates images illustrating the changes occurring at each transition, demonstrating the effects on the system's behavior and predicting upcoming stability shifts. Additionally, we've incorporated features such as parameter-space imaging, allowing users to identify and visualize regions where bifurcations occur without numerical data. We've demonstrated the capabilities of this tool by identifying and visualizing various types of bifurcations, including changes such as the creation of Hopf bifurcations and transitions involving a double limit cycle. As examples, we've analyzed the Mackey-Glass equation, a model describing delayed feedback and instability, and the model of Chacón's global model of malaria transmission. With bifurcation-visual, researchers can quickly visualize and understand complex dynamics, facilitating new discoveries and insights. As a web-based tool, it's easily accessible from a browser, requiring only the Java runtime or Julia for installation. bifurcation-visual is completely open-source, allowing users to customize, extend, or quote its code. In our work, we explore an extension of Quillen-Suslin theory for graded rings, developing a more sophisticated framework that accounts for graded ideals and their impact on the context. This refined approach ultimately enables the resolution of more complex problems encountered in projective geometry, such as the graded case of the Serre Quotient Trick. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the lifting of linear algebra techniques to the relative Quillen-Suslin setting is feasible. These findings are presented in the context of a ring of formal power series with coefficients in a Noetherian ring over which a particular condition involving the Yang-Mills indeterminates is met. We have also successfully expanded our results to include the case of relative Quillen-Suslin theory for graded connections. In addition, the principles underlying our work have far-reaching implications, such as the generality of the Snake Island Conjecture. We further prove that the generalized Nullstell's Theorem for graded rings is valid and establish a connection between the category of graded rings with an ideal and the category of Matrices over free graded rings. This theoretical development is a result of combining two previously independent results by Arnault and Muller in 1996. Our work culminates with the presentation of an intriguing generalized Axelsson-M Müller-Mroue-Mustafa conjecture. This theoretical framework has significant implications, including the generalized Axelsson-M Müller-Mroue-Mustafa conjecture in the ungraded setting, as noted by Daniilidis. This research explores the potential of adapting pre-trained vision transformer models and efficiently integrating them into existing facial verification systems to enhance anti-spoofing capabilities. Building on the pre-trained models' foundational knowledge, our study introduces a concise and adaptable framework for further development. The results demonstrate that transfer learning can significantly facilitate anti-spoofing detection for unfamiliar users, and more importantly, can improve the performance of existing systems with limited training data, thus making a significant impact in the field. The outcome of our experiment shows that using data augmentation in conjunction with fine-tuning the vision transformer model yields the best performance when trained with a small dataset, ultimately providing a valuable contribution to the field. Current end-to-end RL approaches have shown promising results but suffer from several limitations, such as poor generalization and unstable training processes. Furthermore, they are heavily influenced by environmental randomness, a characteristic of partially observable environments that RL agents often struggle with. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an innovative framework that integrates the power of Recurrent Neural Networks, a classic deep learning technique, to enhance the robustness of RL training and improve the learning efficiency. The relative positions and movements of the lensing star and the microlensing event are key factors in determining the mass of the lensing star. A higher accuracy in measuring the mass is achieved with larger optical axis angles and greater amplifications. This study provides theoretical backgrounds on microlensing and the method of mass estimation, while outlining several future plans to combine these measurements with data from the VLT survey. These planned observations are expected to greatly enhance the analytical techniques, allowing for a broader and more in-depth analysis of the events. This, in turn, could provide significant insights into various astrophysical phenomena including planet formation and the early life of stars. By exploiting specific characteristics of microlensing events such as the lens-star's motion relative to the microlensing event itself, the break-down of the lens-star's motion into distinct components can be established. These distinct components are 1) planetary motion within a larger system and 2) the lens-star's motion around its parent star. This study outlines the potential for the VLT survey to detect both stellar and sub-stellar objects that are candidates for future brown-dwarf/planet transit surveys. These candidate objects would be identified based on specific features such as large optical axis angles and the potential for the lens-star to move within its surrounding environment. This study provides an overall estimate of the potential for the VLT survey to analyse nearly 2000 microlensing events while also examining specific characteristics such as the mass of the lens-star and the distance between the lens-star and the microlensing event. Generally, the potential for the VLT survey to analyse these events is notable with the average measurement accuracy being 10 times greater than that of current analysis methods. These analytical measurements will be combined with data from other useful cosmological constraints including weak-lensing and baryonic structure data from the VLT survey. This study proposes the implementation of a analytical software known as the PLATO analysis tool, designed to 1) identify microlensing events with potential planetary movements, 2) calculate analytical measurements of the lens-star's mass based on its motion within these events and 3) combine these measurements with data from other survey analyses to estimate the VLT survey's overall analytical efficiency in understanding cosmological constraints. By using detailed simulation models of the VLT survey, the accuracy of the analytical software calculation is validated and compared with actual survey results. This study outlines the potential for the VLT survey analytical software to provide accurate analytical estimates of 0.03 M for every microlensing event analyzed.

The data were collected by the LHCb experiment at the LHC in two different energy settings: one corresponding to 7 TeV and the other to 8 TeV energy levels. A total dataset of 3 fb^-1 was used for this analysis. The CP-violating process was detected with an significance level of 3.9 sigma, and it matches predictions from the Standard Model. To account for possible effects from non-reversible $\pi^+ \pi^-$ production, the CP-violating process was also studied using partially reconstructed $\phi$ decays. This analysis produced a direct CP-violating process value that is consistent with expectations from the Standard Model. The CP-violating process value was also used to determine the relative size of two different amplitudes in the $\pi^+ \pi^-$ production process. A CP-violating phase value was obtained from a combined fit of the production and decay processes. The results for charge asymmetry and CP-violating process values for $J/\psi K^+ K^-$ are also presented. The analysis produced values consistent with the third generation's unitarity, and they match predictions from the Standard Model. The analysis produced no notable deviations when the results were compared with predictions from different models. The analysis produced results consistent with the notion that CP violation can be explained by the minimal admixture of heavy and light $B_s$ quark components. Classifying images from a target domain can be challenging when the training data lacks relevant labels.  This is a key issue in several real-world applications where there is a significant gap between the source and target domains.  Two main approaches have been developed to tackle this challenge: the first involves transferring knowledge from the source domain to the target domain using image features, and the second focuses on matching the target domain's distribution to the source domain's distribution using data features.  This work combines key techniques from both categories to develop a novel unsupervised domain adaptation framework.  Specifically, it incorporates adversarial learning, batch normalization, and class balancing to improve image classification in the target domain.  Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on two different scenarios: one with single-source data, and another with multiple-source data.  Key contributions of this work include the implementation of a domain confusion loss to aid unsupervised domain adaptation, and the investigation of the impact of different source data quantities on this task.  This work also shows that unsupervised domain adaptation can be used to cross-domain learning, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy when the target domain is comprised of mixed data from multiple sources. The extremal points of solutions to widely-used gradient optimization problems on the unit sphere have significant connections to equioscillation points in polynomial interpolation. These connections enable the derivation of precise spectral limitations for non-derivative free optimization techniques. These spectral limitations are analogous to the widely-known spectral limitations derived from the Chebyshev theorem. This paper will elucidate the mathematical relationships between interpolation, polynomial roots, and optimization, leading to the formulation of questions that may help revolutionize free optimization techniques. It is anticipated that this work will contribute meaningful insights to the optimization community by leverging knowledge from the highly-regarded field of interpolation theory. To validate the relevance of this study, this paper will initially examine the most elementary gradient optimization problem: the unconstrained linear regression, where the objective function involves the Euclidean norm. The first part of the study will provide an in-depth exploration of the polynomial roots associated with the extremal configurations of this problem. The second part will generalize the results to all the maximum modulus configurations of polynomial roots, after which it will establish corresponding limitations for the minimum modulus configurations. The third part of the study will extend the findings to all the gradient optimization problems where the constraint is the unit $n$-sphere for any positive integer $n$. It will also examine the polynomial roots associated with the extremal configurations of these problems. The final part of the study will present theoretical analyses of three optimization techniques: the gradient descent method, Newton's method, and their higher-order iterative counterparts, with a focus on their performance and convergence. The theoretical predictions obtained from the spectral limitations will be validated by numerical experiments based on specially designed test problems. These test problems, although derived in the context of free optimization, have significant connections to other optimization disciplines such as semidefinite programming, quadratic assignment problem, and continuous branch and bound method. The numerical experiments will further reveal the interdomain relationships of the polynomial roots. The study concludes by outlining significant unanswered questions that may help revolutionize free optimization techniques by ushering in a new era of interpolation-based theory. A common issue in remote sensing or medical fields, deblurring of satellite images has received significant attention in recent years. Traditionally, satellite image deblurring has been approached by focusing on image sharpness and detail preservation, often treating the level of blur and image sharpness as fixed characteristics. However, when the amount of blur can vary, resulting in an image formation model that includes a flexible kernel, a more accurate image restoration can be achieved. This paper proposes the use of a structured regularization method for the kernel in the image formation model to improve the results. Since the kernel's shape and size greatly impact image restoration, the level of blur also requires adjustment during the image deblurring process. To address this, we develop a new kernel estimation technique that adapts the amount of blur. This technique combines the idea of sparse representation with a parametric kernel-based model, using a gradient descent optimization that integrates the related parameters. To validate our approach, the level of blur can be automatically determined from the image's edges, and several experiments show that our proposal surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in restoring sharp satellite images from blurred ones. All the source code and implementation details are available for public use. Additionally, our approach opens up new possibilities for treating image blur caused by other factors, such as camera imperfections or atmospheric conditions. The larger the forecasting horizon, the more uncertainties involved. This research proposes Unet++, a modified 2D version of the HitNet architecture, incorporating residual reflections to enhance efficiency. The model adapts the Unet sequence of operations, combining an encoder and decoder with skip connections, to achieve more effective feature extraction and representation. The addition of residual reflections and reflections of reflections significantly expands the model's capacity, allowing it to handle complex scenarios. The increased depth of the model also helps to address the problems of power-law decay in long-term forecasting and inflows. The paper evaluates the performance of Unet++ using Pavia Traffic, Amsterdam, and taxicab data sets, demonstrating superior results compared to HitNet and ConvLSTM. The proposed model achieves an MAPE of 3.0%, which significantly surpasses the MAPE rates of HitNet (3.9%) and ConvLSTM (4.6%). The corresponding L2 error of Unet++ is 0.155, indicating a substantial improvement over HitNet (0.209) and ConvLSTM (0.255). Furthermore, MAPE and L2 error results indicate that the proposed model performs well on all three data sets, with Amsterdam displaying the lowest MAPE and L2 error values. The proposed model's accuracy and efficiency make it a suitable choice for near-term traffic forecasting. resection sizes, and automating patient inclusion in clinical trials. While recent advancements
have led to highly performing segmentation methods, they were primarily tested on individuals with
healthy hippocampi. Consequently, we evaluated their effectiveness in individuals with
hippocampi resections, finding a significant drop in segmentation Dice scores when existing methods
were applied to this altered population. To address this performance disparity, we developed and
tested a hip-pocampus reconfiguration network, KReN, as a post-processing approach that analyzes
hippocampus images to identify and adjust distorted segmentations from previous methods.
Notably, the integration of KReN into existing segmentation techniques resulted in a substantial boost in
segmentation precision, especially in individuals with resection-related hippocampus damage. When
evaluated using the hippocampus automated removal tool, KReN demonstrated a high degree of
effectiveness, achieving a mean and standard deviation of $0.911 \pm 0.040$ in segmentation Dice score.
Furthermore, KReN demonstrated across-modality adaptability when tested in conjunction with
segmentations derived from different imaging modalities, such as 2D T2-weighted and 3D MPR images.
We strongly believe that the use of KReN will have a significant positive impact on hippocampus
related clinical operations when integrated with existing segmentation methods. The source code and
configuration files for KReN are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.

The Most Clicks Problem, developed by Daxini and Dhar (ICICI 2016), has its solution closely tied to the concept of nullity in the context of grid sizes. Specifically, the problem's correctness hinges on the presence of a combination of grid sizes that has a particular property involving the symmetric group's invariants. Inspired by this connection, we establish a new characterization of grid sizes centered around the concept of nullity. Additionally, the property involving the symmetric group's invariants serves as a necessary condition for a combination of grid sizes, and we demonstrate that, under certain limitations, this condition ensures the validity of the Most Clicks Problem's solution. However, in the general case, the characterizations of grid sizes are still closely linked, and we propose a modified version of the Most Clicks Problem's condition that can be characterized in terms of the symmetric group's invariants. Finally, we outline the computational process for determining the Most Clicks Problem's solution in scenarios where the problem's size exceeds the feasibility limit, a threshold reached around the size of 18. To facilitate the computations, we establish a relationship between the problem's equivalence classes and the concept of nullity in the context of split Orlov's conjecture. The specific calculations for sizes ranging from 19 to 21 are presented, and the paper concludes by highlighting the open questions and challenges associated with the Most Clicks Problem. This paper presents a different approach to abstract interpretation that replaces the standard polyhedra used for accuracy in flow analysis with a new concept called truncated rational arithmetic. The system's underlying theory is developed by modifying the kernel of rational arithmetic to incorporate set operations, and proving its soundness. The proposed abstract interpretation is tested on three standard programs, compared to the traditional polyhedra method, and the results show significant precision gains at minimal computational cost. The next stage is to apply this framework to object-oriented programs, incorporating additional features like inheritance into the rational framework, or comparing it to existing non-traditional abstracters. Furthermore, this framework offers possibilities for integrating with set operations in ongoing abstract interpreters. The development of a prototype implementation is described along with performance benchmarks that demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. The framework's theoretical foundations, represented in HOL, are discussed in conjunction with the deconstruction of the Clight compiler used in the Verifying Compilers project. The project also explores the potential for incorporating the rational framework into existing abstract interpreators, as seen in the context of the Steensgaard abstracter used in the Verifying Compilers project. The potential for integrating the rational framework into other abstract interpreators is also examined. The framework's completeness was demonstrated through the construction of a correspondence between the abstract and concrete models. The first author's PhD thesis thoroughly covers the theory behind the rational framework, among other topics, and provides further justification for its use. The paper also discusses how this framework can be extended to other types of numerical data, such as date and time expressions. The research has resulted in the publication of four refereed papers with two currently under review. The next stage of the project is to integrate the proposed abstracter into the Steensgaard and Steensgaard-2 abstracters to further validate its potential. The research has significant implications for the development of software verifiers, as it could potentially replace the polyhedra-based approach to accuracy in flow analysis. X-ray spectroscopy experiments on the hexagonal and tetragonal forms of SrTiO3 reveal the formation of topological phonons (top phonons) following photoexcitation. Further investigation using density functional theory and time-dependent perturbational analysis explains how tetragonal perovskites can host top phonons and how their bandwidth relates to the extent of distortions. In SrTiO3, the transition from hexagonal to tetragonal phases and the consequent top phonon formation are driven by cooling, but also sensitive to the presence of excitations created by photoexcitation. At room temperature, the perturbational analysis predicts that SrTiO3 in its tetragonal phase is at the edge between top phonon and normal phonon behavior, exhibiting a distinct response to photoexcitation. Finally, the almost vanishing top phonon signal in hexagonal SrTiO3 is due to its low-phonon bandwidth, reflecting a reduced top phonon density of states. These observations also indicate that normal and top phonons have different characteristics and require distinct models to describe their separate and interconnected roles in the dynamic behavior of perovskite materials. The distinction between these models is especially crucial when they are combined to explain how SrTiO3 becomes superconducting under pressure. Our investigation lays the groundwork for future research into the top phonon density of states, which may influence the physical and chemical properties of perovskite materials. Theoretical and experimental studies can now explore the potential of top phonons in perovskite materials to support charge excitations, whose presence is known to trigger top phonon activity in other systems (for example, BaFe2(PO4)2). The problem of identifying outliers in massive data sets has received significant research attention in recent years. A typical approach to tackling this issue involves constructing a proximity graph by assigning weights to connected nodes, with outlier detection then being facilitated through identified isolated nodes. Prior methods, however, have struggled with scalability and poor precision in real-world applications. This paper proposes a new outlier detection algorithm, MRPG, which utilizes a more efficient proximity graph, consisting of optimized meta centers, thereby significantly enhancing its performance. Experimental results demonstrate MRPG's superiority over existing techniques, with MrPG showcasing a considerable reduction in execution time and improved precision compared to alternative methods. Specifically, MrPG outperforms Best Horse and Local Outlier Factor with improved precision and reduced time, respectively. Furthermore, mrpg-large.exe outperformes Best Horse and LOF when executed on a local computer but with a much smaller data base. MrPG, rpg code, can be downloaded from https://github.com/HongtaoMao/MRPG. A new search for finding long-lived gluinos in hadron collisions is being proposed using the CMS detector at the LHC. Unlike conventional searches, this one focuses on detecting the final stages of gluino decays rather than their initial forms. By considering various decay modes and taking into account the displacement of gluino decays, this search is unsensitive to the direction of gluino production. It particularly targets the slow-moving decays that occur outside the primary jet region, thereby providing a more comprehensive search for long-lived supersymmetric particles. It is anticipated that this search will be capable of detecting gluinos with decay lengths spanning multiple orders of magnitude. Three distinct search concepts are being proposed, each targeting different regions of phase space: S1, targeting gluinos with short ranges and low momentum; S2, targeting gluinos with short and long ranges and low momentum; S3, targeting gluinos with short and long ranges and high momentum; S4, targeting gluinos with long ranges and high momentum. S1, S2, and S3 are focused on detecting the displacement of gluino decays, while S4 is focused on detecting the survival of long-lived hadronic jets. These searches will be executed via simulated data of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions. It is projected that in the event no signals are found, 95% confidence level upper limits will be set for gluino production rates. S1 aims to set constraints on gluino masses up to 1000 GeV with a lifetime of 0.1 s or longer; S2 aims to set constraints on gluino masses up to 500 GeV with a lifetime of 1 ns or longer; S3 aims to set constraints on gluino masses up to 700 GeV with a lifetime of 1 ns or longer; S4 projects the ability to detect the survival of long-lived hadronic jets with a lifetime of 1 s or longer. These results represent the first direct search for long-lived supersymmetric particles decaying into stable particles. It is anticipated that future results from higher LHC data exposures and second-generation detectors will significantly improve these constraints. These proposed searches will be executed on real data in summer 2018 and results will be presented during the conference. A key finding relates to the fundamental limit of performance for optical communication systems to accurately transmit information about a driving field, as characterized by the transmitted photon number distribution. It is also found that the long-term behavior of these systems is largely determined by the dominant eigenstate of the time-evolution operator. For multi-photon systems, it is shown that the driving field can be effectively transmitted if the coherent state used as the initial state possesses a specific property related to photon number symmetry. This property arises from the inherent parity symmetry of the Hamiltonian of the multi-photon system. Consequently, the long-term performance of the system is largely dependent on how the parity of the coherent state is preserved during its time-evolution. Moreover, the prior research on single-photon systems is shown to be a specific instance of the general findings regarding the parity symmetry of the Hamiltonian. Further research is suggested to explore the crucial role of the dominant eigenstate of the time-evolution operator in the behavior of driven quantum systems. In the realm of code-switching, most current research relies on fully automated methods for generating data, which are subsequently used to train high-performance models. Despite this, the synthesis of code-switching examples often lacks consistency with reality, resulting in difficulties during the training and testing process. To rectify this, our research introduces a semi-automated, segment-based approach to code-switching data synthesis. By replacing consecutive code-switching segments with monolingual ones, our synthesized data conform to naturally occurring patterns, thereby enhancing its overall quality. To determine the optimal size of these code-switching segments, we experimented with varying the length of replacement units and discovered that a segment size of two or three characters yields the most satisfactory results. Furthermore, our synthesized data, comprising over 28,000 code-switching examples, significantly improved the performance of leading neural transfer models, showcasing superior performance in the WSJ dataset with an F-score increase of 17.7% and 12.3% respectively. Moreover, our synthesized data, along with 10,000 real code-switching examples, allowed the model to reach an unprecedented level of performance, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art in the 22K CS English-Hindi dataset with an F-score increase of 3.7% on the same dataset. Finally, our research demonstrates that the synthesized data can be used in conjunction with real data to maximize CS model performance. When combined in equal proportions, our synthesized data, along with 10,000 real code-switching examples, allows the model to reach an unprecedented level of performance, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art in the 22K CS English-Hindi dataset with an F-score increase of 7.2% and 5.6% respectively. However, when the proportions are altered, our results reveal that heavier reliance on synthesized data among English speakers yields better results, whereas a heavier reliance among Hindi speakers yields worse results. Consequently, our research provides novel insights into the understanding of code-switching synthesis. To facilitate future research, our synthesized data, along with the code, is made publicly available at https://github.com/gauravmassar/CSsyn. Ultimately, our research provides novel code-switching synthesis methods, opening up new avenues for further exploration. A mesh's quality greatly affects computational outcomes and researchers have offered various definitions. According to our analysis of multiple strategies, no definition assesses the connection between mesh quality and element-specific errors. To address this gap, we have developed a new quality measure that focuses on estimating local errors made by approximations on a mesh. This approach involves leveraging existing mesh quality metrics to predict the quality of mesh elements and applying a subsequent correction factor. As a result, the local error estimate approximates the actual error made by an approximation on a mesh. We have demonstrated that our quality measure effectively differentiates between good and poor meshes, whereas conventional measures do not. To validate its usefulness, we have utilized this new quality measure to introduce the first mesh improvement method centered around local error reduction. Experimental findings show that this approach leads to superior outcomes compared to traditional improvement methods. We have also investigated the potential for generalizing the local error estimate to incorporate other approximation parameters, such as time steps in time-dependent problems or iterations in iterative solvers. While the generalization concept is intuitive, we have encountered significant challenges in estimating the errors associated with iterations. Therefore, further research is required to explore the feasibility and potential applications of such a generalization. We have conducted several numerical studies to examine the connection between mesh quality and approximation parameters. These investigations revealed interesting connections and highlighted areas that demand further research. Moreover, reducing time step or iteration errors could provide valuable insights for optimizing approximation parameters, such as stopping criteria for iterative solvers. We have also discovered connections between mesh element errors and the elements' geometric properties, such as orientation, normal, and tangents. Investigating these connections could facilitate the development of new mesh improvement algorithms focused on specific application needs. To facilitate future research, we have developed an open-source library that employs the mesh element error estimator, allowing users to easily evaluate and improve meshes. Knowledge graph link prediction, a crucial task for assessing knowledge graph quality, has garnered significant research attention in recent years. It involves forecasting link existence between entities in a knowledge graph, largely based on the output of relation extraction, which has been extensively studied in NLP. Our research introduces the concept of induced subgraphs, which can indirectly retrieve a graph's relation transitions as an aggregation of previous extraction data. This led us to develop a novel model, the Induced Subgraph Alignment Network (ISAN), which reports state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, outperforming existing approaches on FG-BERT and Linear-ECE. Furthermore, ISAN showcases efficiency and consistency in handling various types of link prediction tasks. The project's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zwli/ISAN. Our work has two pivotal contributions: first, we present a groundbreaking model for link prediction, a groundbreaking achievement as it outperforms all then-current non-neural baseline approaches in this domain. Secondly, because ISAN is complemented by relation extraction, it provides a practical link between these two NLP tasks, giving insight into relation extraction's underlying mechanism. Interestingly, when ISAN was reconfigured as a simple transformer encoder, it demonstrated comparable performance to FG-BERT and the state-of-the-art strong baseline models, while also requiring far fewer parameters than the top-performing models on FG-BERT and Linear-ECE. Our results suggest FG-BERT's achievements result from its built-in representation of a knowledge graph's induced subgraphs. Off-policy learning algorithms have difficulty taking full advantage of large continuous state-action spaces, because current methods that estimate projective dynamics or expected action values can be very computationally expensive, limiting the use of these spaces. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a new technique that approximates a coarse approximation of a policy's behavior using a set of rules based on integer-valued decisions. We develop an off-policy learning method that directly optimizes the relationship between past experiences and the value of being close to a target state, which can be more efficient than existing methods in certain situations. Furthermore, our approach, named SortPPO, is similar to PPO but focuses on experiences that are close to the target state, which allows it to achieve good results on tasks with large continuous state-action spaces, such as those involving multiple robotic arms. When tested against behaviors optimized using the PRIORitized experience replay method, our approach was able to significantly reduce the number of experiences required to achieve good performance by as much as an order of magnitude in certain situations, even when all experiences were used. The code used to implement SortPPO is available at https://github.com/wooptse/sort-ppo. The demonstrations of our method's capabilities can be seen at https://youtu.be/Fk0d3OeX3Q. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents typically learn their optimal policies independently, but adapting collaborative tasks requires agents to synchronize their actions, leading to complex challenges and reduced sample efficiency. To address these issues, we propose the Estimation of Gaussian Processes in Latent Space (EGrels) method, a parameterized multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that exploits transfer empowerment to boost performance efficiency. EGrels employs action-conditioned depolarizing quantum circuits to represent latent space embeddings of demonstrated actions. By doing so, EGrels increases sample efficiency by leveraging information from fewer examples, and empowers agents to synchronize their actions collectively, enhancing performance in both self-play and multi-agent scenarios with both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings. We demonstrate that EGrels outperforms existing methods in both single and multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks. Our findings also indicate that EGrels can benefit from quantum capabilities, such as quantum advantage through the application of a quantum optimizer to the action-conditioned latent space embeddings, which in turn showcases better performance compared to its classical counterpart. These results mark the first implementation of quantum reinforcement learning in multi-agent collaborative tasks. All source code sources are available on GitHub at https://github.com/QuantPen/EGrels. Our study contributes to the growing understanding that multi-agent quantum reinforcement learning can leverage quantum mechanisms to achieve superior outcomes. Nonetheless, the extent to which quantum mechanisms contribute to sample efficiency and performance remains to be determined in further research on smaller-scale systems. Moreover, the EGrels source code has been made available under an open-source framework at https://github.com/QuantPen/EGrels. Our study marks the first successful implementation of quantum reinforcement learning in multi-agent collaborative settings. To establish the feasibility of integrating such methods in practice, we have also conducted a user study that demonstrates EGrels's cross-domain transfer capabilities, which is described in detail in Supplement 2. Furthermore, while EGrels utilizes quantum circuits, it does not necessarily benefit from quantum speedup due to its limited number of qubits and dimensions. Nonetheless, our approach offers promising avenues for the investigation of quantum reinforcement learning in multi-agent collaborative tasks in the future. Discovering novel substances is typically a lengthy process, relying on the analysis of numerous samples with various physical attributes, such as color and fluorescence. By using one-shot learning, the discovery of unfamiliar materials in diverse environments can be accelerated. To facilitate this, a data transfer system is proposed that enables the effective exchange of information between high-capacity data storage systems and one-shot learning algorithms, allowing for the discovery of unfamiliar materials in diverse environments. The proposed system is evaluated through experiments on two features: artificial illumination and fluorescent properties. The results indicate that the proposed system is capable of discovering unfamiliar materials in diverse environments with great success, and that the effectiveness of the system depends on the quality of the data, as well as the effectiveness of the data storage system and one-shot learning algorithms. The proposed system is envisioned to have a significant impact in various fields, such as geology, botany, and pharmacology, where the discovery of unfamiliar materials in diverse environments is critical. The proposed system is comprised of two core components: data transfer systems and one-shot learning algorithms. The data transfer systems are responsible for facilitating the data storage and retrieval processes, as well as coordinating the data transfer operations. The one-shot learning algorithms, on the other hand, are responsible for learning from the data retrieved from the data transfer systems. The proposed system is evaluated using two benchmark experiments, one investigating the data transfer systems' ability to transfer artificial illumination properties and the other demonstrating the effectiveness of the one-shot learning algorithms in identifying unfamiliar materials in diverse environments. The results from these experiments demonstrate the great success of the proposed system in identifying unfamiliar materials in diverse environments. The proposed system is envisioned to have a significant impact in various fields, such as geology, botany, and pharmacology, where the discovery of unfamiliar materials in diverse environments is critical. In this work, we explore the idea that Wigner negativity in a specific subsystem can be used as an indicator of quantum correlations shared between parties holding a non-Gaussian state. Our investigation reveals that when two parties possess an arbitrary number of photons, it is feasible to eliminate the Wigner negativity in one subsystem without removing the total correlations, provided both parties retain a portion of the shared state. These findings challenge the notion that nonclassical properties in a specific subsystem serve as a reliable measure of overall correlations. Moreover, our research demonstrates that the Wigner negativity in one subsystem cannot be completely eliminated in the scenario where one party owns the entire quantum system, underscoring the Wigner transform's strength in identifying nonclassical states. Finally, our study examines how closely the Wigner form mimics the actual quantum density matrix when projecting a two-photon state to a specific subspace, thereby validating the utility of the Wigner transform in analyzing nonclassical properties in such scenarios. The Wigner transform has the advantage of bypassing computational difficulties in evaluating the quantum density matrix, especially for systems lacking photon number operators as relevant degrees of freedom. In various real-world scenarios, humans can provide comparative feedback on unlabeled data, but due to time constraints, they can only compare a limited number of items at once. To make the most of this feedback, we can compare the items being compared to speed up the learning process. Our proposed method involves using a batch-mode feedback learning algorithm that estimates the underlying video quality metrics through comprehensive comparisons made by humans. By comparing multiple videos within each batch, the algorithm can learn to predict the effectiveness of video improvements more accurately, thereby requiring fewer comparisons to achieve the same overall quality. Experiments in a real-world scenario have shown that this method can reach the same quality as a fully manual feedback process while only needing half as many comparisons to do so. Furthermore, by leveraging more comparisons, the algorithm can achieve better performance, outperforming a system that uses individual feedback and significantly reducing the need for comparisons to reach the same performance. These results demonstrate that batch feedback can be a valuable approach in certain contexts, but may not always be necessary to achieve optimal results with minimal human input. Our findings also indicate that batch feedback could be an effective means of reducing costs in industry settings where human feedback is necessary to complete tasks. By leveraging batch feedback, the algorithm can achieve the same quality using fewer comparisons, which may translate to reduced costs in real-world scenarios. As such, we believe that batch feedback could be a valuable option for tasks requiring human input. Our proposed method is not specific to our particular domain and can be applied in other areas requiring comparative feedback; for instance, audio, text, or other formats requiring comparisons could benefit from this algorithm. In this study, we investigate how the probability distribution of complex eigenvalues in random upper triangular matrices with non-zero diagonal elements changes as the band width increases from 1 to infinity. The research builds upon earlier work by Bialinskiy and Olshanski, which showed the convergence of the eigenvalue distribution of individual large random upper triangular matrices to a specific limit distribution known as the Olshanski matrix. Extending this to the matrix ensemble defined over the entire real line by introducing i.i.d. complex Gaussian elements on the band's edges, we find that the limiting eigenvalue distribution changes from a trivial case with band width 1 to a specific pattern of arcs on the real axis of the spectral plane as the band width increases. Furthermore, we found that the band width determines the relative sizes of these arcs. We outline the data processing and reduction protocols used for the Hi-GAL survey. Conducted with the GEEPS instrument on the APEX telescope, the survey maps six major galactic regions, and comprises 315 datasets that cover a total of 61,668 areas. Our reduction pipeline involves 50,000 cubes, each with 256 pixels per side, and 1 arcmin resolution, resulting in 3.22 TB of data once processed. The pipeline consists of four stages: first, the raw data from the instrument is corrected, then the data is filtered to remove irregularities, followed by the noise in the data is smoothed, and finally the data is projected onto a HEALPix grid for efficient storage and visualization. Additionally, the pipeline includes advanced data quality checks including the standard photometric analysis tools to ensure the data accuracy and robustness. Overall, the pipeline demonstrates its capability to produce high-quality data while minimizing the impact of technical artifacts. Notably, multiple generations of star formation have been discovered within some metal-rich clusters, while the lighter elements offer rare insights into the early supernovae patterns. Optimizing speed and accuracy often entails a balancing act, and our work demonstrates that this trade-off can be optimized through strategic search strategies. One theoretical model of this optimization is an asymmetric potential, characterized by increasing width in proportion to the square of the speed, a prediction supported by our analysis of random walks. Utilizing path integral techniques allows us to derive mean square displacements for various potentials, confirming that the asymptotic behavior of these potentials depends on the specific speed-accuracy trade-off, a relationship different from that predicted by the standard diffusive equation. Notably, our theoretical findings appear to be confirmed by experimental data from both physical and biological systems. In the case of Caenorhabditis elegans bacteria search, our path integral methods allow for the extraction of search strategy parameters from the bacterial mean square displacement, providing insight into their search strategies and accuracy levels at different speeds. Overall, our work sheds light on the fundamental speed-accuracy trade-off in one-dimensional physical systems. As an extension of this research, we have explored the application of this theory to the optimal strategies employed by C. elegans and E. coli, including a comparison of the search tactics of these species with that of a simple Brownian particle. Our model also allows us to investigate the sensitivity of optimal strategies to changes in accuracy levels, and even makes predictions for a possible optimal limit in the specific case of C. elegans. As the speed-accuracy trade-off has far-reaching implications, our findings have significant relevance to the field of biophysics, as well as to our understanding of random walk behaviors in one-dimensional physical systems. Ultimately, our work offers a valuable framework for studying and analyzing the speed-accuracy trade-off in search strategies. By integrating our theoretical model with an experimental approach, our research confirms that the asymptotic behavior of path integrals provides a precise description of the search strategies employed by E. coli at different speeds. Additionally, our path integral simulations allow us to derive search strategy parameters directly from the bacterial mean square displacement, providing insight into their search tactics and accuracy levels at different speeds. Our work appears to be generally applicable, as our path integral simulations successfully explain the optimal strategies observed in the specific case of C. elegans, accuracy levels, search tactics, and accuracy at different speeds, all of which have been rigorously experimentally confirmed. As the speed-accuracy trade-off has far-reaching implications, our findings have significant relevance to both the biophysics community and the field of random walk behaviors in one-dimensional physical systems.
