The existence of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules is considered natural and can be understood through the principles of QCD sum rules. In this paper, we explore the potential range of masses and the spin of the $\Lambda_{ccc}$ tetraquark as a three-quark system. Theoretical models also suggest that certain states can be identified as narrow, hidden charm three-quark systems. To further establish the nature of these states, we have analyzed the electromagnetic form factors of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules. The calculations reveal a unique configuration for the heavy quarks within the molecules, which is consistent with experimental data on the $X(3872)$ characteristics. Moreover, our research indicates that certain transitions of heavy molecules to baryons can serve as potential methods for detecting these states in future experiments. The predicted values of the magnetic moments of heavy baryons, such as $\Upsilon(11070)$, fall within the range of $0.30-1.30$ lepton mass units. These outcomes seem reasonable, considering the conventional rules of quark model magnetism. Our study also shows that the rule of a factor two in the transition from heavy molecules to baryons is consistent with spin-parity methods, but yields mixed results for the axial form factor, depending on the molecular state involved. Nonetheless, our maximum obtained values for this form factor do not present issues with transition radial structure. These outcomes were obtained using heavy molecules with the $s$ or $d$ quark as the light constituent, a configuration that is also indicated by our prior Faddeev-type three-body models. The derived form factor patterns for these states bear a resemblance to those of the $\Lambda_c^{+}$ baryon. The post-publication discussion of our research has uncovered questions regarding the treatment of the current mass in our model and whether our findings can accurately predict the magnetic moment of the $\Upsilon$ baryon. In addressing these concerns, we have determined that our model's treatment of the current mass is justified, but the simulated characteristics of the $\Upsilon$ baryon do not match its properties as seen in heavy quark effective theory. Nonetheless, our research provides the first theoretical description of the electromagnetic properties of heavy molecules consistent with experimental data on the $X(3872)$ and can potentially detect certain states in future experiments, such as those involving the $\Upsilon$ baryon. The way matter is structured in the universe is key to our understanding of its evolution. Lately, simulations based on the standard model of cosmology have shown that the growth of matter clustering is highly stable, which has significant implications for our understanding of the universe's evolution history. To investigate the impact of observational errors on the growth factor, we analyzed a collection of 425 cosmological models with variations in parameters, focusing on the galaxy redshift distribution and flux. Notably, we found that the errors made in determining the galaxy distribution at higher redshifts have a much lower impact on the inferences made about the universe's evolution compared to smaller redshifts. This is crucial, as it means that the errors made in inferring the universe's evolution history based on galaxy data at redshifts greater than 0.5 are likely to be substantial. Moreover, we found that the errors made at redshifts greater than 2 have a particularly substantial impact on the universe's evolution inferences, which is why it would be very beneficial to have data from galaxies at these redshifts. This is could be achieved through the use of new, sensitive equipment that is capable of detecting large numbers of galaxies at these redshifts. If this is successful, it is likely to lead to significant improvements in our understanding of the universe's evolution. To test this, we used the information from the Planck satellite and 6 other sets of data to see how effective different methods are at making accurate inferences about the universe's evolution. Notably, we found that the errors made at redshifts greater than 2 have a substantial impact on these inferences, which is why future work should focus on reducing these errors. This research is key to understanding how to improve the accuracy of the standard model of cosmology when more data become available. This is key to understanding how to improve the accuracy of the standard model of cosmology when more data become available. The first stage of the LHC upgrade, which involves upgrading the low-energy ion beam injector, has been underway since 2018 at the CERN LHC. As part of this initiative, a new cavity designed to bend the beam in a specific poloidal direction has been installed in the Linac 3, which houses the Linac improvement unit LIA1. A key aspect of this upgrade is the ability to use the new cavity to manipulate the particle beam's phase space through RF scanning technique the new cavity is integrated with. Furthermore, the upgrade includes upgrading the existing RF system to accommodate the scanning technique. Our focus in this paper will be on the details of the new cavity design, the challenges we faced during the installation process, the precision with which the cavity's electrical properties have been measured, and finally the first experimental observations of the beam following the installation of the new cavity. These initial experiments have been conducted as part of a dedicated run in 2022 known as the demonstration run, which took place outside of the LHC's regular cycle. The findings from this experiment have been presented and discussed in this paper. Upon completion of the upgrade, the total length of the low-energy section of the LHC injector, which houses Linac3 and six RF cavities, was extended to approximately 34.5 meters. Furthermore, the upgrade involved upgrading six separate RF cavities to accommodate a total voltage of 25 MV. It is noteworthy that the new cavity has a frequency of 462.5 MHz and is designed to bend the beam through an angle of 36.6 milliradians over a distance of six RF cavities. A key advantage of the new cavity is its compact design, which is largely attributed to its supersingular design characteristics. The new cavity has an effective length of 0.305 meters, a little under the theoretical minimum. The first experimental observations of the beam have demonstrated that the new cavity can successfully transfer approximately 6.7% of the beam's energy as it traverses the six RF cavities. Notably, the initial measurements of the cavity's electrical properties have established a precision of 0.15 parts-per-million (ppm) for the shunt impedance and 0.5 ppm for the frequency. These initial experimental findings confirm that the new cavity's integration has not compromised its overall length, which remains unchanged at 34.5 meters. The task of inferring pedestrian movements from observed trajectories, known as pedestrian trajectory prediction, has significant applications in robotics and autonomous systems. However, the reliance on simplistic statistical and social models hinders the state-of-the-art trajectory forecast accuracy. This paper presents an innovative approach, grounded in physical measurent bias theory, to address this challenge. The new method, referred to as the physically valid and distinct risk-aided trajectory prediction (PV-DRPT), views pedestrian motion as stemming from continuous state adjustments. By incorporating an integrated continuous motion prediction framework, PV-DRPT outperforms existing approaches, as evidenced by our experiments, yielding notable gains in terms of trajectory distance and intersection overlap during prediction. Specifically, PV-DRPT achieves a 2.4% reduction in Adam Szot Bell tracklet final trajectory distance and a 8.3% improvement in mean Calibrated Intersection over Union value compared to the view-point trajectory forest (VPTF) method. Furthermore, our PV-DRPT code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/paulpierina/PV-DRPT. This code facilitates comparisons with other top approaches in the field, such as social-laneflow, social gan, social gmm, social sam, socgnn, social transformer, LSTM, SARNet, liver, new ssgan, new social gan, new social gmm, new socgan, new sarcnet, and new social transformer, as detailed in our results section. A Boltzmann machine's dynamics can be viewed as a continuous transformation on its energy function, and this viewpoint offers a natural way to study how the system's complexity changes over time and in response to changes in its parameters. By using a variation of the Haar measure, we define a measure of complexity for the temporal evolution of the system's state. This measure indicates that, generally, the system's complexity decreases as it evolves, but it also reveals situations in which the complexity remains stable or increases. In particular, we find that in an infinite Boltzmann machine, the complexity can remain constant over time within the space of cycles in the dynamics. Furthermore, our results provide a foundation for a method to optimize Boltzmann machine parameters. This method involves initializing the parameters using a random, uniformly distributed configuration, and then refining them until they reach a stable state that minimizes complexity. Notably, this approach leads to results that closely mirror the topological kernels found in recent studies. Finally, we also explore how the complexity of the model's state changes over time can be used to monitor the learning process in the model. By tracking the complexity in a VAE, we are able to identify distinct phases in its learning cycle, including an initial phase characterized by rapid decreases in complexity. These findings offer new insights into the behavior of neural networks. All of the code used to implement the research in this work is available for public viewing on GitHub at https://github.com/jmjj/jarvetly.jarvetly/latest#boltzmann-machine-complexity. To increase a swarm of robots' efficiency, we've developed an adjusted inter-robot distance approach. A key element in this approach is maintaining a specific distance between robots, which is crucial for optimizing swarm performance. However, this strategy often results in collisions, especially when the distance between robots varies. To resolve this issue, we've developed a distance-adjustment method that takes into account the influence of neighboring robots. By incorporating these effects, the approach ensures that the desired inter-robot distance is maintained, reducing collisions and increasing efficiency. A simulation of this method revealed significant improvements in both convergence speed and overall efficiency within the robot swarm. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that the determined inter-robot distance affects the dexterity of robot movements, allowing for more precise task execution. As examples, the approach was applied to a swarm of robots picking up objects from a grid and positioning them at targeted locations or sorting them into distinct categories based on color. The results show that our method outperforms existing techniques, providing optimal inter-robot distance and improved swarm performance. To verify the approach's effectiveness, it was successfully implemented using real-world robotic systems. Automating the analysis of blood test results enhances accuracy, reduces costs, and elevates healthcare efficiency. Current industry trends rely on deep learning methods for image processing but they fail to account for extensive knowledge about diseases, which contributes to uncertainty in medical diagnoses. A new approach 'Probabilistic Deep Bayesian Network Learning' combines the advantages of deep learning and Bayesian networks, by disambiguating uncertainties in disease diagnoses using a probabilistic Bayesian network, and then training it with deep learning. This novel technique demonstrates an impressive improvement on three critical datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches and offering a promising future direction for making more informed medical diagnoses. Quantum theory is often assumed to be nonlocal, yet a proposed local model called objective collapse theory seeks to explain quantum phenomena locally. To compare these theories, we investigate the concept of measurement, particularly how measurements are related to changes in system state and what value they possess. Our study focuses on two key concepts: counter-factual measurements and measurement independence. Historically, the former has driven discussions about nonlocality while the latter is essential to understanding and altering system states. By applying our general framework, we found that measurement independence cannot be achieved without counter-factual measurements and that achieving the latter necessitates the former. These findings hold true for a broad range of physical systems, including those with multiple components. Moreover, our research reveals the essential role of the probability rule in connecting system changes to measurements, a role that is distinct from the function that maps system states to measurement outcomes. Our results have significant implications for understanding the differences between local and nonlocal aspects of quantum theory. They also shed light on the essential requirements for nonlocality and outline the criteria necessary for realizing counter-factual measurements and achieving measurement independence. Furthermore, our study offers a unique perspective on the process of system evolution, demonstrating how changes to system states are influenced by both counter-factual measurements and the probability rule. Our work ultimately compares the local behavior of the objective collapse theory to its nonlocal behavior, with special emphasis on the role of counter-factual measurements, which are absent in the local description but essential for understanding the nonlocal aspects of quantum theory. By contrasting the two descriptions, we gained insight into three distinct aspects of quantum theory: its nonlocality, the role of the probability rule, and the function that maps system states to measurement outcomes. Our study has substantial consequences for understanding these components of quantum theory. Our work also raises fundamental questions about the process of system evolution that are relevant to both local and nonlocal descriptions. We have developed an extended version of the Group Lasso method, which incorporates prior knowledge of variable correlations to enhance variable selection and sparse modeling in Bayesian continuous or categorical data. This enhanced Group Lasso, referred to as Group Lasso with Correlated Data (GLCD), takes into account arbitrary prior distributions for variable correlations. Using a penalty function that is proportional to the correlation matrix's trace, GLCD ensures the convergence of posterior mode estimates to the true parameter values under certain conditions. Additionally, the proposed method maintains sparsity and enables computationally efficient inference on variable inclusion. Our theoretical findings are substantiated by simulated scenarios and real-world data analysis. Notably, the posterior mode and the lasso estimator both exhibit fast convergence rates. Furthermore, the method appears robust to issues of perfect or partial singularity within the correlation matrix. Our case study found that GLCD improved variable selection and disease risk prediction accuracy for prostate cancer, achieving a 85.3% classification error rate compared to 86.7% for popular genomic risk model PREDICT-Prostate, and 86.6% for the lasso method. The R package, GLCD, is publicly available to facilitate the implementation of our method. In this research, we explore the stability of chimeras within networks of three oscillators, where each node displays stability-induced chimeric behavior. Our study examines the influence of heterogeneity in parameter sets on the chimeras' collective behavior. Building on existing research, which established that modest heterogeneity enhances the stability of chimeras, we further investigate how this phenomenon behaves under different degrees of heterogeneity and couple types. Notably, we discover that in many cases, an increase in heterogeneity ultimately leads to the disappearance of chimeras, which we demonstrate using both theoretical and numerical approaches. Our findings are also supported by a practical example. Moreover, our results show that not only the type of coupling but also the number of nodes in a network can significantly impact the chimeras' stability. Our study contributes not only to a deeper understanding of chimeras but also to the development of robust chimeras, by revealing how to create stable solutions in complex network systems. Our study may serve as a foundation for similar investigations into robust chimeras in more intricate networks.

One significant advantage of using neural networks to model dynamics and learn controllers is their potential to handle unknown systems. However, most of the current research in this field still relies heavily on assumptions regarding the accuracy of the models. Others have explored ways to make controllers more robust in the face of model inaccuracies, but usually, there's no limit put on the likelihood of errors, which can negatively impact performance. In our research, we've found that enforcing a minimum limit on the likelihood of errors in the dynamics model significantly enhances the robustness of the learned controllers, even when the model isn't very accurate. Our study is the first to investigate the effects of this constraint and we've applied it to high-fidelity wind turbine models to demonstrate its practical benefits. Our results show that a similar level of error can be achieved in real-world applications without the need for precise model accuracy, thanks to this approach. Furthermore, our research has successfully simulated the practical advantages of this noise regulation, even in complex scenarios where the model isn't a perfect representation of the actual system, acting as an robustness insurance policy against potential simulation inaccuracies. In contrast to other methods, our approach has the advantage of not requiring the simulation model to perfectly replicate the actual system, but rather, it ensures the learned controller's performance capabilities. Our results also show the effects of this noise regulation on the learning outcomes of the neural dynamics models and the robustness of the controllers. Ultimately, our approach has important implications for the practical use of neural networks in controller design and learning. Despite the widespread application of Deep Neural Networks across various fields, achieving optimal classification accuracy can be challenging, especially with large and complex datasets. To enhance the likelihood of finding a network capable of accurately categorizing data, multiple networks are trained and their outcomes compared. However, a more robust ensemble approach has been lacking. This research introduces an innovative ensemble method, dubbed K-SDRE, which leverages the strengths of multiple networks to produce a robust decision. Inspired by the SDRE philosophy, which simplifies the classification process by projecting data and classes into a reliable low-dimensional subspace, the proposed ensemble method further refines the accuracy of each network's classification by projecting the data into the robustly determined class subspace. Experimental results demonstrate that K-SDRE consistently outperforms traditional ensemble techniques, frequently delivering an accuracy of 99.5% or higher on the MNIST dataset, while also surpassing the state-of-the-art accuracy of 99.44%. Moreover, in contrast to other advanced methods, the robust accuracy of K-SDRE was achieved through the selection of just two networks. Furthermore, this robust ensemble method was validated on real-world datasets, namely the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. It is noteworthy that the robust accuracy of K-SDRE was consistently higher than other approaches, while also robust against overfitting. Control Optim., 2000) scheme for Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, and is further connected to a linear integro-differential equation through an ideal interface. The scheme leverages the flexibility of Generalized Viscosity Solutions and offers a computationally efficient way to solve the given equations, thanks to its independence from particular solutions of the equations and an approximate separation principle. By applying the Generalized Viscosity Solutions theory, we demonstrate the asymptotic convergence of the scheme to a Generalized Viscosity Solution of the equations, and show that this solution is uniquely determined up to an additive constant. Moreover, we derive an approximation of the solution by iteratively applying a linear approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations on a bisection of the time domain, and provide a stochastic interpretation of the scheme via SDEs. Finally, we implement the scheme in a MATLAB tool to derive an optimal control for a distributed control system. This analysis is backed up by numerical tests of the method's convergence and efficiency. The research is an extension of previous work on Generalized Viscosity Solutions for Hamilton-Jacoli-Isaacs equations, and builds on prior results for linear integro-differential equations by Pizzaro and Sanchez (2019). A simulation test was conducted using the MATLAB Simulink software platform to compare the performance of GFBC and conventional FBC. The results indicate that GFBC exhibits superior control capabilities, with successful regulation of the quadcopter's rotation and position despite the presence of external disturbances. Furthermore, GFBC displays more stable and robust convergence in comparison to FBC. A comprehensive evaluation of GFBC is presented through a statistical analysis of the root mean square error scores obtained from the simulation trials. The outcomes of this investigation reveal that GFBC is a dependable control strategy capable of reducing the influence of noise and system uncertainties. Moreover, GFBC exhibits potential as a adaptive control system, enabling online adaptation of its gains through the recovery of its predictive model. A theoretical examination of the necessary and sufficient conditions for the local asymptotic stability of the GFBC closed-loop system was performed, defining the region of parameters within the local asymptotic stability of the GFBC closed-loop system. Consequently, the local asymptotic stability of the GFBC closed-loop system is confirmed when the control parameter falls within the specified range. Moreover, the robustness of the GFBC was evaluated and demonstrated through simulation trials conducted under various adverse conditions, including changes in weather and mechanical failure. The robustness test of the GFBC revealed that the control system is capable of maintaining its stability and control capabilities even in extreme scenarios. Consequently, the Genetic Filter Backstepping Control is a dependable and robust control strategy, offering enhanced robustness and robustness capabilities, with potential for adaptation and learning. The genetic filter-based control method is a versatile controller, compatible with a wide array of nonlinear dynamic systems, including MIMO systems. The application of the genetic filter offers the advantage of adaptability and learning over traditional control strategies. The integration of the genetic filter into the control system allows the automatic fine-tuning of the control gains online, eliminating the need for prior knowledge and further stabilizing the control loop. The robustness of the GFBC was evaluated through simulation trials conducted under diverse fault conditions, revealing the mechanism's capacity to withstand mechanical failures. The SPD's improvements allowed for the implementation of longer readout cables (ROC), thereby improving readout speed and reducing radiation damage issues. On the edge of the 2016 dataset and following a major upgrade for the start of the LHC's Run 2 in 2017, several components based on silicon carbide were substituted with those using silicon carbide antiparticles (BISI) to further minimize degradation. These developments led to improved signal quality, increased sensitivity, and enhanced durability. The enhancements to the SPD signal quality allowed for the implementation of more stringent data quality selection criteria even in situations of intense luminosity and substantial radiation exposure. The longer readout cables and improved FE amplified signals resulted in the reduction of hit uncertainties, while measures to mitigate radiation damage led to the improvement of signal quality in the most heavily irradiated layers. The replacement of several components based on silicon carbide helped preserve the signal quality in the most irradiated layers, and the strategic placement of BISI components on the edges of the detector minimized readout system inefficiencies. The SPD's enhanced design and performance resulting from these improvements have significantly contributed to the current detector's operational capabilities and the achievement of accurate and reliable experimental results. The SPD's current state serves as the foundation for its upcoming upgrade to the end-of-the-roadmap exploration phase, in which two thicknesses of doped analog front-end amplifiers will be replaced with digital FE. We present the existence of distinct periodic solutions for a general, given time-periodic parabolic equation within a bounded domain, assuming the coefficient of dissipation possesses a positive maximum. Furthermore, we examine the implications of initial condition prevalence on the nature of these periodic solutions: in scenarios where the prevalence is high, solutions converge to a global equilibrium; however, for low prevalence, solutions may persist in periodic orbits. In line with earlier findings for linear equations, the rate at which the prevalence shifts and the size of the time period determine whether solutions converge to periodic patterns or an global equilibrium. Ultimately, we establish the existence of periodic solutions in a range of contexts, including those described by the Hunter-Saxton equation and the quasi-geostrophic equations. Due to the absence of traditional dissipation in these equations, the nature of their solutions is closely related to those of their strongly damped counterparts. As such, the periodic solutions exist regardless of the initial conditions and prevalence of the dissipative factor within the equations. Moreover, our research into periodic solutions in strongly damped quasi-geostrophic equations offers a novel perspective on the rapid dissipation of two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic solutions at critical latitude. Recent breakthroughs in generative models using autoencoders and GANs have significantly improved the quality of unsupervised speech synthesis. This paper demonstrates that an unsupervised speech synthesis system can rival a supervised system, producing speech that is both clear and easy to understand. In particular, we enhance the quality of synthesized speech by incorporating a vocal tract optimization module that adjusts acoustic features to better match the target speech. Unlike the conventional approach of fine-tuning existing models using large datasets, our approach utilizes a combination of a pre-trained variational autoencoder and a single-emotion procrustes loss, as well as the vocoder, to refine the acoustic features of the target speech. In comparison to a supervised system, our approach achieves similar mean opinion score results, according to the average speech perception score. Additionally, our results show that our approach can tolerate some remaining differences between the generated acoustic features and the true speech in terms of spectral representation. In the framework of Tsallis holographic dark energy model with interaction, we explore the possibility of achieving a stable de Sitter ground state consistent with current observational standards. The research is conducted in a universe described by a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker spacetime and characterized by a general interacting dark energy equation of state. Specific details about the equation of state and the coupling parameter are considered in two separate analyses. The analyses demonstrate that under certain conditions, the universe can asymptotically reach a stable de Sitter state. The research further reveals that these stable states are in accordance with current observational constraints as represented by the Riess $H_{0}$ value. The findings also show that there exists a relationship between the coupling parameter and the constant parameter of the Tsallis holographic dark energy model. The research ultimately indicates that such stable states can be achieved either by introducing interaction between the dark energy and the dark matter or by adjusting the characteristic length scale of the Tsallis holographic dark energy model. The outcomes of this research provide valuable insights into the evolution behaviors of the two-parameter Tsallis holographic dark energy model. The potential applications of this model in understanding the accelerating universe are also explored. The potential candidates from the string landscape that may accommodate such a stable ground state are briefly discussed. The research opens up more questions regarding the theoretical underpinnings of these stable states, such as whether they represent stable minima in the effective potential or temporary stable states in the trajectory of the model's evolution. The differences in behavior between the Tsallis holographic dark energy model and the phantom energy model are particularly highlighted. The research suggests that a broader examination of the effective potential and trajectory along with various parameters is required to gain a deeper understanding of the evolutionary dynamics of these models. The potential usefulness of this approach in observing the cosmic evolution and extracting parameters is also identified. The final part of the research explores the theoretical underpinnings of the photon Boltzmann-Hawking (BH) length as well as its generalization and potential applications. The last part of the research particularly investigates the BH length in its pure form and demonstrates that the introduction of interaction or modification does not significantly alter its fundamental principles. The outcomes of this research show that the BH length serves as a fundamental standard in understanding the evolutionary behaviors of matter and dark energy states at the horizon of the universe. The overall goal of this research is to contribute to a deeper understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of the BH length and its related concepts, as well as to open up new avenues

We have developed a new family of test functions (TestFun5) that demonstrate the potential of the SCS method to outperform SDP in terms of the IR score. Additionally, the IR metric has been used to compare the performance of the SCS method across various preprocessing options. The computational results show that different parameter settings within the SCS method yield various solution quality and run time characteristics. Consequently, the IR can be utilized as an objective function that guides the parameter selection among thousands of possible configurations in the SCS method. Moreover, the IR has been found to be strongly convex, enabling the use of accelerated first-order optimization techniques to find its minimum value. This efficient minimizer, which takes just a few seconds to operate, has been used in a model-based optimization framework to identify optimal parameter settings for the SCS method. Notably, the optimal parameters thus identified are on average 12 times better than their default values in terms of the IR score. Finally, the optimal parameter settings found have been shown to reduce the number of required matrix-vector products in the SCS method. This approach has significant implications for distributed computing environments where such products are often the primary cost factor. Therefore, the IR has significant potential to contribute to the field of numerical optimization for optimization of composite or binary sensing problems. In synthetic differential geometry, different approaches have been developed to introduce a geometrically meaningful ring of functions. We discuss these methods and introduce new terminology, including the source path and source groupoid, to describe the flow of information within these geometric structures. These concepts lead to the development of a hierarchy of functions, and the choice of a source groupoid defines the domain of functions on a presheaf. When a sheaf of functions is formed from a presheaf of functions, the geometrically significant functions are those specified by functions of sheaves with a specific property related to the source groupoid. Building on this framework, we investigate the notion of differential geometric atlas by generalizing the concept of an atlas from differential geometry to differential geometric atlas. A differential geometric atlas is a source groupoid with a local basis consisting of elements with high differential order. As a practical application of this theory, we describe the source groupoid of functions associated with the standard Grothendieck sheaf of differential functions and demonstrate that this sheaf is differential geometric. Importantly, this means that the concept of differential geometric atlas can be defined using standard methods of differential geometry. Finally, we consider the extension of these ideas to more general topological spaces and discuss the challenges associated with defining differential geometric structures on such settings. A novel approach is proposed, which involves equating differential geometric structures to those satisfying a specific condition related to ideal sheaves, and this method is proven to be equivalent to the original definition for certain types of topological spaces, namely, when the X-space is locally compact or when the x-valued function vanishes when composed with any morphism f in the category of topological spaces. The last section of the work explores the concept of differential extensions in the context of topological spaces with a rich ring of functions, which is achieved when the differential structure extends the differential structure of the ring of functions on X. A local description of differential extensions is provided and the concept is proven to be equivalent to the differential structure of a sheaf of functions in the case of compact Hausdorff X-space. The work also discusses the concept of differential extensions in the case where the X-space is locally compact and the sheaf of functions on X is defined as the sheaf of germs of functions on open sets of X. A key discovery made in this context is that the differential structure of the sheaf of functions on X is the maximal differential extension of the differential structure of the ring of functions on X. Researchers are eager to explore the potential of non-commutative geometry in quantum systems, and for this reason, we develop a theoretical framework under the name $\Lambda_q$-approach. This framework applies the non-commutative geometry to coupled cavity systems with a qubit, and shows the intricate relationship between tunneling strength, optomechanical coupling, and an external driving field. By adjusting the tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, we can control the probe field's behavior, and the presence of tunneling leads to a suppression of heating in the system. Additionally, we control the center frequency of the probe field by tweaking the optomechanical coupling and study how different parameters influence the generation of two-photon states. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this framework can be used to build an entanglement source for quantum networks. By carefully manipulating the optomechanical coupling and tunneling strength, we can control the source's efficiency and optimal driving strength. Moreover, we find the robustness of entanglement generation under different optomechanical couplings and reveal the role of an exact solution in this process. This provides a foundation for further exploration of $\Lambda_q$-approach in various applications. In particular, future studies could incorporate quadratic potentials to investigate lattice sonics, which may uncover novel and unexplored features. Furthermore, the possibility of connecting distant quantum systems could be explored through the concept of qubit teleportation. Possible experimental implementation of $\Lambda_q$-approach could be realized in dielectric micro-spheres by incorporating qubit degrees of freedom. Future studies could also investigate the role of quadratic potentials in this context. In conclusion, we find that $\Lambda_q$-approach is a versatile tool for understanding non-commutative geometry in quantum systems and the potential roles of lattice sonics, qubit teleportation, and qubit degrees of freedom in these systems. The presence of an exact solution in this context facilitates the exploration of various applications and parameters. We demonstrate the importance of careful tuning the optomeomechanical coupling in order to achieve optimal entanglement generation in real-world applications. This relationship also holds for real-world applications and future studies should investigate the role of quadratic potentials in the context of qubit degrees of freedom. We are eager to see the outcomes of potential experimental investigations into the important aspects of $\Lambda_q$-approach and the collaboration between theory and experiment will be highly encouraged.

Accurate segmentation of various brain tissues is crucial for understanding brain diseases and determining measures such as brain volume. While Gaussian Processes possess the ability to generate accurate segmentation, the resulting forecasts often struggle to incorporate future knowledge. In an effort to rectify this, we developed a time-adaptive model that combines a Gaussian Process with a sequence of adjustments, allowing us to incorporate expert knowledge about the brain's structure and its changes over time. This expertise is incorporated using a mixture of Gaussian Processes, each representing a distinct aspect: one for the overall brain shape, one for the amount of brain fluid, and one for the cortex thickness. Our model's results on multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over conventional segmentation techniques. Using this framework, we were able to create detailed maps showing how the cortex changed over time for over 5,000 individuals, revealing correlations between brain structure and measures such as education level and brain volume. Code and the final dataset can be found at https://github.com/tiloFJG/GP-CCVI. This work has been supported by the NIH grant R01MH107249.  Please note that our approach can be extended to any multi-dimensional image analysis task that accepts point-wise annotations.  Future work will explore utilizing our framework for making precise predictions about an individual's risk of cognitive decline.  We anticipate our approach to be applied in multiple domains where forecasting based on images is crucial, including astronomy, biology, medical imaging, atmospheric and biological drift studies. We explore the interplay between heat generated by an external field and energy loss due to its interaction with an environment in a one-dimensional gas of bosons. By applying the density matrix formalism, we derive an analytical expression for the temperature of the system over time. As the strength and duration of the interaction with the environment increase, we observe a transition in the system's behavior, from equilibrium to non-equilibrium statistics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, a system that experiences strong dissipation and periodic heating can exhibit a Bose-Einstein condensation that surpasses the typical temperature range for the process. Interestingly, this type of condensation occurs at a fixed fraction of the period of the driving field. Our results are verified through numerical simulations at various levels of system-bath coupling. Ultimately, we analyze the conditions under which equilibrium statistics emerge in a system that is coupled to a bath. Importantly, we find that strong dissipation and periodic heating can lead to unique statistical behaviors. To extend this work, we investigate the numerical and experimental boundaries of system-bath coupling in the context of quantum systems. As a specific application of the presented findings, we examine the influence of system-bath coupling on the entanglement of two Bose-Einstein condensates during a process of interaction and exchange. Importantly, we demonstrate that strong dissipation and periodic heating can lead to unique statistical behaviors, surpassing the typical temperature range for the process. The approach and findings of this work are adaptable to other quantum systems, such as fermions, that exhibit dissipation and periodic heating. Moreover, we identify the potential of developing novel quantum technologies that leverage dissipation and periodic heating to produce unique states of quantum systems. Importantly, the numerical and experimental boundaries of system-bath coupling are evaluated, and current challenges in the field are considered. As a specific case study, the potential applications of the presented findings to the experiment with a Bose-Einstein condensate produced by the optical melting of a Bose-Josephson ring are examined. The optical melting of the ring is used as a specific example of the complexity of the simulations involved. Importantly, the potential applications of the presented findings to other areas of quantum system research, such as the simulations of quantum baths, are considered. A new framework is developed to understand the role of dissipation and periodic heating in the quantum systems. Importantly, the approach and findings of this work are seen as a significant advancement in the numerical and experimental boundaries of system-bath coupling in the context of quantum systems. This paper presents a novel online OpenFlow Energy-aware Path Setup (OFES) algorithm that takes into account real-time network conditions, including real-time traffic flow, link energy consumption, and node reliability. To improve efficiency, we've modified the OFES algorithm to reduce its time complexity from polynomial to a more manageable linear time. The adapted version, called Heuristic OFES (HFES), rapidly establishes energy-efficient, reliable paths under varying network conditions. By comparing HFES with other algorithms, such as OpenFlow-based Energy-aware Path Setup and Flow-based intrusion detection, we've demonstrated that HFES achieves nearly equivalent flow set-ups as the original OFES algorithm while outperforming it in reduced energy consumption and higher flow set-up rates. Furthermore, HFES shows a substantial increase in scalability over OFES with its simplified computations. Notably, when comparing HFES to other algorithms, it outperforms them in all aspects of the experiment results. The proposed HFES algorithm offers a practical solution for reducing energy consumption and network reliability issues in flow setup problems within software-defined networks. Our experiment findings show that HFES can reallocate paths in under 50 microseconds, providing an online algorithm with considerable advantages over other energy-efficient flow scheduling methods. The OpenFlow-based energy-efficient flow scheduling problem shares similarities with various network resource management challenges in software-defined networks, and its key advancements in flow setup efficiency could be applied or adapted to other related issues. A future plan is to investigate how the energy consumption and reliability features of this problem can be extended to other network resource management tasks. As a contribution to the research community, we've made our source code available online. Our potential future line of investigation includes exploring how the characteristics of this problem can be expanded to other network resource management challenges. A detailed comparison of the proposed algorithm's performance along with other energy-aware algorithms is presented in this study to highlight its advantages. This research introduces an innovative approach to speeding up metric learning for image retrieval. The proposed method focuses on breaking down the loss gradient components from pair-wise loss functions and utilizing the dominant direction in these gradients to accelerate metric learning convergence. In doing so, convergence can be achieved even faster than the original loss function. The approach has also been combined with existing acceleration techniques such as the leading edge method to further boost its performance. Comprehensive experiments conducted on CARS196, Clever Systems, and the sistemberg datasets demonstrate that this approach alone results in better or comparable image retrieval results than other acceleration techniques. Notably, when combined with the leading edge method, the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CARS196 and Clever Systems datasets. The source code for this research is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/leechan420/MeanLeadingEdge. Moreover, a Tensorflow implementation can be found at https://github.com/leechan420/MAPLE-TF. This work aims to provide valuable insights for future advancements in metric learning acceleration. Additionally, the proposed method has significant potential to speed up other deep learning tasks utilizing pair-wise loss functions. Finally, the term 'MeanLeadingEdge' refers to the project's name, suggesting a mean to leverage the leading edge of convergence. In contrast to the original leading edge method, MAPLE requires only access to the gradient of the loss function during training, making it a versatile approach. Following a review of literature on consensus controllers, this paper proposes an iterative convergence theory for power flow management in community networks, facilitated by a centralized leader. Building on this framework, two consensus control strategies are introduced - one centralized and one decentralized - to address the limitations of consensus theory, where some nodes refuse to cooperate. Simulations using a small community grid validate the effectiveness of these controllers in achieving stability within specified voltage ranges. What's more, this study shows that conventional consensus controllers can lead to unstable outcomes in inverter-based grids with significant loads, but the proposed control strategies can mitigate this issue. Finally, this research evaluates the resilience of these controllers in the face of communication delays and uncooperative nodes, providing a foundation for future load modeling and analysis. We focus on multi-round multi-armed bandit issues where a key problem is minimizing regret. In our research, we have made significant contributions by broadening the applicability of existing outcomes in scenarios where losses for the top arm can only be bounded by a conditionally Bernoulli random variable, taking values in the range [0,1] or [0, $\Delta$]. This extension encompasses various more general scenarios, including: (i) infinitely many arms where the top arm's losses can only be bounded, (ii) arms with unique loss distributions, and (iii) scenarios where the loss for each round is dependent on previous outcomes. Based on our new general outcomes, we have derived faster regret bounds that are particularly efficient when the top arm's loss is far from optimal. To achieve these outcomes, we have developed two new types of policies: (i) a policy that dynamically adjusts the set of arms to be simultaneously played each round, (ii) a policy that dynamically adjusts both the set and probability of arms to be simultaneously played each round. These two types of policies cover our multi-arms scenarios and play a central role in all of our outcomes. Furthermore, we have proven that in general scenarios where there is no lower bound on the mutual information between arm $i$ and arm $j$ (denoted as $I_{i,j}$), a lower bound can be established for this mutual information, significantly broadening the applicability of existing outcomes in scenarios where this mutual information's lower bound can be easily determined (e.g., when arms' loss distributions are Gaussian with well-known covariance matrices or play unique roles in solving the bandit issue). In addition, we have derived a new outcome in scenarios where there is no lower bound on the mutual information $I_{i,j}$; this outcome is based on our new policy and plays a central role in all of our outcomes. To the best knowledge, all of our outcomes are the first to solve these general scenarios that are currently unsolved. Lastly, we have verified that our policies are feasible to implement when arm $i$'s loss distribution is known to be $\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)$, by showing that its infinite support implies that the lower bound of $I_{i,j}$ can be easily determined as an $\Omega(\min\{i,j\})$. This is particularly efficient in solving the classic smooth bandit issue where arms' loss distributions have unique means $\mu_i$ and covariance matrices $\Sigma_i$.

Since its introduction in 1972, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) has been the sole
theory governing strong interactions. However, for nearly five decades, the
world has lacked a reliable and precise numerical solution to QCD. As a result,
numerical approaches have focused on non-perturbative QCD, while leaving precise
solutions out of reach. On the other hand, light-confronting operators and QCD at
vanishingly small energy densities have been explored using alternative methods.

In this study, we make a breakthrough by solving the QCD Yang-Mills equation,
which describes energy densities of QCD at low energy densities, and our
solutions appear robust and precise. Moreover, our work at zero temperature
reveals that QCD energy densities are, at very low energy densities, proportional
to the fourth root of the QCD running coupling constant's value. Our data also
corroborate that QCD undergoes a transition from non-interacting to strongly
interacting at low energy densities, and such interactions become universally
applicable across all spin states. 

We take a dimensionless perspective on QCD coupling constants by expressing
them as functions of energy densities, and our results may offer a fresh point of
departure for exploring QCD's non-perturbative behavior and further refining the
QCD phase diagram. Our approaches might also bear the potential to significantly
facilitate numerical solutions to QCD. We verify that the QCD Yang-Mills equation
are free from order-by-order divergences in certain limits and expand solutions
to incorporate quantum electrodynamics (QED)-like interactions. We model the QCD
running coupling constant's behavior using an approach incorporating an analytic
tamper and apply it to both the continuous quantum phase transition of QCD and QED.

The energy industry is experiencing a rapid growth in demand for powerful offshore wind turbines, yet these machines are prone to experiencing failure due to turbulent sea conditions caused by wave interaction with the shore. Since the shore can generate turbulent flows in various stochastic ways (such as irregular waves and river inflows), the loads on offshore wind turbines become increasingly unpredictable as they move further away from the shore. To better understand and model these unpredictable loads, this paper explores a statistical approach, involving a state-space model, that makes use of specific turbine sensors (AC power data) to make accurate predictions about unknown variables (turbine loads). The proposed methodology relies on generating artificial data through advanced computer simulations and uses a machine learning method to determine the best predictive model for turbine loads, while also accounting for changes in turbine dynamics over time. The proposed methodology was successfully tested on simulated data from three different offshore turbines, with the results showing that the accuracy of the predictions improved significantly when the method was combined with historical data. The outcomes of this study present a promising statistical approach that can effectively account for the influence of complex stochastic sea conditions on offshore wind turbines. The findings suggest that there is considerable potential for this method to produce accurate predictions of turbine loads in various scenarios, such as changes in power production and structural health monitoring. Therefore, the method could have a positive and efficient impact on reducing offshore maintenance costs, increase energy production and compliance with maintenance standards. The study's code and data are freely available online. The wavelet-based state-space model developed in this study has the advantage of being simple and easy to understand, which is not typically the case with neural network-based methods. The COVID-19 global outbreak has prompted the widespread adoption of contact tracing technologies driven by digital tools, government initiatives, and healthcare expertise. While this rush to scale the rollout of contact tracing technology is underway across many countries, there is currently a lack of comprehensive, upfront analysis of the long-term implications for society that go beyond the immediate health crises. This research aims to fill the gap by examining the potential consequences of large-scale contact tracing technology for individual rights, governance, and society as a whole in the longer term. By investigating the impact on individual privacy, justice system governance, and society, we provide insights into both the positive outcomes and potential drawbacks of large-scale contact tracing technology systems. Furthermore, we discuss critical design factors and trade-offs that can minimize negative consequences and maximize benefits, suggesting that a multi-faceted design approach is essential to ensure the long-term durability and success of contact tracing technology initiatives. By exploring critical design elements and societal considerations, we provide guidance for policymakers, governments, and healthcare institutions to implement contact tracing technology systems while upholding essential values. Finally, we outline areas worthy of further exploration and research. By highlighting critical design elements and societal considerations, we provide guidance for policymakers, governments, and healthcare institutions on the safe adoption of contact tracing technology to contain the COVID-19 crisis, while upholding crucial values. Additionally, we outline areas worthy of further exploration and research in the future. Furthermore, by systematically reviewing the impact of contact tracing technology on the individual, governance, and society, we provide comprehensive guidance for governments, policymakers, and healthcare professionals on its effective use to contain the COVID-19 crisis, by identifying crucial design factors and trade-offs to minimize negative consequences and maximize benefits.

However, researchers have since discovered that this process can be reversed and still benefit from it:
translated proof scripts can serve as a basis for generating a target language implementation.
We outline a general framework that uses annotated proof scripts to drive the translation of other languages.
We then apply this framework to the specification and development of a C11-compliant runtime environment for Go.
Our method encompasses the translation of Go's runtime complexity analysis as well as its code generator. 
We have successfully implemented and validated this framework within the Coq proof assistant. 
As a result, Coq provided both a formally correct C11 runtime environment and a tool to generate native C code based on these specifications. 
Our approach featured explicit representations of program state and procedures, with annotated proof scripts serving as a bridge between Go and Coq/OCaml. 
By combining formal verification with program synthesis, we could ensure the correctness of Go programs that use the specified C11 API. 
This method allowed us to validate a wide range of examples, including multi-threaded programs that leveraged C11's atomic safety features. 
These verified examples could be visualized using the Verity visualizer, with both their source code and formal proofs seamlessly integrated. 
Furthermore, our implementation included an interactive compiler from Go to C, C code from Go, and even a C code verifier based on C11 specifications. 
All our sources, including both manually written and automatically generated code, proof scripts, and formal verification, are available online through the Coq database. 
Additionally, our recent publication detailing the verification of a Go program drove discussions about the program's atomic misuse and contributed to broader discussions about the atomic library in the Go community. 
We have also shared our research with the Go team, including a proposal for incorporating formal verification into the Go project.
We believe our approach has significant potential for future use in verifying real-world programs across multiple languages and domains.

Consequently, the proposed $\ViViT$ approach may open up new avenues for optimizing deep neural networks. The primary goal of single-image pose estimation in object detection is to accurately determine a target object's orientation. Most current techniques rely on direct output, whereas others employ two-step processes involving an initial width and height estimation followed by a width and height-dependent orientation prediction. In this research, a novel method, known as L-Dense2Pose, is presented to significantly enhance orientation estimation capabilities. The proposed technique is inspired by the dense prediction approach and combines multiple object size-dependent sub-pose estimators to generate robust orientation results. To address the inherent size-related ambiguities in pose challenges, sub-pose estimators are carefully fine-tuned to accommodate size variations. The proposed method incorporates size-dependent sub-pose estimators, size-independent pose aggregation, and size-dependent final pose aggregation to substantially improve orientation estimation accuracy. In-depth experiments were conducted on the widely used Layttop-42K and challenging KITTI datasets to compare the proposed method's performance with that of existing baseline approaches. The results indicate that the proposed L-Dense2Pose method significantly enhances orientation estimation accuracy by 1.4% and 2.3% relative to the best baseline performance on Layttop-42K and KITTI datasets, respectively. However, our detailed linear stability analysis in multi-dimensional spaces reveals that damping within Froude cycles is not the primary mechanism preventing instability. Instead, it is mainly due to geometric damping caused by orthogonal power network topology and line characteristics. Furthermore, our results show that secondary frequency controls do influence voltage dynamics but incur robustness issues if power transfer becomes too large. To address these concerns, our complementary robust control design ensures that decentralized secondary frequency controls remain stable over a wide range of power transfer and network impedance. We've developed and analyzed several online schemes designed to identify the most similar state from a collection of pure states with constant overlap among all pairs. These schemes are akin to the online version of the collision estimate. With constant overlap, we found that no online scheme can identify the closest state with certainty and confidence as the number of states and identifications approach infinity. In contrast, model-guided control is an innovative learning-based approach that empowers us to discover controlled policies while only requiring partial model information. Following its initial development for linear systems, we have adapted this technique to work with parametric nonlinear systems that have limited model knowledge. This entails training a model that estimates the policy that maximizes a user-defined cost function. Notably, model-guided control for nonlinear systems allows us to incorporate constraints on the control inputs when formulating the optimization problem. Our approach offers several key advantages, including the ability to outperform conventional reinforcement learning even under data scarcity. Furthermore, it exhibits resilience during tasks involving incomplete state observations and uncertain dynamic system models. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through simulations of various benchmark tasks. Notably, our technique successfully controls the double integrator system with no model knowledge using the policy evaluation method for learning, and it achieves comparable performance to reinforcement learning under sufficient data conditions. Moreover, it turns out that model-guidance significantly boosts the robustness of the learned controller when the system is subject to noise and random disturbances. While initially designed for online learning, our approach can also operate in an offline setting, given the precomputation of multiple system models. This facility allows our model-guided control method to handle tasks involving incomplete state observations and uncertain dynamic system models. In these cases, our approach outperforms reinforcement learning by learning multiple control policies corresponding to different system models and selecting the most suitable one based on the current estimate of the state. Our model-guided control method offers an attractive trade-off between requiring knowledge of multiple system models and the high costs associated with it. To further illustrate the capabilities of our approach, we have demonstrated its effectiveness on several benchmark tasks involving uncertain dynamic system models and incomplete state observations. Notably, our model-guided control method learns to solve the challenging task of autonomous flight, where we only have access to the readings from the accelerometer and gyroscope. These sensors provide an incomplete estimate of the state and are subject to significant noise and random disturbances. A widely used method for object detection known as pseudo bounding-box annotation, or soft-box, has been proven to boost the performance of detectors significantly. This method involves using detailed information about box shapes and can be derived from the detection dataset without manual annotation. In this research, we present an advanced framework for creating high-quality pseudo boxes for both individual images and groups of images. Our approach draws on visual evidence by regulating the box shape, cross-image correlation, and temporal coherence. To optimize the pseudo boxes accurately, we employ a learning-to-rank method to fine-tune the box shape according to classification performance. Our framework has been extensively tested on two challenging vision tasks: object detection and vehicle re-identification. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art pseudo-box methods while surpassing weakly-supervised end-to-end detectors significantly. Notably, our framework established a new record on the MS-COCO 2017 detection benchmark by delivering a mAP of 21.6 without manual annotation. Additionally, our framework's effectiveness in vehicle re-identification was confirmed by achieving top ranks on the VeRi and VeRi-W dataset. Overall, our approach represents one of the best combinations of efficiency, simplicity, and performance achieved so far in pseudo-box-based weakly-supervised object detection. The code and dataset used in this research are available at: https://github.com/EliranBen-Ari/BoxYourBrains.

Completing a neural architecture search (NAS) task within a predetermined time constraint is crucial for real-world applications. Since the output space of a top-ranked model can exceed 10^10, significantly accelerating search is essential. Although utilizing pre-trained language models (PLMs) has significantly improved performance, their complexity and time-consuming training make them less suitable for efficient in-place text prediction during NAS. To overcome this, we investigate the feasibility of condensing the PLM's capabilities into smaller, faster models, while preserving its data's predictive power. Our method for achieving this involves an innovative type of attention that uses the input data to select relevant past experiences. We evaluate this approach using a leading PLM based on the BERT family, and our results show that a substantially smaller model can achieve nearly identical performance, outperforming existing methods on a range of PLMs, including variants of the BERT and Transformer-XL. To accelerate NAS, we also investigate alternative techniques such as early stopping, continuing from previous checkpoints, and combining these with data augmentation and transformer-based models. Our results indicate that a method combining continued training, data augmentation, and a expert-guided sampling strategy can substantially accelerate the search process while maintaining performance, even when using smaller models. When applied to a range of NAS tasks, our approach enables significantly more efficient in-place prediction, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. For example, while it currently takes around 130 seconds to predict a top-ranked model using an ELECTRA-based model on a NVIDIA V100, our accelerated method can complete the task in a mere 10.5 milliseconds, at a cost reduction of 88%. We demonstrate that in a convex CAT(0) space, geodesic completeness is not solely determined by the Hilbertian nature of its fundamental group, contradicting a previous claim by Misha Gromov. Notably, our counterexample involves a proper action of a group on a metric space, which suggests that the relationship between asymptotic collapse and stable isomorphism for group boundaries explored by Eric Leemans, Lucja Pawliuk, and Mike Susterson has broad implications across various settings. Additionally, the characteristics of the proper isometric action of a group on a metric space, as well as the properties of the boundary itself, are essential in defining a geodesically complete space of its type. Consequently, our findings imply that under certain conditions, the boundary itself cannot be expressed as a Hilbert space. Lastly, our construction yields a new instance of a non-hyperbolic group whose growth function is polynomial of degree 2, which has implications for discussing non-positive curvature metrics on the circle. The proof relies on the principles of model category theory, specifically the application of proper homotopy equivalences as computational models for the fundamental group, as outlined by Galatovits and Quillen. The work can be further expanded to non-uniform free groups through an analogous argument. The authors are seeking to establish a detailed description of geodesically complete spaces of the type described in this report. Further research is intended to extend the results to other types of non-hybrid spaces, such as CAT(0) length spaces with upper curvature restrictions. The concept is also being explored in the context of char $p$ theories. The question of geodesic completeness remains to be answered in the case of uniform finite group actions. The connection between eigenchannels and energy distributions has been established in several studies, which provide a useful perspective for understanding loss in photonic systems. In this research, we have developed an alternative approach that links eigenchannels to wave phase information. By deriving eigenmode profiles at multiple points in space using the Riccati equation, we can track the evolution of eigenchannels throughout an optical device. Applying this method to a large-scale optical interferometer, which is used for testing quantum gravity, we obtained the eigenmodes of the input and output channels. By comparing the results with loss estimates derived from random matrix theory, we have validated the utility of this phase-based framework in analyzing loss mechanisms in complex optical systems. Moreover, we have discovered that phase information can be utilized to confirm the accuracy of random matrix theory predictions. Besides its applications in physics, we believe that this phase-based framework has the potential to simplify the simulation and design of mechanical and electrical channels. Furthermore, we propose its extension to other disciplines, such as bosonic quantum channels, where eigenchannels may provide valuable insights into quantum advantages over classical communication. As such, the phase-based framework offers a versatile tool for various fields of study.

Conventional methods of pruning neural network weights, which require manual
specification of the level of pruning, have been a major limitation. Researchers
have made recent attempts to overcome this by introducing methods that can automatically
determine the optimal amount of pruning. However, these attempts have primarily
focused on binary decisions, and the relationship between the amount of pruning and
performance in visual tasks remains unclear. By leveraging SuperNet, which is an
advanced technology capable of efficiently representing various network architectures,
we gain insights into how different pruning methods impact performance. Our analysis
discovers that iterative magnitude pruning in visual tasks exhibits an inverted U-shaped
trend, where excessive pruning leads to significant performance degradation despite the
capacity of the network to recover using SuperNet's properties. Furthermore, our
findings indicate that using SuperNet to restore the effects of pruning actually reveals
more severe performance deterioration than what is observed immediately after pruning. 
These counter-intuitive outcomes can be attributed to two key factors: (1) the iterative
pruning process being potentially a form of overfitting prevention, and (2) the effects
of pruning being reversible when it comes to the quality of the network's output. 
Combining these insights with our knowledge about the effects of pruning in a diverse set
of visual tasks, we draw a crucial distinction between techniques that are open-loop and
closed-loop, and draw the line based on whether the method forces the network to adapt
to changes in data. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that applying pruning methods
that are adaptive in this manner does not necessarily mean that the network has
become more invariant to the effects of data augmentation, and thus current methods
of evaluating the benefits of pruning are imperfect and in need of improvement. 
Ultimately, our research challenges some of the most widely accepted assumptions about
the benefits of pruning deep neural networks. These findings serve as a strong argument
for the importance of formulating a unified framework that captures the effects of
pruning that are dependent on the specific characteristics of the method used, the type of
task being performed, and the degree to which the network is being modified in terms of
its capacity and data.

address: https://github.com/ufoor/counterintuitive-pruning.

A companion paper with the full details of our research is currently under review at

Research into valley Hall transport, driven by minor Berry curvature fluctuations, is gaining momentum.  Although current KUBVH theories assume smooth potential variations, real-world valley metal materials are plagued by nonuniform strain.  Strain effects are well-documented in two-dimensional materials, but their impact on valley transport remains poorly understood.  Here, we explore the effects of nonuniform strain on valley Hall transport by considering a scenario where this strain originates from a randomly positioned etched pit.  Employing the nonequilibrium Green's function method, our results reveal that valley Hall conductivity is not solely determined by Berry curvature, but also by this nonuniform strain through its influence on wave function phase shifts.  Consequently, valley mobility is significantly reduced by nonuniform strain.  Notably, while valley Hall conductivity may appear to be topological, it is actually vulnerable to minor perturbations by nonuniform strain.  These findings offer valuable insights for designing practical topological valley Hall devices.  

See also our related publication, "Valley Hall effect in 2D Dirac-Coulomb systems with nonuniform charge perturbations", published in Physical Review B (2021). 

Please note: This work primarily focuses on the impact of nonuniform strain on valley Hall transport, rather than addressing the related phenomenon of valley Hall effect.  Moreover, the terminology "KUBVH" refers to a knowledge underlying valley Hall effect, not a known underlying valley Hall effect.  As such, the term "KUBVH" should be regarded as an arbitrary acronym rather than an established scientific concept.

This paper revisits the t-SNE algorithm originally designed by J. J. Lewis and J.V. Stone to tackle the challenge of visualizing high-dimensional data graphically. The method relies on the premise that proximate data points in lower and higher dimensional spaces are statistically independent and follow specific distribution models. Unlike the traditional assumption of Gaussian distribution, this paper advocates for the use of a K\"onnig-Huber loss instead, providing analytical proofs for the optimization of log-likelihood values. Three experimental datasets are used to demonstrate that by applying a weighted version of K\"onnig-Huber loss, which takes into account data point distances, t-SNE's success is actually achieved. Moreover, this approach allows us to develop a spherical version of t-SNE, thereby offering an innovative visualization tool for embedded data. The algorithm's stability is further ensured by introducing a small perturbation in its loss function. Interestingly, this work reveals that to optimize the negative log-likelihood of t-SNE, a system of non-linear equations needs to be solved, rather than a single non-linear equation. The method's relevance to unsupervised learning domain and the inherent theoretical differences between stochastic gradient descent and Stochastic Average Gradient methods are also explored and discussed. Two experimental datasets and the UMAP algorithm, which is known to perform well on unsupervised embedding, are employed to evaluate the performance of Spherical t-SNE. The results indicate that despite its simplicity, Spherical t-SNE is able to achieve comparable performance to that of t-SNE, while providing more accurate visual representations for spherical data. Additionally, this approach suggests using a specific distribution models to model data proximity, offering an alternative to traditional Gaussian assumptions. The corresponding C-code and MATLAB code are made available for their simplicity. The research further investigates the relevance of K\"onnig-Huber loss to handle data proximity in Euclidean and spherical settings, thereby offering new and better methods for t-SNE. The work also reveals interesting differences and similarities between stochastic gradient descent and Stochastic Average Gradient methods. These results are first to separate beauty and charm production in high-mass regions above 10 GeV/c^2. Within a broad area of experimentation, these findings are in line with the standard model's predictions. The decay length of beauty particles was discovered to be around two and a half times longer than that of charm particles, while being significantly greater than background particles. This study also produced an estimation for the number of beauty-hadron interactions, comparing it to the total number of charm interactions, which is roughly two and a half times greater. These findings were further used to determine the reliability of the detector's vertex finding algorithm. Furthermore, these results led to the discovery of a new standard model process, which is the direct decay of a W boson into two muons, along with a statistical significance of 8.7σ (including systematic uncertainties). The analysis also provided an updated limit for the coupling between a new photon and the muon, which remained unchanged at 0.12 (at 95% confidence level). The final result can be viewed as constraining the two-lepton invariant mass regions of the process beyond the standard model. The next step will be to expand these findings to the region of lower charge squared value. The study also made available a complete list of beauty and charm hadron decays used in these findings. Persistent homology extends this topological space by considering the characteristics of its connected components. A critical point in image analysis is detecting interactions between color classes in a real-world image.
