The resolution of hourly renewables in power system models has been closely examined. This study investigates whether and how a higher temporal resolution influences the efficiency of power system investments. Such models evaluate the expenses of building power lines and storage, considering the value of unserved energy and carbon emissions. We discovered that increasing the resolution results in greater costs of building power lines and storage, but these enhanced costs are lower than the costs of not having these infrastructure assets. Although the method to achieve efficiency might change with a higher temporal resolution, the overall efficiency gains are primarily driven by the expansion of renewable energy sources. In contrast, the efficiency gains related to energy storage are minimal. A higher temporal resolution is also linked to a higher misallocation of generation capacities, but this misallocation comes at a lower cost than the costs of not having these infrastructure assets. This implies that power system planners should prioritize acquiring more precise renewable energy data, but this added value also comes with a higher investment cost. Ultimately, the trade-off between the additional efficiency and costs of power line and storage investments requires close examination. A well-balanced analysis of these factors is crucial for power system expansions. We suggest policymakers consider the trade-offs between different sources of data such as wind forecasts, spatial weather maps, and historical weather data to make informed investments in these data sets. Additionally, carbon pricing and unserved energy values could also influence the trade-offs between efficiency, misallocation, and investment costs. These factors could alter the overall investment outlook for renewable energy, storage and transmission by 30-40%. A thorough investigation of these factors can help reveal crucial policy questions that need to be addressed. For instance, how can policymakers improve the quality of power system investments? Can improved forecasts directly increase the efficiency of power system investments? Do improved forecasts indirectly improve the efficiency of power system investments by reducing public investment needs? Can policymakers leverage improved forecasts to reduce investment needs while maintaining current service standards? Answering these questions could help policymakers gain deeper insights into the trade-offs between the quality of power system investments, efficiency, misallocation and investment costs. A better understanding of these trade-offs could also inform decisions to invest in different data sets, forecasting methods, models, and other tools for supporting power system operations. Moreover, these results could aid in the development of national and international climate change mitigation policies by providing quantitative estimates of the potential economic benefits of improved weather and energy forecasting. A better power system efficiency also means a lower carbon footprint power system which can contribute to global climate change mitigation efforts. To identify relevant search terms for modifying software components, researchers have developed various techniques that leverage available documentation, such as method names and field comments. Two prominent approaches, TextRank and POSRank, focus on analyzing software code snippets as text data to determine their relevance and prioritize the resulting search terms. Despite their widespread use, these ranking algorithms lack a thorough examination of their ranking processes and the effectiveness of their suggested search terms. In contrast, our study investigates how effectively TextRank and POSRank rank various search term candidates within the context of software repositories. By applying these algorithms to nearly 250k actual search terms gathered from Practical Text Search datasets and comparing them to human-evaluation metrics, we discovered that TextRank yields results comparable to those of experienced software developers, but falls short of average developer performance. Additionally, we developed and released Ranksnake, a search-term ranking algorithm that combines characteristics of TextRank and POSRank with the goal of achieving better results. Our empirical assessments of Ranksnake revealed significant improvements in its suggested search terms compared to those generated by TextRank and POSRank. Ultimately, our study aims to provide software engineers with a clearer comprehension of the strengths and limitations of popular algorithms used to extract relevant search terms from code comments. Based on our conclusions, we propose alternative approaches to manually or automated search term selection. These new approaches are designed to extract relevant search terms from available documentation. Our study also issues a call for further research on this topic. The research artifacts can be found at https://github.com/tech-smp/search-term-rank. As of March 2021, this repository is dormant. The data and code for reproducing the paper's results are stored on the https://archive.is/pie-sharing website. The final version of this paper has been published in the 2020 ACM Symposium on Software Science. A preprint of this paper can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.11953. 

Keywords: search terms, software maintenance, TextRank, POSRank.

This study investigates the application of a low-frequency ultrasound field to control gelatin gel dry powder mobilization within a two-dimensional conveyor belt system. The initial analysis focuses on the effects of ultrasound on gel pellets and powder, revealing similarities in gel pellet melting points and the acoustic intensity required to maintain a fluidized state. The powder mobilization dynamics and its responses to varying ultrasound frequencies and acoustic powers have been characterized comprehensively. The research discovered a low-fidelity model that effectively simulates the behavior of a single, slowly-moving wave of fluidized material in the conveyor belt system. The complexity and nonlinear characteristics of two-dimensional powder mobilization systems are also explored, revealing the coexistence of stable state branches, the presence of acoustic pulses at the system's edges, and an acoustic environment rich in fluctuations. Moreover, the research demonstrates how changing the system control parameters can trigger a transition from stable fluidization to unsteady fluidization or even powder mobilization. The study finally reveals the existence of a universal transition mechanism that remains unchanged regardless of the system's control parameters. The discovery of this universal transition is characterized by a critical fraction of fluidized material, denoted as theta_c, where theta_c is also found to be directly linked to the acoustic intensity required to maintain a fluidized state. The outcomes of this research also expand existing knowledge on complex acoustic powder mobilization dynamics, thereby offering opportunities for optimized control strategies and academic advancements in the field. Automatically generated summaries are assessed by human evaluators who consider
their relevance, coherence, and overall quality. Current computer-based evaluation
metrics focus on the logical connection and grammatical correctness of the summaries,
but do not account for their unique content. Furthermore, existing metrics do not
accurately reflect human judgments, as they are inconsistent with human evaluation
criteria. We have developed a new, reference-free evaluation metric called SummScore,
which uses a unique approach to break down summaries into underlying meaningsthat consider the overall meaning and structure of the text. We then compare the unique
characteristics of human-written and automatically generated summaries to assess
their similarity. SummScore outperforms previous computer-based evaluations in its
accuracy and correlation with human judgments. Additionally, experiments have shown
that models fine-tuned using SummScore produce high-quality, diverse summaries
that align with human expectations. We have made the SummScore implementation
available for public use at the URL c4c4est.github.io/SummScore. We encourage the
use of SummScore to assess automatically generated summaries. In the future, we
intend to expand the scope of the SummScore evaluation metric to encompass more
features of written language. We hope that our new approach will inspire the
development of the next generation of language generation systems that produce
high-quality, engaging summaries. (Abstract in 250 words)

Our empirical findings also validate the reliability of this theoretical guarantee, even with the presence of random errors. Moreover, we observed that the sparse deconvolution algorithm performs better for complex scenarios compared to the standard deconvolution method, producing higher quality results, especially with larger amounts of cross-related data available. Moreover, we noticed that the percentage of recoverable sparsity increases with the amount of available data. On the other hand, when there is no prior knowledge about the system, the sparse deconvolution algorithm performs poorly in the absence of additional information. In cases where the system does not possess structured noise, we proposed a modified algorithm to improve the performance by utilizing second-order expectations. The interaction between laser light and particles in a heated fluid is studied by observing the patterns resulting from the scattering of laser light. Due to variations in the fluid's temperature and concentration of suspended particles, the laser light is scattered in ways that depend on its intensity and wavelength. This scattering is measured in experiments using He-Ne and GaAlAs lasers, which emit light in the visible and near-infrared spectra. The resulting patterns exhibit periodic variations in space and time, with their periods dependent on the characteristics of the laser and particle scattering mechanisms. Notably, in experiments involving the He-Ne laser, higher spatial harmonic components of the scattering pattern become more prominent at increased temperature differences, indicating an influence of Brownian motion on particle dispersion. In contrast, in experiments involving the GaAlAs laser, the dominant spatial harmonic remains constant over a wide temperature range, but its intensity varies in a complex manner due to particle clustering and the effects of concentration gradients on scattering. These findings suggest significant effects of particle clustering and the non-Gaussian nature of particle distributions on scattering mechanisms. Moreover, since these effects are also observed in experiments involving the spontaneous spontaneous Brillouin scattering in narrow temperature intervals, the influence of particle clustering on this scattering mechanism is also considered. The observed time-dependent variations in scattering intensity, which arise from time-dependent changes in particle concentration gradients and fluid velocity gradients, are found to be consistent with the expected behavior of fluid dynamics at microscopic and mesoscopic scales. These findings may have implications for the understanding of shear mixing in fluids with suspended particles, which could otherwise lead to energy dissipation. However, in the present studies, such mechanisms are found to be ineffective due to the presence of inherently non-homogeneous particle clustering and fluidic effects. To further explore this phenomenon, future simulations will be conducted to examine the connection between shear mixing and fluid dynamics using a model that accounts for particle clustering, which has previously been overlooked in the literature. The observed spatial modulation of the scattering pattern may also be exploited as an opto-thermal imaging technique to map temperature and particle density across microscopic and mesoscopic scales, which could provide valuable insights into the behavior of complex fluid systems. Additionally, the spatial variation of the scattering pattern may be used to manipulate laser beams with complex patterns, which could lead to novel applications in the field of laser technology. Our tool, called FieldTools, is designed to automatically retrieve this information. By examining CS categories and their connections to publishing venues for each field, we aim to provide an accurate and structured view of the field's development. Our methodology can be applied to any academic field with a publishing system similar to Computer Science, enabling a comparative analysis of its growth. A web-based visualization, called FieldWatch, has been created to display the evolution of each field. It combines statistical data on CS categories over time along with their corresponding venues, providing a dynamic and interactive view of the fields' growth. To facilitate long-term analysis, this tool can help transition from categorization based on algorithmic associations to associations derived from both algorithms and expert input. Furthermore, it is anticipated that FieldWatch can enhance collaborations between academics and their university partners by facilitating data-driven strategy discussions. To measure its effectiveness, we compared our analysis of CS categories using FieldTools to the classifications from two prominent databases, DBLP and Scopus, with our results mirroring each other's categorization structure almost perfectly, but with our method identified nearly all new research venues not captured by Scopus. This paper explores recent advancements in verifying the robustness of neural networks, which could be applied to the training of control systems' neural network controllers. The deep learning community has made significant strides in generating challenging data and evaluating adversarial robustness, while the control community continues to develop sophisticated algorithms for training resilient neural network controllers. Research on the robustness of neural networks has closely mirrored the growth of control systems' adversarial robustness, with key differences in the approaches used. By synthesizing these findings, we identify crucial areas for future research, shed light on the distinctions between adversarial and adversarial-like robustness, and highlight the advantages of leveraging techniques from computer vision and machine learning for enhancing neural network robustness, particularly in scenarios where robustness is inherently difficult due to data limitations and dimensionality. We also investigate potential applications of verification in enhancing sampling-based controller training, which could contribute to the development of adaptive and model-based controllers. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the verification of neural networks may facilitate a deeper understanding of their robustness, reliability, and trustworthiness. Ultimately, integrating insights from the literature on adversarial robustness may accelerate the achievement of robust neural network control. We demonstrate the practical utility of verification-based training in promoting robustness, based on its theoretical underpinnings. We conclude by identifying promising avenues for future research, including the potential role of verification in promoting neural networks with fair and transparent outcomes. We aim to make crucial contributions to the development of neural network-based control systems that prioritize safety, reliability, and human life. We've developed two novel equivalence relations, known as functorial clustering schemes, which cater to general metric spaces. One relation aligns with most experts' notion of a cluster, where all elements within a group are grouped together. The other relation includes elements from multiple clusters in a subgroup. In the context of traditional single-linkage clustering, the first relation's approach to element grouping suffers from positive errors, where some elements end up in separate groups. To address this issue, we've modified the functorial clustering schemes to combine them in a way that merges certain elements from different clusters. What's more, we've established the conditions under which the resulting clusters in the combined scheme correspond to local maxima in the space's optimization landscape. Finally, we've validated the efficiency of our new schemes with actual computations, including some new findings in the process. The corresponding code can be accessed at https://github.com/olahcsan/cluster/tree/main/journal-cluster. Furthermore, our evaluation method confirms a previously suggested link between the Askey-Wilson algebra and the level-k Fuchsian Liouville Q-matrix. Moreover, with the aid of the state-sum model, we propose an alternative description of the Askey-Wilson algebra, proposing that the algebra's action on a particular wavefunction describes a linear flow on the classical regime of the deformed holomorphic part of the Bertola-Masoref model. In the dual picture, the findings imply a connection between the wavefunction evaluations and the expectations of Wilson loops in the bulk limit of the BTZ model. Ultimately, the Wilson loop evaluations may potentially be utilised as an efficient means of computing the exact partition function of the BTZ model. We've developed a unique computational basis for quantum Monte Carlo simulations comprising three individually linked spin units. This 'trimer' basis allows for flexible analysis of the correlated hyperpolarizability properties of paraanlene, a prototypical model of strongly correlated organic systems. Our study focuses on the ground state of paraanlene under the gapped scenario characterized by low-temperature super-symmetric behavior. The quantum Monte Carlo sign problem is assessed in relation to different trimer configurations that cut and connect the original double-cyclic chain structure. The research delves into the underlying physics of trimer-based computational bases with various symmetries and comments on their potential applicability to trimer-based molecular quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The findings indicate that the ground-state densities resulting from positive trimer-based configurations are in agreement with those generated by density functional theory, a standard method. However, the results for negative trimer-based configurations are seen to be inaccurate due to their connection to particular wave function patterns that contradict the trimer-based sign structure. In line with the generally negative wave function values, these outcomes are consistent with trimer-based quantum Monte Carlo simulations, but they also highlight the need to address the sign problem. The research shows that the signing of trimer-based wave functions is complicated by their disparate trimer configurations. Consequently, a single overall signing of trimer-based wave functions is insufficient, instead, all possible signings must be accounted for. For paraanlene simulations, our findings confirm this general insight, linking the paraanlene correlation gap to the signed trimer-based wave function properties. The research explores the applicable signings in trimer-based quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The findings indicate that the trimer configuration comprising three individually linked spin units in a chain has the lowest sign problem among all the studied trimer bases. Consequently, this configuration is suggested as an effective option for future quantum Monte Carlo simulations tackling the ground-state properties of trimer-based molecular systems. The growing concern with language model privacy has prompted an investigation into the effectiveness of truncating model outputs for predictive assessments. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of truncation's impact on the reliability of language models for zero-shot classification. Utilizing the GLUE suite as a benchmark, our findings reveal that larger models consistently achieve higher AUC-ROC scores when their output lengths are increased, albeit at a diminishing rate. Notably, our results demonstrate that truncating high-dimensional models does not necessarily compromise their performance across all tasks, a contrast to prior findings on the performance degradation law for fully-trained models. Additionally, our work explores the feasibility of privately transferring knowledge from one task to another using masked language models as the donor. We found that all the considered tasks could learn to utilize the donor model for prediction, and that increasing the donor model's output size would enhance the recipient model's performance. We observed a similar trend with the donor model's complexity and the number of training examples. Moreover, our results indicate that using a small, tightly-focused set of outputs from the donor model can yield the best trade-off between accuracy and output length while preserving the recipient model's accuracy within acceptable limits. The method of kernel ridge regression is compared to traditional parametric projection techniques like the Galerkin method in this study. It is revealed that under certain conditions, these methods converge towards the exact solution at essentially the same rate, yet the kernel ridge regression offers significant advantages in terms of computational complexity. Furthermore, the stability of the kernel methods is discussed along with the effects of using different kernels on the solution, illustrating how the choice of kernel greatly impacts the solution, underscoring the need for a systematic approach to kernel selection. To showcase the method's capabilities, the kernel ridge regression is applied to the theoretical Laplace equation, demonstrating that nearly identical results to linear multigrid methods can be achieved with minimal grid data. Moreover, the method was also successfully applied to the solution of a real-world biomedical problem, specifically the problem of imaging brain activity through Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), with the objective of inversely calculating neuronal current densities from external EM field measurements. To solve this nonlinear inverse problem, the kernel ridge regression was employed in a manner similar to the multigrid method. In this context, the method was referred to as the multigrid kernel coherency functional. By repeatedly applying an iterative process, the method was able to find a stable solution that effectively minimizes complexity, and when compared to a nonlinear least squares approach, the results demonstrate that the kernel ridge regression is a highly effective technique for this complex biomedical application. The method was further validated in several other applications, confirming its remarkable effectiveness in a multitude of different test cases. As such, the kernel ridge regression is a highly valuable tool for complex problem-solving in a multitude of domains. Furthermore, the method's simplicity and ease of use make it an exceptionally accessible and versatile computational methodology. The code used for the study has been made publicly available at: http://www.gharbieh.com/codes.html. A new approach, KROTE, for improving temporal knowledge graph embeddings is introduced. It utilizes time-related and structural knowledge graph information in a holistic framework. Unlike other models, KROTE is grounded in two key principles: combining temporal and structural knowledge to a single temporal knowledge graph representation, and incorporating temporal knowledge into the structure of the knowledge graph. Compared to state-of-the-art models, KROTE's representations demonstrate better consistency with real-world knowledge graphs, leading to enhanced accuracy in completion and classification tasks within knowledge graph prediction. Specifically, KROTE outperforms other methods by achieving an impressive 12.1% increase in edge ranking for the entity-relation link prediction task on the TKG-Benchmark. Moreover, KROTE's developments have broader implications for the development of graph neural networks. Interestingly, analyses show that traditional knowledge graph neural networks can be viewed as special cases of KROTE, where the temporal component is absent or minimal. We propose that incorporating temporal knowledge is crucial for effectively capturing real-world knowledge graph structure. Moreover, a novel TKG benchmarking and evaluation platform were developed to independently assess TKG models. The benchmark, called TKG-Benchmark, is composed of four diverse noised TKG benchmarks, each with distinct characteristics and origins, and is designed to evaluate various TKG models under different and realistic conditions. The benchmark, along with accompanying resources, can be accessed via https://github.com/dwmol/TKG-Benchmark. The source code for KROTE can be viewed at https://github.com/dwmol/KROTE. The research is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01425.

The first virtual pioneer in the field of complex dynamics was the 19th century mathematician Felix Klein. He initiated an exploration of the dynamical behavior of the exponential map. Building on his legacy, this study delves into the dynamics of the map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^2+\lambda+1$, alongside its iterations, and their corresponding elliptical representations. These functions hold a profound connection to the dynamics of the exponential map in the complex plane and have been discovered to possess remarkable properties, such as being non-constant, globally defined solutions to the differential equation $z''=-z^3$. Moreover, the study of their trajectories in the complex plane offers an elegant resolution to a longstanding problem in the field, attributed to the influential mathematician Josef Hofmann. Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for the analysis of dynamical systems within loop-glass bodies in the complex plane, an area of research previously studied by Hofmann for the case of double pendula. Interestingly, the solutions to the differential equation $z''=-z^3$ may be regarded as the complex equivalents of the well-known Carnot curve and the Lenz vector in quantum mechanics. Additionally, the study finds connections to the recently discovered strong global asymptotic stability of rational maps with connected Julia sets, providing insights into the Julia and Fatou sets associated with the map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^2+\lambda+1$. A comparison is made with the dynamics of the exponential map and an in-depth examination of the coefficients of the map in relation to the arithmetic properties of the minimal fields arising from the algebraic closures of the rational numbers is presented. Lastly, the study discovers novel relationships between the coefficients of the map and the geometry of the trajectories, employing novel mathematical techniques, including generalized Fourier-Legendre expansions. These expansions were found to be particularly useful in the study and are recognized as a new mathematical contribution. They have further exponential properties, expounding on previous studies by the second author. Specifically, the study discovers novel connections between the Fourier-Legendre expansions of holomorphic functions and their formal power series expansions, previously studied by Hofmann. Interestingly, the top Fourier-Legendre coefficients of the map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^2+\lambda+1$ are found to be ultimately periodic in nature. A theoretical explanation for this phenomenon is developed within the framework of the study. The results indicate a significant impact of Gd3+ ion size on the lattice parameters and indicate that GdInO3's electronic properties are largely influenced by its 4f electron configuration. To clarify the material's electronic nature, various theoretical approaches are used, which in turn enable the examination of GdInO3's magnetic properties. The research finds evidence of ferromagnetic ordering and a resulting saturation magnetization of 330 emu/g. By applying the Heisenberg Hamiltonian, the study finds the exchange interaction to be positive, at approximately 2.58 meV. Consequently, the research yields valuable insights into the optimal treatment procedures for GdInO3 and its potential technological applications. The simulations' findings are further reinforced by comparing the material to its isotypic compounds in the LnInO3 series (Ln = La, Pr, Nd). In the past few years, graph embedding has received a great deal of attention for its wide range of practical uses. Nevertheless, the conventional methods designed for large networks are inadequate for networks with sparse connections. This research introduces a novel method called Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM), developed specifically for handling the challenges presented by sparse networks. By utilizing local neighborhood information and a series of iterative procedures that enhance the degree sequence, SNHAM aims to provide a more accurate representation of the network. Utilizing the real-world networks, the proposed method has been shown to surpass current state-of-the-art techniques, including the DeepWalk, Node2Vec, and GRAPE, as measured by the node classification task. Additionally, SNHAM's efficiency has been further demonstrated through its application in the prediction of network size. Furthermore, SNHAM offers a level of adaptability in its parameters, allowing it to effectively handle networks with varying sparsity levels. Various case studies have been conducted to illustrate the effectiveness of SNHAM. Firstly, a comparison of SNHAM and GRAPE based on different orders (h) for a sparse network of 64 nodes and order 3 (h=3) has been performed, resulting in SNHAM requiring 30% fewer floating point operations. Secondly, the proposed method was applied to a sparse subgraph of IMDB with 625M edges and order 10 (h=10), showing a significant reduction in time complexity of 65.88% compared to GRAPE. Lastly, SNHAM was used to compute the co-authorship network of PLOS ONE with 40 million nodes and order 5 (h=5), taking approximately 5 minutes to complete the computation, which is 65% faster than GRAPE. These experiments have consistently shown the superiority of SNHAM over state-of-the-art methods in terms of computational efficiency. Furthermore, SNHAM's potential for handling the challenges presented by sparse networks has been explored by applying the method to a network with a specific degree sequence. By manipulating the network degree sequence, SNHAM's ability to accurately learn node representation has been validated, while failures in learning the node representation result in incorrect reconstruction of the network's degree sequence. Ultimately, SNHAM's applicability in a wide range of real-world sparse networks has been demonstrated. By combining the node representation learned from SNHAM with the node attributes, the proposed method has been able to effectively recommend comparable papers to a given article for the PLOS ONE dataset. It has multiple applications in remote sensing, surveillance, and robotics. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of different image fusion techniques, including traditional and deep learning-based methods, in generating composite images. Multiple sensing modalities offer a variety of image fusion scenarios, and we focused our analysis on multi-spectral and panchromatic image fusion. The performance of six traditional image fusion methods, including Principal Component Replacement, PCA-SR, IHS-Clover, IHS-RPCA, Chi-Square, and Linear Combination, was compared with that of two deep learning-based techniques, the Deep Image Fusion (DIF) and the Multi-Scale Dense Neural Network (MSDNN). Our results indicate a significant impact of the IGMR-IGQR coupling on energy structures, especially in low-lying excitation energies of deformed nuclei. The strength of the interaction is found to increase with deformation. We also discover coupled peaking-isomer energies in IGMR and IGQR, which arise from the coupled resonance character. The influence of the IGMR-IGQR coupling on the nuclear structure is expected to be even more pronounced in superdeformed nuclei, where a energy gap between IGMR and IGQR facilitates their interaction. Our study is the first to analyze the coupled character of the IGMR and IGQR in deformed atomic nuclei within the TDHFB+RPA framework. The findings suggest that the energy structures in deformed nuclei could be significantly modified by the interaction between the IGMR and IGQR, which can be associated with the isomer energies, especially in the lower excitation energy range. Moreover, the IGMR-IGQR coupling could be a key factor influencing nuclear relaxation phenomena, especially in the isoscalar CDCD channel. The coupling does not affect the energy structure in spherical nuclei, as the IGMR and IGQR do not overlap in energy. The proposed coupling phenomenon is relatively universal and may be experimentally verified through measurements of E1 strength distribution following a gamma-ray burst, such as in $^{124}$Xe. The study has also explored the effects of the coupling on the fragmentation of the resonance, as the IGMR-IGQR coupling modulates the energy structure and strength distribution. The phenomenon is expected to occur not only in atomic nuclei but also in the isospin sector due to the isospin conservation in the RPA. The influence of the IGDR-IGQR coupling on the energy structure is however relatively small compared to the IGMR-IGQR coupling. The impact of trading costs and liquidity constraints on market dynamics is examined in this model, which utilises a continuous time framework. The model presents two feasible approaches for constructing a complete market model from the partial equation describing the net supply of the second trader, by incorporating their respective reaction functions and individual optimization objectives. The first method involves employing stochastic Riccati equations to solve an optimal control problem, while the second approach uses a classical linear control theory for second-order volatilities, resulting in dynamic portfolio equations that can be expanded into a comprehensive market model. Both methods demonstrate a similar dynamic behavior, with the second order equation serving as a fundamental component. The emergence of a spreading process in the market, characterized by a symmetrical score, is associated with a cost function optimized by the first trader, in a scenario where the second trader lacks sufficient order flow. Conversely, when the second trader generates sufficient orders, the market displays a asymmetrical score, illustrating a shift towards a mean-field type model. The model's validity is supported by a method based on duality, while specific stochastic process equations for both approaches are presented and their similarities and differences are compared. The outcome of this research reveals additional insights into the relationship between the second-order equation and the score's spreading process, as well as the first trader's optimal behavior, through the fundamental propagator and the score's asymptotic behavior. The model's extension to the N-trader case involves a generalization of the model's equation and its propagator, leading to a comprehensive market model construction. In this expanded scenario, the model's propagator and score are fundamentally altered by the presence of N traders, while an explicit equation can be derived for second-order volatility terms for N traders, showing a similar behavior in the market's dynamics. We investigate a low-rank matrix recovery scenario where a specific matrix is represented as a linear combination of several known rank-one matrices, and we consider a PCA-based estimator applied to a dataset consisting of multiple independent observations following this linear model. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis that the PCA estimator achieves near-optimal performance when the observations' number exceeds a certain threshold, which is defined in terms of the coefficients of the linear combination and the geometry of the set of rank-one matrices, and we analyze the impact of varying these coefficients on the threshold, highlighting a more stringent threshold when all coefficients are equal and equivalent matrix weights. Moreover, our findings remain valid in two distinct contexts where the PCA estimator suffers from estimation bias: data corrupted by Gaussian noise and data contaminated by outliers. In these situations, our results show that a simple modification of the PCA-based approach can achieve optimal performance as the number of observations tends to infinity. We substantiate our claims through extensive numerical illustrations. Moreover, our method is exemplified through real-world data applications. The research presented in this article bears a striking resemblance to a recently published study (Tsao and Vempala, 2020). We start with a thorough examination of the determinants of our findings, delineating three primary research trajectories. Firstly, we explore how altering the coefficients of the linear combination influences the PCA estimator influences its performance and establish its applicability to recovery issues with orthogonal matrix templates. Secondly, we inquire about the statistical equilibrium of this influence, posing the question of whether the coefficients' magnitudes ever reach zero, and revealing that this phenomenon doesn't occur in the orthogonal matrix scenario but does occur in the non-singular matrix case. Thirdly, we investigate the practical implications of our results for PCA-based techniques and demonstrate through numerical simulations that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach (Vempala and Yin, 2020) designed for matrix recovery under a specific weighted average framework. Unlike traditional research focusing on attacks launched by someone in close proximity to the speech source, our study considers the possibility that an attacker may have limited or no familiarity with the language being spoken. To address this scenario, we evaluate several existing attack techniques that utilize either audio or text contexts, with the goal of assessing their effectiveness and similarity to legitimate speech produced by the model before and after the attack. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of crafting customized attacks tailored to specific languages an attacker is unfamiliar with. The results of our investigation indicate that adversaries with minimal knowledge can effectively launch successful attacks, although these attacks tend to have a greater impact on the audio waveform rather than the underlying semantic content. Moreover, we discover that the most effective attack techniques in cross-language scenarios involve manipulating pitch. The findings from this research aim to broaden the horizon of adversarial attacks on speech representation models by considering the dynamics of adversaries with varying levels of expertise. We have introduced an E-value extension that enables the use of causal information, even in cases where data is incomplete. Unlike previous approaches which could only handle certain types of missing data, our method can handle a broader range of situations. Key benefits of this expansion include its ability to handle multiple types of missing data, its simplified calculation which requires only marginal and conditional probabilities, and its potential to quantify the reliability of causal conclusions. We have also explored the potential of E-value thinking in automated inference, highlighting that E-values can provide essential insights in time-series analysis, particularly when dealing with missing data or partial scope. Moreover, this concept offers new avenues for exploring causal dependence limitations, which may contribute substantially to the development of automated inference methods. We demonstrate the practical applications of our E-value extension through three case studies involving missing data: one with synthetic data, another with COVID-19 statistics, and another with partial dataset simulations. Each example showcases our method's capabilities and potential future research opportunities. All related code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/jkmiech/E-value. We have further published automated inference code incorporating the insights from this work at https://github.com/jkmiech/dse. These wavefunction overlaps can be used to compute various conformal data. For the Ising chain in a specific context, we were able to compute the magnetic charge by applying a specific trick, and our results show agreement with theoretical predictions at the conformal point. However, our approach also allows us to investigate how the magnetic charge varies against the central charge $h_{\phantom{1}\mathcal{Z}}$ for non-conformal observables. Moreover, we were able to compute the magnetic charge for the $n$-subspace of a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain for small values of $n$ and derived a relationship that can help expand the density matrix to higher $n$. These findings showcase the wide applicability of our method to investigate the properties of quantum spin chains. Moreover, we computed other conformal data such as the energy of excitations above the ground state and the wavefunction overlap known as the string fidelity, with results consistent from different computational approaches as the size increases. These findings reinforce our understanding of quantum spin chains and provide valuable insights into their properties.

To validate this optimization, our results consist of two parts. Firstly, we investigate the average convergence rate in relation to various parameters, such as the depth of the quantum circuit and the precision of the density matrix, and demonstrate that our mitigation strategy accelerates the average convergence rate by multiple orders of magnitude when compared to prior versions. Secondly, we test the robustness of the algorithm in scenarios where noise is present using the parameters of the IBM Q protocols. By simulating the IBM Q qubit circuits, our results reveal that our mitigation strategy enhances the average convergence rate by nearly four orders of magnitude and, in addition to this, reduces the number of iterations needed to achieve convergence by more than half when compared to prior implementations. Furthermore, our results confirm that the mitigation strategy can enhance the computational speed in experiments involving noisy quantum hardware by transferring our algorithms to the IBM Q qubit platforms, including the IBM Q Copenhagen and IBM Q Rome devices. Our results reveal that our mitigation strategy allows for accurate calculations of various physical properties, such as ionization energy, potential energy curves, and dipole moment. Notably, our results show that our mitigation strategy enhances the computational speed by over ten times when compared to prior implementations. By leveraging our mitigation strategy, our protocol demonstrates the capable performance of accurate calculations of various physical properties, such as ionization energy, potential energy curves, and dipole moment, on the IBM Q Copenhagen and Rome qubit platforms. Our results demonstrate the promising potential of our mitigation strategy in enhancing the computational speed and efficiency of VQE algorithms on the latest IBM Q qubit platforms. By leveraging our mitigation strategy, our protocol has the potential to sustain accurate computations of various complex problems despite the presence of noise and limitations in current noisy quantum hardware. Our results yield novel insights and understanding of the practical effectiveness of our mitigation strategy in enhancing the computational speed and efficiency of quantum algorithms, especially for realistic scenarios where noise and gate inaccuracies are present, and may find applications in analogous quantum algorithms that rely on parametric quantum circuits, such as the imaginary time evolution (ITE) algorithm. Although the metric is not the vacuum solution of the Einstein equations, and is thus not invariant under diffeomorphisms that preserve its structure, it is shown that these diffeomorphisms play a role in maintaining invariance of key horizon characteristics. This is shown through a mathematical argument that uses a deformed star as a reference point on the conformal section of the Schwarzschild metric, and another that uses the hypersurface of asymptotic flatness in the FL model. These arguments demonstrate that, despite initial invariance uncertainties, the horizon's location is fixed once the metric's structure is specified. This is further demonstrated by an analysis of a deformed Friedmann-Lemaitre metric, which shows that the structure of the deformed models' inner boundaries matches that of Schwarzschild, and that the location of this boundary is determined by the location of a specific surface on the FL model's hypersurface. The study of the horizon's area and area entropy also reveals that, although the metric is not the vacuum solution, the horizon's characteristics converge to those of a static black hole. This behavior is distinct from that of null geodesics, which, when simulated, demonstrate that photons passing through the metric will appear to emerge from a location corresponding to the location of the horizon's boundary, and that this location is fixed by the metric's structure. The study of the curvature properties of the horizon's location also reveals that, although the metric is not the vacuum solution, the horizon's characteristics converge to those of a static black hole. This behavior is distinct from that of concentric spheres within the model. The study of these characteristics, and of the curvature properties of the horizon's location, shows that key aspects of the horizon's behavior are determined by the metric's structure, and that certain transitions between states of different topological orders are determined by the metric's structure, and that the area of the horizon and its associated entropy converge to those of a static black hole in the model. The study of the horizon's properties also reveals that the metric's structure determines key aspects of the horizon's behavior, and that the area and entropy of the horizon converge to those of a static black hole in the model. The work presented here offers a novel approach to the study of the horizon's location, and one that is distinct from previous studies of the curvature properties of the horizon's location.

We demonstrate a relationship between the $q$-analogue of chromatic symmetric functions and the combined product of $q$-hit numbers and elementary symmetric functions, achievable through reduced Schur functions. This connection mirrors the identity established by Stanley for ordinary chromatic symmetric functions. Utilizing this association, we demonstrate equivalence among certain poset-related events. Furthermore, we leverage reduced Schur functions to offer an alternative expression for the $q$-analogue of homogeneous elementary symmetric functions. Building upon this insight, we derive various $q$-analogues of Cauchy identities involving Schur functions and elementary symmetric functions. Notably, the $q$-analogue of the Adams-Wynton-MacDonald identity requires the $q$-analogue of elementary symmetric functions in its expression. A permutahedral decomposition of $q$-elementary symmetric functions is also provided, showcasing its similarity to the permutahedral decomposition of homogeneous elementary symmetric functions. In addition, we explore $q$-analogues of Melham's identities for even powers of elementary symmetric functions and even elementary symmetric functions. By incorporating additional parameters, we can recover the $q$-analogue of the Adams-Wynton-MacDonald identity through reduction. Ultimately, the approach allows for the recovery of the generalized Frobenius norm via the $q$-analogue of the Frobenius norm. Utilizing the $q$-analogue of minor indices of a hook-shaped shape and its Schur functions, we establish identities including $q$-analogue homogeneous elementary symmetric functions, odd or mixed symmetry Schur functions, and Foulkes' $q$-analogue of the Frobenius norm. Reductions to special cases of these identities are also undertaken. In addition, an invitation is issued for exploration of involution-based proofs in reduced Schur function expressions. A novel AI model has been developed to accurately diagnose individuals with respiratory illnesses, including those with COVID-19, using limited clinical data from lungs. This model leverages clinical images and symptoms to confidently rule in or rule out a diagnosis, while also providing probabilities for various conditions. In the event of a potentially fatal diagnosis such as COVID-19, the model generates specific lung area predictions to inform treatment decisions. Following training on a large dataset with diverse respiratory conditions, the model was assessed on two distinct benchmark datasets and demonstrated exceptional performance, with some conditions yielding near-perfect diagnostic accuracy. Notably, the model performed well even when the available clinical data was limited, making it a valuable diagnostic tool for hospitals with limited resources. By integrating the model with clinical data, such as heart rate and oxygen levels, the model achieved high diagnostic accuracy while also identifying potential inconsistencies in these supplementary metrics. Finally, the model was modified to generate actionable information for healthcare professionals by identifying areas of lung damage specific to certain conditions, with promising early results. Future research aims to build upon this advancement by incorporating additional relevant data. The source code for the model is openly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ashishpandey661/Lung_Diagnostic_Net. This model has the potential to be utilized as a quick and reliable diagnostic tool when clinical data is limited. By combining the model's diagnostic output with the corresponding clinical data, healthcare professionals may be better equipped to make more informed treatment decisions. Over the past few years, numerous satellite projects have been initiated to form massive satellite fleets, with more than 10,000 planned satellites, to support widespread access to communication services. While these initiatives have potential economic benefits, their scale could potentially lead to severe environmental degradation if left unmanaged. To mitigate this concern, a novel orbit category called minimum space occupancy (MiSO) orbit has been proposed. By requiring satellites to maintain a minimum distance between each other, MiSO orbits constrain the density of satellite placement. This raised speculation that MiSO orbits might limit megasatellite clusters to increase costs, thereby encouraging more sustainable deployment practices. This study investigates the miSO orbit constraint effect on satellite placement and the resulting increased inter-satellite transmission loss in typical scenarios, demonstrating that such constraints could have a significant impact on satellite deployment scale. As a result, early consideration of miSO orbits could facilitate more sustainable and environmentally friendly satellite mega-constellations, ultimately benefiting both the space community and end-users. Additionally, implementing miSO orbits could pave the way for the decolonization of geostationary orbits, as these orbits could provide an opportunity for developing nations to establish their own sustainable space infrastructure frameworks. Moreover, the decomposition algorithms used to place satellites in miSO orbits could be exploited to support the deployment of traditional satellites in these orbits, thereby benefiting both developing and developed nations alike. Experimentally, this study utilizes 3566 satellites from two mega-constellations to examine the miSO orbit scale factor's impact on satellite placement and the resulting increased loss probability. Based on these findings, several optimization problems are proposed to minimize loss probability or downlink data rate in miSO orbits, and a novel deployment strategy is introduced to achieve an optimal trade-off between transmission loss and satellite number. Furthermore, backhaul capacity-fair user association and hybrid analog digital beam division multiple access (HAD-BDMA) are developed to support miSO orbits and the fair transmission to all users on the line-of-sight. Using the miSO orbit orbit-fair association (OFA) algorithms from the previous study, these methods demonstrate the effectiveness in reducing transmission loss and increasing system capacity, with HAD-BDMA offering an 8.64% increase in average capacity compared to conventional BDMA. As another novel contribution, the fairness in awarding uplink transmission to users under miSO orbits is redefined, with miSO orbit fairness redefined as minimizing the total miSO orbit scale factor, and a user association scheme is proposed to achieve this redefined

Recently, the mesh generation process was simplified by introducing the notion of quad layouts, which organize the elements of a T-mesh in a particular configuration. However, the flexibility of quad layouts is still restricted, requiring o(n) operations to determine the neighbor information of each element. In our study, we have introduced the concept of crossable quad layouts, capable of providing the necessary neighbor information in an efficient manner, thereby enabling simplified divisions of T-meshes. Additionally, we have established the criteria for the class of crossable quad layouts, which are essential for Topological Data Analysis applications. By combining our findings, we have concluded that a T-mesh is quadifiable if and only if it can be quadrangulated into a crossable quad layout of quadrangulations. First, we develop the $S$-matrix formalism for Schwarzschild black holes in combination with the Hamiltonian approach. Then, we apply this methodology to the model of degenerate hollow black hole, placing the model within the framework of quantum $S$-matrix theory. The key aspect of this work lies in the technical challenge of adapting the $S$-matrix approach for spacetimes with non-traversable horizons. When putting recommendations into practice, there is often a common hurdle to overcome: making end-users understand the behind-the-scenes decision-making process. To address this, a new approach has been developed, aiming to empower explanations for self-driving recommendation systems. This approach involves incorporating explanations into the recommendation system's training, as opposed to relying on post-hoc methods, which are often plagued by inconsistency and a lack of clarity. Unlike existing post-hoc methods that provide explanations after the recommendation model has made its decision, our approach integrates explanations directly into the training of the model. By doing so, it achieves explanations that align with the recommendations they predict and are also robust to inconsistent data. To demonstrate this, a new dataset has been created that includes scenarios where the features and recommendations do not align, followed by a comparison of integrated and post-hoc explanation training on both the dataset and a real-world recommendation system application. The results show that the integrated explanations align with the recommendations they predict and are also more robust to inconsistent data. Conversely, the post-hoc explanations are inconsistent and do not boost the performance of the model. Ultimately, our approach contributes to a deeper understanding of recommendations by providing explanations that are consistent and reliable. These explanations can also be used to improve the transparency of recommendations when they are accessed by humans. This threshold is significant because its value not only determines the sample size requirements but also dictates the learning parameters, such as achieving a low generalization error without assumptions. The Fast Sinkhorn II algorithm enhanced the efficiency of optimal transport calculations, but its underlying theory has yet to be thoroughly explored. Our analysis clarifies the meaning and purpose of FS-2, modifies the original implementation to streamline it, and confirms that its revised version reaches equilibrium as anticipated. Notably, we found that FS-2 converges at a $O(1/n^2)$ rate, which surpasses the original Sinkhorn method's $O(1/n)$ rate. Our analysis supports the hypothesis that FS-2's performance benefits from canceling out error terms from the Sinkhorn method. Our findings are further demonstrated by numerical examples that verify our theoretical conclusions. Ultimately, our validation strengthens the validity of using sinkflow profiles as groundings for quantitative imaging measurements. Our updated FS-2 code has been made publicly available at https://github.

We have conducted the first examination of AU Mic b under extreme stellar flare conditions using the Gemini/PIONIER closed-loop mid-infrared astroimaging technique. A combination of the target and its companion - a 0.078 mag brown dwarf located 21 arcseconds away - served as a fixed reference point in the images captured throughout a 4.5 hour flare event. We obtained 7 images taken at the center of the flare, out of a total of 13 available frames, including 5 obtained before the flare began. These images were employed to determine the atmospheric loss of AU Mic b, estimated to be 10^8 times the mass of our sun, under steady state conditions, increasing to 10^10 times the mass of our sun during the early stages of the flare. Furthermore, we calculated the sub- stellar mass loss to be around 10^10 times the mass of our sun, at a rate that is 3.5 times the mass of our sun per year, under both steady state and early flare conditions. It's worth noting that AU Mic b exhibits a significantly low sub-stellar mass compared to other exoplanets, with a high atmospheric loss during the flare event, that is three orders larger than the mass of the planet itself. In the event of a giant outburst, the atmospheric loss of AU Mic b could potentially result in a significant loss of the planet's mass. In order to gain a better understanding of this phenomenon, we employed the results of the SIMON2 model to determine the effect of various particle characteristics on the atmospheric loss, with the outflow continuing until the planet's distance to the star reaches 0.1 AU. At this point, the model predicts that an outflow of particles with an energy of less than 10^3 KeV will result in a significant loss of the planet's mass, with the outflow of particles with higher energy levels resulting in a much less significant loss. In a real-world scenario, the model predicts that an outflow of particles in the event of a giant outburst will result in a mass loss of up to 60 times the mass of AU Mic b, with the outflow potentially rendering the planet's status as a sub-stellar entity futile. As the expected mass loss of the planet during a giant outburst is significantly less than other exoplanets, the outflow of particles in the event of an outburst may potentially be a viable mechanism to destroy exoplanets with masses greater than the mass of AU Mic b. When radiation penetrates a conductive medium, it encounters particles moving through it that create variations in the medium, thus affecting radiation interactions and resulting in a form of friction affecting the particle's trajectory. This phenomenon can be described using relativistic hydrodynamics and solved numerically for moderate to high density environments. However, in situations involving low densities and interplay between photons and neutrons such as in supernovae explosions or neutron star mergers, a new analytical model is proposed that considers the distinct behaviors of photons and baryons separately, yielding a wavelength of radiation that scales inversely proportional to the density of the medium and the particle's velocity. As a consequence, when a particle moves through a static radiation field, the particle's shadow causes a shift in the center of mass of the photon gas, leading to a circular trajectory for the center of mass, in turn influencing the dynamic behavior of the particle and the surrounding radiation interaction. Moreover, particle motion in a static magnetic field generates distinct patterns of current and polarization in the photon gas, thereby producing a magnetic field-driven dynamics in the dynamic equation and resulting in a spiral trajectory for charged particles. Importantly, the dynamic friction effect becomes more pronounced at low velocities and manifests as a velocity-dependent term in the dynamic equation that can be reinterpreted as relativistic friction effect that accounts for both radiation interaction and thermodynamic properties of the medium, with a modified Lorentz factor. Numerical assessments of the numerical scheme and applications to scenarios involving supernovae, neutron star mergers, quark gloves and dense laboratory particles have been conducted, yielding significant insights into non-equilibrium radiation interaction and thermodynamic properties of the dynamic equation. These findings reveal the significance of non-linear feedback and radiation interaction in determining the dynamic behavior of particles and result in outcomes that often surpass equilibrium limits, with potential implications for supernovae, cosmic ray production and laboratory particle research. Additional investigations into radiation interaction and the dynamic behavior of particles are needed to advance our understanding of intense radiation interactions and result in outcomes that often surpass equilibrium limits. Over recent years, numerous oversampling methods have been developed to address the issue of class imbalance in machine learning, specifically for detection tasks. Unlike traditional approaches that create new instances by interpolation, some recent methods utilize genetic algorithms, which generate new instances by modifying existing ones through genetic operations. This new classifier also addresses the issue of duplicate instances by utilizing a clustering-based oversampling method that identifies and creates new instances from clusters with low confidence. By doing so, the proposed classifier differs from traditional oversampling methods, as demonstrated by its utility in detection tasks where datasets are highly imbalanced. Experimental results show that the proposed classifier surpasses its counterparts in multiple datasets. This paper suggests a new strategy for incorporating prior knowledge about the distribution of response times in Bayesian Generalized Linear Mixed Models. Unlike conventional approaches, this method facilitates direct specification of the prior probability density function or its density derivative. As a result, commonly observed distributions such as log-logistic, log-normal, and gamma can be easily modeled, all while maintaining a standard linear predictor for response variables. Furthermore, this approach enables flexible accommodation of various covariates effect sizes by tailoring prior mean and variance. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method in a simulation study and illustrate its practical value in real-world scenarios, including an analysis of the effect of educational reforms on students' test scores and another on the time patients spend under intensive care. We compare these findings to traditional approaches, revealing the proposed strategy's superior performance. We also note that this method is equivalent to a Bayesian nonparametric mixture model, offering an alternative perspective on the significant challenges posed by the substantial overdispersion observed in the second case study. We specifically examine the magnetic levitation used in recent studies on the geometrically forced Ginzburg-Landau Taylor dynamo in reference [PJ Jadhav et al., npj Conf Sci 2, 9 (2018)], with particular emphasis on how it can be adapted for dynamic manipulation. With dynamic magnetic levitation, we propose a few potential strategies for creating stable, inverted, and rotating initial perturbations within the cylindrical container. These Emotion-driven designs do not rely on any part of the cylindrical container, but rather solely on the dynamic magnetic levitation for support. Additionally, we outline the basic concepts and principles governing magnetic levitation in a cylindrical container, with a view to broadening its applicability to diverse research areas in fluid dynamics. We believe that the dynamic magnetic levitation approach will accelerate the exponential growth of the field, with potential applications extending beyond magnetic levitation to other areas, such as shape-memory alloys, for creating complex initial perturbations in various geometries. The underlying physics of basic magnetic levitation in a cylindrical container is also re-examined, with the aim of furnishing a practical handbook for designing magnetic levitation in a cylindrical container, as well as highlighting intriguing aspects unique to rotating fluids in a cylindrical container. The study specifically explores the numerical simulation of dynamic perturbations in a cylindrical container, with a view to facilitating the design of magnetic levitation in a wide range of formats. The work presents a new perspective, the perspective of the user, in designing magnetic levitation in a cylindrical container, with a view to fostering active participation from researchers working in different areas to expand the current applications of magnetic levitation in fluid dynamics. The study specifically employs the dynamic magnetization approach, with a user-defined target force rather than a specific temperature in a shape-memory alloy. Due to inherent differences in the materials' electronic structures, slight chemical potential differences result in the equilibrium of charge and spin transport, rather than uniform Fermi levels. Consequently, these conditions create distinct energy dependencies in the transport characteristics of graphene when in contact with a traditional conductor. Additionally, these conditions create unique equilibrium occupations in the case of a traditional conductor, characterized by a non-zero finite energy dependency. This study demonstrates that these conditions create consistent results in the transport characteristics of graphene when in contact with a traditional conductor, as well as in the traditional conductor itself when in contact with a solution. To thoroughly understand how quark-gluon plasma behaves when it rapidly cools down, researchers need to analyze the dynamic process of its collapse into a vast number of hadrons. A novel numerical model investigates this phenomenon, beginning with the QGP's initial configuration and tracing the evolution of its fluid dynamics until it eventually reaches a state of thermal equilibrium. By optimizing parameters such as the ratio of quark and lepton densities, the model simulates a scenario in which the QGP's initial structure consists of two distinct regions: a dense inner core and a less dense outer shell. The simulation shows that this unusual initial setup leads to an irregular distribution of forces within the QGP's fluid dynamics, causing pressure to increase at the edges and decrease at the center. Consequently, an inward force forms at the boundaries of the central region, generating substantial velocities among the fluid's particles. The results of the simulation indicate that this behavior contributes significantly to the production of high-energy particles at the edges of the QGP. A comprehensive analysis of the various parameters of the QGP's fluid dynamics is conducted, revealing the intricate relationships between them. The models also show that when the QGP rapidly cools, the produced hadrons undergo an extensive process of resonance, resulting in substantial production of baryons. The results of our simulations align with experimental data on hadron production, while also accounting for differences in the production dynamics of pions, kaons, and other particles. The models' predictions regarding the significant production of certain particles at high energies are particularly noteworthy, as they have not been extensively explored in previous studies. The models' ability to forecast the degree of polarization within the production of certain particles at mid-energy is also a key achievement. We introduce the SASK approach, a novel, high-performance FEM technique for solving PDEs that operates in a kernel matrix level. In the context of time-dependent PDEs, it employs an adaptive time-scheme where fine-grained steps are taken at early time points and coarsening occurs at later points. Each time step is accompanied by a corresponding choice of finite element space. Additionally, the SASK approach features an optimized data management system, known as the Matrix Accumulator, designed to minimize memory access inefficiencies. These advancements enable the SASK approach to achieve greater efficiency compared to traditional adaptive finite element schemes. Moreover, the SASK method has been successfully integrated with quasi-contour element methods, which themselves have been proven to have exceptional error reduction properties. We demonstrate the SASK approach's robustness through numerous numerical demonstrations across a diverse set of PDE examples. These experiments reveal the SASK method's capacity to achieve significant acceleration while maintaining accuracy. In fact, the SASK approach often achieves accelerated convergence or reduces computational costs by up to 90% in some instances. Moreover, the SASK method's findings reveal a strong correlation between time step size and resulting solution error. The Sinkhorn algorithm, an efficient method for solving the Schrödinger problem in optimal transport, has been found to converge to a suitable solution using purely first-order computations, despite relying on a diverging series in its original implementation. By modifying the algorithm to include a weak closure condition on the cost function and implementing a stopping criterion, the Sinkhorn algorithm can safely ensure convergence to a well-defined solution. This approach also allows for the algorithm to terminate if no solution exists. Moreover, by combining the Sinkhorn algorithm with a specific model-based approach, a practical method for solving the Schrödinger problem was developed, evaluated, and compared with the Gottfert algorithm in various numerical experiments. This new method was found to converge in most cases within a few iterations, even when starting from an arbitrary initial position. It was also found to approximate the solution obtained through the Sinkhorn algorithm nearly exactly. While the Gottfert algorithm showed faster convergence in some cases, the new method was found to outperform it in practical applications due to its better theoretical properties. It was further observed that the new method facilitated a straightforward extension to the t-Sinkhorn algorithm, a fast tool for open-set classification. This new method is believed to be a reliable and efficient solution to the Schrödinger problem in optimal transport. It was implemented in an open-source code, called TorchOpt, for easy replication and exposition. This code is currently available for public use at https://github.com/chomnes/TorchOpt. Top-quark pair production cross-section has been measured in the single-top-quark events with a lepton from the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Using 2017 data with 36.1 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, the research analyzed single-top-quark events in the ATLAS detector. It distinguished between three events involving a single top quark and a lepton: $t\to l^-\nu_l$ (where $l$ can be either an electron or a muon), followed by the incorporation of two or more jets. These events were categorized as either having a $W$ boson from the top quark or from the other quark in the pair. Using this information, the cross-section of the process was measured as 75.8±19.9 pb and compared with quantum chromodynamics predictions based on the fifth-generation two-Higgs doublet model as well as the Standard Model itself. The measurement also revealed a discrepancy of about 2.3 standard deviations between the theoretical and experimental cross-sections. Additionally, the research introduced a new method to correct for detector inefficiencies. It also verified, with high confidence, the expectation of an asymmetry in the production of same-sign top quark pairs, predicted to be around 0.3-0.6% by the relevant quantum chromodynamics theories. No evidence of same-sign top quark pairs was observed in the analyzed data. Given its larger phase area, the exclusion limit for the same-sign top quark pairs cross-section was set at 60 and 40 fb at a 95% confidence level. These results are expected to be part of a broader understanding of the top quark's properties. Further research into the analyzed data could provide insights into the non-standard model four-top-quark production process, predicted by similar quantum chromodynamics theories. It is expected that a more precise measurement in the process could either exclude completely or further restrict the predicted cross-section value. As a result, the analyzed data could provide valuable insights into the properties of the top quark and ultimately contribute to understanding the quantum chromodynamics theory. Moreover, the research identified an anomaly in the incidence of events involving an extra electron or muon in the parton-shower simulations. Truncated correlations in these systems allow for analyzing entanglement evolution, and our results show that, as might be expected, the amount of entanglement that develops is limited by the system's internal interactions and external disruptions. Notably, when the surrounding environment consists of non-interacting spins, the amount of entanglement that develops tends to increase over time, and our results reveal that this entanglement has a regular oscillating pattern. On the other hand, when the surrounding environment consists of interacting spins, the amount of entanglement that develops tends to decrease over time, and our results show that this entanglement has a more irregular, random pattern. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the effectiveness of using entangled spins to enhance quantum information transfer between a central cavity and a central qubit is severely impacted by the surrounding environment's internal interactions. A specific property of left- or right-handed light is usually considered the key chiral component in physics, but researchers now reveal that it is also possible to have macroscopic chiral properties at a fundamental level. For example, a planar mirror can reflect both left- and right-handed light in the same way, but still maintain a handedness due to the inherent properties of circularly polarized light. Recently, a new class of chiral optical cavities was developed, which were initially single-handed but gained the ability to transmit both handednesses; this was achieved by modifying the cavity's properties. In the study, the researchers show that these cavities interact more strongly with chiral emitters in a handedness-specific way, which was not dependent on the coherent properties of the emitters. Instead, the interaction was influenced by the probability of the emitters being in a handedness-specific state. A limiting threshold was also identified for the cavities' properties beyond which the handedness-specific interaction becomes dominant. In the future, the researchers' findings can be applied to various applications that rely on the handedness-specific interaction, such as controlling the rotation of molecules and creating advanced light manipulation systems. This article explores a specific aspect of two-dimensional anti de-Sitter spacetimes in the context of two-dimensional string theory. A general approach is developed to compute the thermal entropy of these AdS_2 spaces within the framework of the geometric action formalism. The outcomes reveal that AdS_2 thermodynamic properties are closely linked to those of spherical sections within the associated higher-dimensional anti de-Sitter spaces. A thorough examination is also provided of the holographic entropy convergence in the semi-classical limit, supported by specific case studies. Our goal is to determine the extent to which the electromagnetic field can concentrate at sub-wavelength points, and how this influences the electromagnetic responses. We have also investigated the non-local electromagnetic properties of dielectric materials and their implications for TERS. Our findings show that the electromagnetic field can focus at sub-wavelength intervals, but not necessarily at a single point. Conversely, the electromagnetic responses in TERS can occur in areas much smaller than the wavelength of light due to non-local effects. These outcomes demonstrate the distinct roles of the electromagnetic and chemical effects in TERS, which can be viewed as complementary phenomena. To further illustrate this, we have reinterpreted a range of TERS studies, revealing a simple relationship between the electromagnetic responses, the optical properties of materials, and the geometrical properties of the materials under investigation. Our hope is that this will inspire researchers to effectively combine the capabilities of near-field optics and quantum nanophotonics to facilitate the production and study of artificial atoms and molecules at the single-particle level.
