The acceleration of quantum computing progress has sparked a renewed interest in exploring quantum systems for their potential to model complex phenomena that defy classical solutions. The process of measuring these quantum models, however, is subject to error and can be mitigated using techniques such as unfolding. While conventional methods unearth underlying distributions through iterative applications of Bayes' theorem, the complexity and cost associated with measuring these distributions often restrict their practical applications. We have developed an algorithm that unfolds iterative Bayesian measurements on multiple qubits without requiring frequent, high-cost measurements. The algorithm instead utilizes a probabilistic map of distributions pre- and post-measurement, thereby significantly reducing the costs involved. We have evaluated the scalability and efficiency of this approach by applying it to various datasets, which we have simulated on multiple quantum computers. The results indicate that the algorithm yields reliable results quickly, including for larger datasets, thanks to its capacity to process probability distributions as a whole rather than individual data points. We have shown that the algorithm can process datasets consisting of millions of data points on multiple qubits in a matter of seconds, which could facilitate its adoption in the measurement process of quantum circuits. The code for reproducing our results is publicly available. The research has broader implications for quantum computing-based services, which will soon be offering access to complex quantum models despite the limitations imposed by measurement noise. The development of the unfolding algorithm will therefore contribute to reducing the scalability and efficiency costs associated with these measurements. In addition to its practical applications, the research delves into the conceptual foundations of Bayesian unfolding in the context of quantum computing-based services. The study provides an in-depth analysis of the trade-off between the Bayesian evidence and the Bayes factor, which are both crucial in understanding the quality of fit and model selection. The research demonstrates that the Bayesian evidence can be an unreliable metric for assessing models when the data is imperfectly known, which may contradict existing knowledge. The study, however, reveals a possible remedy: introducing prior knowledge of the data to the Bayesian evidence to balance the quality of fit and model selection. The researchers further discovered that the Bayesian evidence can be an efficient way to evaluate model scalability, which aligns with computational complexity theory. The study also confirms that the Bayesian evidence can overestimate model performance if the Bayesian assumption that all data is perfectly known is incorrect, which may lead to model misselection. The researchers therefore recommend using unbiased estimates of the Bayesian evidence to reliably evaluate model performance. The study provides an explanation for the phenomenon of the rapid increase in the number of models needed to be simulated as the accuracy of the models increases

Users' ability to solve problems with the aid of a computer is optimised when the system provides clear and explicit instructions on the specific problem-solving strategy required to achieve a high efficiency rating. However, in the context of interacting with a computer-controlled robot, we investigate an alternative scenario in which the robot does not function as a perfect guide but instead as a task-supporting device. Specifically, we design the Action Choice Learning Environment (ACHE) in which a user learns an arbitrary sequence of actions necessary to complete a task as instructed by an informed agent. Our results demonstrate that, even though the robot does not function as an ideal tutor, still it enhances users' performance rates when users have some general knowledge about the tasks. Moreover, we found out that the robot's effectiveness as a helper is significantly decreased if we make its action choices choices transparent to its agent. Based on these outcomes, we propose two possible designs for the interaction flow: one that utilises the robot's ability to offer helpful suggestions and clarify its intentions, and another that focuses on making the user an informed actor by revealing the robot's control mechanisms. We finally establish a fundamental boundary for the effectiveness of interacting with a robot that serves as a general-purpose device. Our study shows that, regardless of any other factors, a robot is able to boost a user's efficiency when its control program has no more than four actions, and if the user has some general knowledge of the tasks, then the robot is able to boost the user's efficiency to the optimal level. Our study, therefore, provides valuable insights to inform the interaction design for general-purpose collaborative robots. Our work, however, leaves many other important design considerations unresolved and, thus, presents several potential avenues for further investigation in the future. Our study's data and all the relevant tools to reproduce our findings are publicly available at this website: https://sites.google.com/view/robothelpsuser/. Our work, however, was limited to examination of keyboard-based interactive tasks and future studies could reveal whether our findings hold true for other physical input modalities that are used to accomplish the same type of tasks. Moreover, although our study's results suggest that the robot's ability to enhance user efficiency could be significant in contexts where the user's task-related skills are either very limited or very extensive. This study presents HiTMap, a novel 2D representation for agent navigation that facilitates the transfer of learning between metric topologies, unlike previous global metric maps which assume fixed navigation pathways. By employing a hierarchical attention mechanism, HiTMap can focus on significant scene features and leverage temporary memory to navigate more efficiently. In comparison to leading agent navigation methods, HiTMap's learned features demonstrate better alignment with human metrics, as measured by the intrinsic curvature of the navigation path. Agent collisions are also significantly reduced, with HiTMap achieving a $66.53\%$ lower collision rate in the Square dataset and a $53.52\%$ lower collision rate in the Complex dataset. Notably, HiTMap's performance approaches human-level metrics in the more challenging Complex dataset and surpasses other agent navigation methods across all datasets. HiTMap's source code is openly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/optimizedplace/hi_tmap. The paper includes a visual demonstration of HiTMap's performance at the URL: https://youtu.be/tybPcH7RF4. Please read our accompanying technical report for further details at arXiv:2207.15304. This research receives no external funding. Optimized-Place is an open and community-driven research platform located at optimizedplace.github.io. Our research focuses on developing cutting-edge approaches for autonomous agent navigation that also address critical real-world concerns like energy efficiency and reduced computational latency. In the past, our research team successfully introduced the HiStar approach, which enables star metric topologies for agent navigation while leveraging end-to-end reinforcement learning to optimize agent navigation efficiency. Our recent studies expand upon this foundation by introducing HiTMap, which enables the transfer of learning between metric topologies for agent navigation. Our research also explores the critical connection between agent navigation metrics and human perception. By introducing HiTMap, we demonstrate that our representation can learn features that better align with human metrics. Compared to other top-notch agent navigation methods, HiTMap exhibits reduced collisions. Finally, our research shows that HiTMap's output approaches human topological maps. Our visual demonstrations display how HiTMap's features compare to human visual navigation and how HiTMap's output resembles a human topological map. Our research also demonstrates HiTMap's efficiency by showcasing its comparative runtime in the paper. Our research receives no external funding. A new class of 2-D Z-complementary array codes, known as ZCACS, has a unique property where the sum of elements in each row or column is zero, resulting in a perfect complement to existing arrays. Traditionally, Boolean functions used in array code construction were restricted to finite fields, but recent advancements allowed for functions defined over finite rings to be used. This paper takes the next step by utilizing Boolean functions with coefficients from finite fields of ring $Z_p^{n/m}$ to construct 2-D ZCACS with m variables. By doing so, it is shown that there is a direct correlation between the number of variables with non-zero coefficients and the value of m. The proposed construction is then used to develop optimal ZCACS of different lengths. The approach is further demonstrated with several examples. Furthermore, a modified version of this method is applied to develop different ZCACS of varying lengths. The approach is illustrated with several numerical examples. All the developed arrays are verified using Verilog codes, which are simulated to confirm their correctness. The overall objective is to expand the capabilities of traditional Boolean functions to produce 2-D ZCACS with diverse lengths for diverse applications. It is noteworthy that this work has been accepted at the 2021 International Symposium on Multiple Valued Logic.

RegCT's unique image formation model incorporates sparsity and low-dose elements to mitigate data disruption caused by limited measurement and measurement error, addressing Poisson noise through a maximum likelihood approach and chromatic noise via a nonlinear correction process. We reframe CT image formation as a multi-task optimization problem influenced by systematic biological processes, which we apply to the CT image reconstruction task. We also leverage the system matrix's unique properties to reparameterize the model, transforming the CT image reconstruction into a set of coupled nonlinear equations. We implemented a novel primal-dual algorithm to solve the CT image reconstruction problem. The task of contextual named entity retrieval (CONER) involves finding entities in free text context, where a specific context is used to narrow down the search for entities. understanding temporal connections and creating a comprehensive data analysis. However, 
current technologies fail to provide an effective way to link temporal plots to other graphical 
objects, making it difficult to study the dynamics of systems over time. Our solution, called timelinked.html, 
enables seamless linking of temporal plots to other graphical models through an HTML extension. 
This technology facilitates the creation of connected visualizations that grow and change in sync, 
like animated chemistry diagrams that update alongside temporal plots of molecule transformations.

Automatically distinguishing multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions from white matter hyperintensities in brain scans is crucial for providing valuable insights into MS diagnosis. Since scanning protocols vary between hospitals, this task is even more complex. To address this challenge, we integrated our recent multi-hospital lesion detection model with an experience replay strategy, alongside modified lesion segmentation and classification approaches. Our modified approach identifies areas with different data distributions as separate categories. In this study, we expanded the scope of the original task by incorporating these complex data patterns. First, we refined the lesion detection model to recognize outliers in the white matter. Next, we integrated Experience Replay (ER) to enhance the robustness of the lesion classification. Our modified dataset, called E-R-Multi, along with the original Multi-Hospital dataset, were used in an experimental comparison that demonstrated the superiority of our E-R-Multi approach over conventional multi-class lesion classification methods. The E-R-Multi model achieved an impressive 90.6% lesion detection rate, 73.0% lesion segmentation accuracy, and 86.3% lesion classification performance. These results indicate that our Experience Replay strategy contributes to more effective MS lesion segmentation. The E-R-Multi approach also performed well in a simpler lesion classification task, reporting an accuracy of 94.5% and 99.5% respectively on the primary Multi-Hospital dataset. Our findings suggest the potential of incorporating Experience Replay into multi-hospital datasets to address complex data distribution issues. Many glass-formers exhibit time-dependent behavior that follows a universal pattern,
correlating temperature variations with time scales and dynamic properties.
This pattern corresponds to a specific thermodynamic process and can be observed
when comparing equivalent processes in different systems. The correlation suggests
that a range of dynamic phenomena rely on the fluctuations of certain fundamental energy factors.
To investigate this further, we analyzed the behavior of a two-body interaction in sugar syrup and polymer solutions, observing how particles move closer to each other.
We compared this to simulations of liquid molecules, observing similar dynamic behavior in different systems. The results confirm that the behavior of complex fluids can be explained by the fluctuations of the two-body interaction potential. Additionally, we identified the observed phenomenon as part of a broader group of processes that follow the same universal pattern, suggesting a link between these processes and the stability of liquid form, as well as the role of these processes in understanding the transition from liquid to glassy states. Furthermore, the study highlights the value of observing the time-dependent behavior of different systems on a universal time scale to understand the behavior of complex fluids. 

Keywords: glass-formers, time-dependent behavior, thermodynamic analysis, complex fluids, universal time scales.

Recent transformer models, such as BERT and ELECTRA, exhibit strong performance across various natural language processing tasks. However, these models struggle with negation due to limitations in their pre-training data and resulting black-box inference capabilities. As a result, they often fail to distinguish between negated premises during a natural language inference task. In contrast, we propose utilizing non-autoregressive transformers to bypass the limitations of autoregressive architectures and non-decompositional representations. By introducing a novel transformation module to address negation, our proposed framework, named NERWI, demonstrates significant improvements over enhanced BERT and ELECTRA models, achieving a new state-of-the-art performance on the SemaForNLI benchmark for full NLI task implementation. Furthermore, ablation studies on individual negation categories reveal that NERWI outperforms these models across all categories, with notable gains of 0.7-3.8 EM and 0.6-3.9 F scores for categorical negation categories. Quasi-categorical negation categories showed a 2.3-4.4 increased F score. Additionally, a thorough analysis of NERWI's performance highlights the impact of pre-training data quality on this model, emphasizing the need for comprehensive pre-training data to address negation. Lastly, NERWI's source code will be made available for public use.

In inflation theories with complex features such as sharp peaks or rapid phase variations in some regions, similar non-Gaussian signs can appear in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), which is challenging to differentiate. We've found that these features' effects on the bispectrum can be broken down into distinct components: local parts that depend on sound horizon scales $\Lambda_{\phi}$, and non-local parts that also rely on how these scales interact. We've developed a method to isolate these individual contributions and compared them to predictions from a standard inflation model with two distinct features - a peak and a rapid phase shift. We've discovered that both scenarios share a similar local response but have distinct non-local characteristics that can be distinguished by simple measurements. Moreover, our analysis reveals significant uncertainties in determining the non-Gaussian signs, which means that in some cases, these features' impacts can't be confirmed until the error margins are reduced to under 1$\%$. We also propose a new approximation for approximating the non-Gaussian signs which can accurately predict the CMB spectra' C_ℓ values up to C_ℓ for l=20 with minimal error. This non-local correction, depending on how specified scales interact, can shift predicted non-Gaussian signs in the CMB from negative to positive when the interaction level is above 5$\%$. We suggest designing experiments that can estimate the interaction between scales to better comprehend the non-Gaussian signs in the CMB. This new approximation and separation of features' effects on the CMB can be found in additional figures and tables in the supplementary materials. Convective dynamo models developed so far have highlighted various turbulent effects' roles in setting up poloidal and toroidal magnetic fields, crucial for solar and stellar activity. Nonetheless, the complex nature of turbulence still requires thorough exploration to assure an accurate physical representation, which is essential for understanding solar-weather phenomena and star formation. Consequently, the goal of this paper is to investigate the impact of turbulent effects beyond those previously studied, with a view to shedding light on the unknown processes governing the dynamos. The paper compares different convective dynamo models to determine how each component influences simulated solar and stellar magnetic fields. The adopted framework incorporates the R\"udiger and Brandt, Balency, and R\"eggiani-Low R\"eggiani schemes for diffusivity and resistivity, in addition to the Bard Rouby, R\"eggiani-Low R\"eggiani, and R\"eggiani concepts for energy dissipation. The results of the simulations demonstrate the relative efficiencies of the dynamo models in reproducing the observed properties of the Sun's magnetic cycle, with successful models displaying good agreement with observational data of the Sun's large and small-scale magnetic fields, in addition to the constraints set by helioseismology. By contrast, the models incorporating new effects show varying performance, with the Bard Rouby, R\"eggiani-Low R\"eggiani, and R\"eggiani convective dynamos exhibiting potential for future star modeling. The investigation's outcomes indicate the difficulties in replicating the simulated characteristics of the Sun's magnetic cycle, in line with the advances made in theoretical dynamos, which is a clear indication of the crucial nature of further research into the complex turbulence effects in dynamos. NGC4945 is a prototype lepton-jet galaxy that is optically active, featuring a centrally positioned nuclear spot and extensive ionized gas emission. Located approximately 3.2 megaparsecs away, it is notable for strong emission lines 40 times greater than the solar nebula. A comprehensive analysis of the nuclear region of NGC4945 was conducted, combining data from high-resolution spectroscopy, X-ray observations, and radio astronomy. Our findings reveal a massive outflow of molecular gas in the central region, with a rate of 15 solar masses per year. This is comparable to the observed ionized gas outflow, with both likely driven by superheated gas near the nuclear spot and powered by an active galactic nucleus. A massive central black hole, with a suspected mass of 20 to 38 million solar masses, is consistent with the observed data, while the nuclear spot's luminosity, despite some scattered light, is primarily the result of shielding the central region from the galaxy's intense starlight. A new model of the nuclear region's geometry allows for direct comparison with different energy scenarios, including active galactic nuclei and supernovae. Although the ionized outflow appears stronger than the molecular outflow, we propose that the molecular gas is denser and forms a relatively thick shield, while the ionized gas creates a thinner layer. Furthermore, the absence of HCN and CO luminosity suggests a relatively hot and diluted gas environment. A comprehensive analysis of the nuclear region's energy diagrams indicates that the molecular gas outflow is likely driven by a radiative active galactic nucleus. Finally, NGC4945's central region displays properties of a quasi-starburst galaxy, featuring a massive outflow of gas and strong starbursts activity. Although an accurate measurement of the star formation rate is beyond our capabilities, we observe notable molecular and atomic gas emission, consistent with a star formation rate of 2-6 solar masses per year. These tools hold significant potential to uncover physics beyond the Standard Model. This study investigates an investor's wealth management, focusing on the use of a non-linear combination of an investor's absolute and relative wealth as the sole asset pricing factor. A particular utility function is proposed, which emphasizes an investor's percentage wealth who possesses a larger share of total market capitalization. In this research, we explore the potential of leveraging large, publicly-accessible datasets, such as Wikipedia, in conjunction with a Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) model, like the one developed by Google. By combining RAG with external knowledge and text, we seek to augment the capabilities of contemporary transformer-based language generation models, thereby expanding their cognitive capabilities. Nonetheless, fine-tuning an RAG architecture in this manner poses specific challenges, primarily stemming from the models' inherent propensity to memorize incomplete answers. To mitigate this shortcoming, we develop an efficient, online-based pre-training approach, which we pair with diverse offline fine-tuning methods. Our experiments reveal that the fusion of external knowledge and text enhances the overall performance of the models, both in qualitative and quantitative assessments. Notably, the online-based pre-training strategy, when combined with knowledge retrieval losses, proves particularly effective in generating more coherent and cognizant text, one example being the production of human-style abstracts. The resulting findings are then translated to examine the asymptotic behavior of related sections in the fermionic Foulkes matrix, a topic that has been studied by other notable researchers such as Isozaki and Kamae. Large language models have achieved great success in various text tasks but there remains a significant issue with their ability to generate accurate and relevant summaries. Current approaches rely heavily on human-provided references for evaluation, which is costly. To address this limitation, we've created a qualification pipeline that obtains high-quality annotations from human experts. By employing a knowledge distillation strategy with these human annotations and subsequent peer-review feedback, our model outperforms its initial performance in summary quality, achieving a 9% relative improvement in COCO-19 evaluation. Furthermore, our qualitative analysis of the data reveals an interesting insight into the type of errors made by language models during the summarization process. This study aims to demonstrate that incorporating qualitative annotation and peer-review feedback into large language model training can, in fact, enhance model performance. Therefore, our approach can be seen as a viable alternative or complement to existing training methods. We explore the properties of a network that combines two types: those with preferential attachment and those with a specific block structure. When nodes are added to this hybrid network, it acts like a pure preferential attachment network until a certain point, after which it forms a specific block structure. Unlike purely preferential attachment networks, this hybrid network's in- and out-degree distributions aren't identically the same, instead, they each have unique exponents. We find that, over time, the exponents for the in- and out-degree distributions both change and approach a certain value. We looked at many different properties of this hybrid network and discussed how they compare to networks that purely follow the preferential attachment principle. Furthermore, we investigated the rate at which the hybrid network's properties change when its parameters change. This hybrid network is meant to model a certain type of system where the assumption of preferential attachment doesn't hold. We found that the degree distribution for this assumption is much slower to converge than other network properties, which could have significant implications. We propose that this type of random network is a more realistic model than purely preferential attachment networks and should be considered when modeling systems that change over time. Moreover, studying this hybrid network may offer valuable insights into the flexibility of degree distributions in random networks and shed light on various network dynamics. We provide some final considerations and potential future directions for further investigation. A potential area for photon physics research is a muon collider, which could serve as an energy upgrade over existing electron-positron colliders. However, the photon beam produced by scattering on a tungsten target in a muon collider is contaminated by in-flight muon decays that can be detected in the same beam line, obstructing the photon research process. The goal of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of various methods for eliminating these in-flight muon decays before they interfere with the photon research. Simulations were conducted using the LUXE detector's layout and the specific muon collider configuration for LUXE, which involves a 100 GeV muon beam and a tungsten target, to analyze the impact of decay muons on the photon research. The results showed that a dedicated decay muon detector positioned close to the target, combined with a ring imaging cherenkov detector upstream, can completely eliminate the decay muons' influence. Additionally, the study found that the remaining decay muons' influence can be minimized through the use of the tungsten target's built-in shielding. While many existing graph representation learning methods focus on static graphs, recent advances have led to the development of several techniques for dynamic graphs. However, existing methods often struggle to capture temporal correlations and can be difficult to interpret. This study introduces a new approach, Temporal Piecewise Gaussian Attention (TPGA), incorporating both local and global temporal cues through the fusion of spatial and temporal attention mechanisms. Local attention captures subtle temporal patterns, while global attention captures the overall temporal correlation. Experimental results demonstrate TPGA's effectiveness on predicting future links in citation and knowledge graphs, and its scalable implementation allows it to operate efficiently on large scales, outperforming existing methods on multiple tasks. Thanks to the advancement of deep learning, state-of-the-art performance has been achieved in visual classification tasks, including person re-identification. To further improve the accuracy in this field, researchers are seeking novel end-to-end methods for learning discriminative embedding spaces. To address this, a novel loss function, known as the Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), is proposed. DCDL measures the discrepancy in class centers within the embedding space and introduces a regularization method to enhance learning. Experimental results demonstrate that DCDL is capable of extracting more discriminative features than traditional identity-based methods and lattic-based methods. Moreover, DCDL is adaptable to various deep network architectures and can be seamlessly integrated into existing visual re-identification systems. To facilitate the reproduction of results, the proposed approach, along with related source code and datasets, is made publicly available online. Various benchmark experiments were conducted to validate the effectiveness of DCDL, including evaluations on the VIPER benchmark and the challenging BANVS dataset. DCDL achieved top performance on VIPER, ranking 4th in the 2019 competition, and demonstrated superior performance in the BANVS dataset, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art method, BodyNet. A comprehensive analysis of the proposed approach was also undertaken to examine its robustness against different noise levels and network architectures. For instance, the approach demonstrated robust capacity when trained with 90% label noise on the VIPER dataset. Moreover, the learning performance of DCDL was compared with various deep architectures, including the widely-used ResNet-50, SeNet-111, and the relatively new AutoNet, showing its effectiveness across different regions of the architecture space. To further verify the robustness of DCDL, various adversarial attacks, including the fundamental Fast Gradient Sign method and the more sophisticated PGGA, were employed. A robustness test under PGGA revealed that the approach could still achieve an accurate accuracy-to-attack ratio of 0.916, even when subjected to a high attack ratio of 0.9. A similar robustness test using the common white box attack revealed a comparable ratio of 0.95. Moreover, the approach demonstrated robust performance when evaluated against several state-of-the-art attack methods, including the evolution-based black box attack, ranked 3rd in terms of accuracy-to-attack ratio and 5th in eigenvalue. A comprehensive evaluation of the learning quality of DCDL was also undertaken to examine its effectiveness in terms of several key metrics

A persistent issue in network analysis involves developing metrics that accurately measure the extent of information transfer between connected elements within complex systems.  A specific approach, known as the Zhang-Horvath clustering coefficient, utilizes a continuous method for assessing the clustering properties of these networks. However, our analysis reveals that this coefficient can be easily manipulated and is sensitive to its time parameters, resulting in overestimation of clustering behavior in certain scenarios.  In contrast, our investigations show that the clustering coefficient falls short, especially in situations involving short signal durations or low signal amplitudes, which can lead to an underrepresentation of the true clustering behavior.  Our research proposes a new continuous clustering coefficient that demonstrates greater robustness and accuracy in various testing conditions compared to the existing measure of Zhang-Horvath.  A comparison of these two coefficients is shown through their application on artificial signal datasets as well as real EEG data.  Our findings indicate that the proposed coefficient yields more accurate outcomes that align more closely with the underlying truth.  Specifically, our results show that the proposed coefficient offers superior correlation with human-identified clustering patterns in EEG data.  While the current measure of Zhang-Horvath achieves a correlation of 0.40, our new continuous clustering coefficient achieves a significantly stronger correlation of 0.40.  Our investigations suggest that our proposed technique offers considerable potential for use in the automated detection and quantification of clustering phenomena in EEG data. Refining machine learning models to ensure reliable predictions is possible by 
converting inherent uncertainties into probabilistic formulations. 
Physics-informed neural networks offer a unique advantage by incorporating 
physical laws into their training, making them more accurate. 
Despite their potential, determining the accuracy of these networks beyond 
training data is challenging. To address this limitation, we introduce a method 
that calculates the error of physics-informed neural networks after training 
using data-driven techniques. This method, which we call PILNE, adjusts the network 
slightly to fit a predetermined error estimate derived from the network's 
parameters. By doing so, PILNE provides a certified confidence bound for the 
network's predictions and helps identify potential issues with the network or 
the predictive model. We apply PILNE to several problems involving ordinary and 
partial differential equations and demonstrate its effectiveness by validating it 
with exact solutions and comparing it to other error estimation methods in various 
scenarios. Moreover, PILNE demonstrates its practical applications by providing 
accurate predictions for a temperature-dependent heat conduction problem and a 
free surface flow problem involving shallow water dynamics. These examples 
demonstrate that refining machine learning models using PILNE can significantly 
enhance their accuracy and establish a reliable framework for use in practical 
applications. Moreover, our study highlights the practical challenges and 
potential issues that can arise during the implementation of PILNE, making it 
suitable for theoretical and practical applications. By doing so, PILNE offers a 
theoretical advancement in the field of machine learning for solving complex 
physical problems and facilitates its application in practical, real-world tasks.

  1. The set of cardinals that are not achieved by any subset of $\kappa$ has a cardinality of $\kappa$, 
  2. The set of cardinals that are not achieved by any subset of $\kappa$ less than $\kappa$, and 
  3. The set of cardinals that are not achieved by a subset of the successor of $\kappa$ is not achieved by a subset of $\kappa$. Furthermore, the presence of the first property with a certain condition indicates the presence of large cardinals, while the absence of the first property with a certain other condition is equivalent to the absence of the first property. The techniques used involve the study of whitehead-type theorems for extensions of theorems by Erdos and Tarski. The proof also involves the construction of a model through elementary transfinite recursion in a suitable model of $ZFC+GCH$. The model has the property that it satisfies the conditions for the first property and also does not satisfy the conditions for the fourth property, which is a consequence of a theorem by Erdos and Tarski. The proof further shows that the fifth property implies a certain type of "generalized singular" cardinal, which implies the presence of a large minimum. The techniques and methods used have some broader applications. The methods used are shown to work in a class with at least $2$ elements and possibly up to $c$ (the cardinality of the continuum) elements. The phenomenon of thermal diffusion in a binary mixture of identical hard spheres under a constant temperature difference is investigated using molecular dynamics simulations. A standard model implements a thermal gradient across the fluid, while the potential energy remains unaffected. Rather than introducing significant temperature fluctuations, the application of the thermal gradient in this model primarily shifts energy among particles. A method to calculate the thermal diffusion factor is developed by correlating energy and particle density changes. The flexibility of molecules and the presence of vacuum gaps between them are found to impact thermal diffusion, but such effects are minimized when particle density is high. At higher temperature differences, the thermal diffusion factor exhibits more substantial variations. Additionally, the theoretical work of Ginzburg and Galilei is related to our findings, as they can be incorporated into a unified expression that accounts for certain molecular properties and non-zero vacuum gaps. Such a unified expression provides insight into factors contributing to significant thermal diffusion, which is otherwise difficult to interpret due to complex thermal energy distributions. A new theoretical model for thermal diffusion in the absence of external fields has also been developed, yielding results comparable to existing research. Nonetheless, the application of the thermal gradient in this model primarily affects the flow of energy rather than causing direct particle movements. Consequently, the diffusion process is largely governed by thermal gradient-induced changes in the energy distribution. A separate study is called for to explore the influence of centrifugal forces on thermal diffusion. Moreover, the models used in these simulations assume non-interacting particles; the introduction of chemical interactions and their effects on thermal diffusion are also investigated, revealing that existing research does not accurately capture the effects of identity interactions on thermal diffusion. Such interactions, primarily affecting the movement of particles, are observed to have a negligible impact on thermal diffusion factor, but they do contribute to modifying underlying theoretical models and the establishment of boundary conditions at high particle densities. Finally, the practical implications and challenges associated with accurately modelling thermal diffusion are discussed and considered. These aspects encompass broader topics such as the modelling of gas mixtures, simulations of gas mixtures, and the analysis of molecular data and predictions of thermodynamic properties. In order to enhance simulations of gas mixtures, the development of theoretical models for thermal diffusion is crucial. Such models enable the prediction of thermal diffusion factors and help to establish the validity of underlying theoretical assumptions and model structure. Furthermore, the analysis of molecular data and predictions of thermodynamic properties are within the reach with the assistance of these models. In contrast, the absence of practical implications and challenges does not entirely preclude the development of general theoretical models for thermal diffusion.

Most natural language processing models were initially developed using English datasets, making them less effective on other languages.  Aiming to improve efficiency and effectiveness across languages of varying resources, this study investigates post-training quantization and Knowledge Distillation as potential compression and bootstrapping techniques.  By experimenting with these methods on multiple datasets in multiple scenarios, our findings suggest that Knowledge Distillation consistently delivers better results but post-training quantization demonstrates more consistent performance despite achieving lower results.  Furthermore, our results illustrate that quantization retains more of the original model's performance while Knowledge Distillation appears to extract less relevant information.  A crucial insight from this research stems from examining the knowledge retained by the compressed model: our data indicates that the Knowledge Distillation method tends to retain core semantic associations more effectively than quantization.  Meanwhile, quantization was found to retain more data-related information such as word co-occurrences.  A possible direction for further exploration is delineating the specific types of knowledge retained by each compression technique in order to better understand their mechanisms and achieve more efficient communication between languages of varying resource levels.  Ultimately, our research aims to offer practical guidance for using these compression methods to successfully deploy high-performance models on languages with limited data availability. Baber and Talbot recently established an upper limit on the Turan density of 3-uniform graphs of order n, which was previously unknown. Their result, derived from a dense subgraph of a certain structure, demonstrates that the previously estimated 3-uniform graph Turan density, roughly n^2/n^3, was accurate. This led us to investigate whether similar methods can be applied to determine the Turan density of 2-uniform graphs of order n, which has been defined as the maximum proportion of n-edge subgraphs in nK_r given to nK_r-1. Our investigation, based on previous lower limits by Yang and Tolkanina, largely resolved this problem. Specifically, we refined the upper bound to be no more than n^2/n^2 with a remaining adjustment of o(n^2) and confirmed that previous lower bounds are in fact accurate, establishing the exact density to be n^2/n^2 for r equal to 2. We also began exploring the feasibility of extending this approach to determine the Turan density of r>3, specifically considering 4-uniform graphs. Our key finding showed, however, that an earlier lower bound by Dong, Liu, and Wang was not the best possible lower bound but rather a value significantly higher than the actual bound. This development leaves open the question of exact density calculation but raises the accuracy of the current upper bound to be n^2/n^r with a remaining adjustment of o(n^2), which is an improvement from the previously established limit. Causal reasoning has the ability to determine cause-effect relationships, enabling more effective decision-making in various tasks including logical deductions and scenarios where multiple explanations are possible.  Within the context of off-policy learning, causal reasoning allows for better assessment of interventions, resulting in improved task generalization.  Recent attempts at integrating causal reasoning into off-policy learning have been centered on the concept of contrastive causation.  Contrastive causation represents a concept developed by Pearl that emphasizes causes over effect-producing factors, highlighting the distinction between causes and mere correlations.  Highlighting contrastive causation emphasizes how actions produce desired outcomes and demonstrates its relationship to utility by showing that the actions most likely to produce these results are those which are caused by the presence of specific pre-conditioning factors.  While such concepts are valuable in theory, they are difficult to evaluate empirically.  Research published in 2019 and 2019 introduced new methods for assessing contrastive causation through the application of equivalence constraints on the concept of interventions.  These equality checks on the outcomes of certain actions when certain conditions are known or unknown were used to evaluate policies in new and unseen scenarios.  Although the method demonstrated the ability to identify causing factors, it was prone to overestimation, as stated in the paper's key findings.  This overestimation occurred because the method did not take into account the concept of unparametrized null-hypotheses.  Our current work addresses this issue by developing a new class of equality checks that are more effective in determining contrastive causation.  By introducing the concept of null space projections, the method demonstrates the ability to identify causing factors while avoiding overestimation.  Our current work also demonstrates the method's ability to intervene on lower dimensional causes, the results of which outperform existing methods when evaluating task generalization in off-policy learning.  These findings were demonstrated in our experiments involving the path planning and robotic manipulation tasks.  By enhancing the method's ability to identify causing factors, the results show that the concept of contrastive causation can contribute to reducing adverse outcomes in real-world decision-making systems.  By understanding harm as a contrastive concept, the results demonstrate the method's ability to identify causing factors relevant to preventing harm. The tradition of deriving heat conduction equations based on Fourier's law being consistent with the linear thermodynamics of irreversible processes has been followed for over a century. However, this approach has been shown to be insufficient in the presence of memory, requiring modification of the first law of thermodynamics and introduction of the concept of internal temperature, ultimately leading to a system of heat conduction equations. A pioneering paper published in 1981 used this approach to investigate the thermodynamics of fading memory in an isolated system, which led to a unique set of heat conduction equations applicable only in a limited space domain. Following the emergence of the theory of classical generalized materials, the described method was revised, and the novel approach to modeling the conductive heat transfer in materials with memory was introduced. Classical generalized materials were defined as materials for which the constitutive equation can be represented as a relation between the memory function and the time component of the relaxing elementary volume's temperature. Given that the traditional heat conduction equations apply only in a confined space, and the time component of the relaxing temperature in the confined space is the effective temperature, the concept of classical generalized materials with fading memory leads to the development of models based on the theory of classical generalized materials. A significant paper published in 1992 introduced the notion of relaxation times being much longer than those contained in the traditional heat conduction equations, and the modeling of a wide range of materials with memory, which was shown to be consistent with the principle of minimum energy dissipation. A later paper published in 2020 demonstrated the potential of the described method to extend the theory of classical generalized materials to the case of a free boundary being exposed to the environment. Building on this foundation and incorporating the newly introduced concept of intrinsic stability, the final paper published in this series aims to explore an array of topics related to modeling the conductive heat transfer in materials with memory. A significant paper published in 2020 revealed the limitations of the Maxwell-Cattaneo equation, which were also identified in a comprehensive review published in 2019. As an alternative, the combination of the local time-microstructural invariant equation and the non-local parabolic equation has been proposed. In addition to the first law of thermodynamics, the time-microstructural invariant equation can be interpreted using the entropy production inequality, which is a fundamental property of non-equilibrium systems. Consequently, the time-microstructural invariant equation applies not only to modeling the conductive heat transfer in materials with memory but also to a broader range of non-equilibrium systems. Recent research on polariton condensates in microcavities has revealed novel phenomena in quantum cavity physics, encompassing aspects of condensed matter and solid state physics. Our investigation focuses on the yet-theoretically-untreated effects of vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field on the stability of the inflow of coherent photons into the cavity. To address this, we have applied the method of systematic perturbation in the framework of the Tavis and Szymansky-Lax model, describing a multi-level quantum system interacting with a single electromagnetic mode. The perturbation method revealed that vacuum fluctuations could lead to the destabilization of the polariton states, imposing limitations on their stable operating range. Moreover, it became apparent that the statistical properties of the polariton states can be predicted solely based on the initial characteristics of the targeted quantum system, without considering the influence of electromagnetic mode fluctuations. Our theoretical model, providing an exhaustive description of the polariton states, has shown that theDestabilizing effects of vacuum fluctuations are minimized in specific operating conditions, typically encountered in the experimental settings utilized in the study of Szymansky-Lax model. Consequently, it became apparent that the typical practices in the preparation of the initial quantum state could adequately mitigate the destabilizing effects of vacuum fluctuations on the polariton states. Our research, contributing significantly to the understanding of the fundamental aspects of quantum cavity physics, has provided a comprehensive and accurate description of the polariton states, encompassing their statistical attributes and the limitations imposed by the limits of stability. Moreover, our investigation has shed light on the multidisciplinary nature of the research, encompassing the study of condensed matter and solid state physics, the study of electromagnetic fields, and the study of quantum cavity physics, highlighting the far-reaching implications of the phenomena explored in the research.

Passive springs are efficiently utilized in active-suspension systems to counter balance the forces generated during motion. Researchers have applied a similar concept to actuation systems in order to develop more efficient and lightweight actuators. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators demonstrate considerable advantages due to their capacity for high power and efficient energy transformation. Additionally, they facilitate accurate force control and a more natural and lightweight design for the actuators themselves. Notably, these characteristics enhance overall system resilience and flexibility. Straight spring actuators are an inexpensive, simple, and cost-effective solution that effectively integrates these characteristics. They are now being used widely in the field, with notable examples including the M7A humanoid robot and the squat-driven walking of spring-loaded komodo dragons. In this paper, researchers investigate the theoretical and practical applicability of straight spring actuators in legged locomition. They introduce an innovative class of spring actuators that utilize a single spring and two mechanical elements capable of resisting the spring's restoration force. These elements, known as passive damper-filters, significantly improve the control precision of the actuator. Combining active damping with variable filtration capabilities allows for precise force and position control, while passive filtration enables energy recovery and reduces the energy lost due to the restoration spring. Researchers also demonstrate that a purely passive system, based on specific system parameters, is able to maintain equilibrium during stationary periods. Ultimately, computational simulations confirm the practical efficiency and sustainability of the straight spring actuators, while successful experimental testing validates the theoretical findings. These findings showcase the immense potential of straight spring actuators in legged locomotion. They are now being offered as an open-source design, opening opportunities for the integration of active-suspension systems in the development of more resilient and adaptable robots. Existing designs have failed to fully leverage the potential of spring-based actuators, with significant capabilities being left untapped. Researchers now seek to apply the straight spring actuators in various legged locomotion frameworks, such as bipeds, quadrupeds, and seal-like creatures, in order to explore novel design possibilities and trade-offs between efficiency, light weight, and system resilience. In the context of robotics, straight spring actuators offer an appealing solution, particularly in the design and development of more efficient and sustainable robots. Researchers aim to contribute to the ongoing debate on the optimal actuation system for legged locomotion and, in the words of Prof. Hatfeild, ask "why not use springs?" rather than continuing to explore "why not use muscles?" This research delves into the realm of fashion instance-level image retrieval (FIR), a crucial task with significant practical implications. As the world's leading e-commerce platform, AliGmall incorporates the FIR challenge by incorporating product image databases and product page images gathered from the website. The aim of FIR is to identify and rank the most relevant product images from the database matching a query image. The model evaluation is conditioned on a latent variable - the type of display platform from which the query image was sourced. The research introduces two novel FIR tasks: FIR with semantic guidance and cross-view FIR. The paper proposes two cutting-edge approaches: the first utilizes contrastive learning and the second employs meta-training, both leveraging the structural advantages of the Gmall e-commerce database. The research establishes seven semantic query groups and four display view groups, making Gmall's database the first to possess these dual semantic and view dimensions. In the context of ill-posed problems, standard gradient flow methods inevitably produce poorly accurate solutions. To address this, researchers have developed alternative techniques, such as early stop methods, which rely on different stopping criteria instead of convergence norms. Despite this change, issues persist, and approximated solutions remain poorly precise. This work focuses on refining early stop methods by introducing adaptable stopping times based on the problem's solution distance or magnitude of its curvature. It also modifies the early stop method to incorporate a balanced approach, which combines distance and curvature factors. Furthermore, a flexible version of the early stop method is proposed, allowing for a weighted balance between past and future information. This approach is demonstrated on discrete problems from optimal mass transfer, which do not have well-defined solutions due to non-convergence of the problem. Consequently, early stop methods also fail to produce precise solutions. To mitigate this, a temporal splitting strategy is introduced, resulting in the formation of an almost monotone solution with respect to time. This method is evaluated with various stopping weights, demonstrating its potential to improve approximations. In addition, a general flexible stop algorithm is formulated for continuous problems and compared with a solution obtained through deep learning techniques. This comparison highlights the potential of the flexible stop method to provide reasonably accurate and robust results under highly irregular conditions. To further solidify its relevance, the early stop approach is also applied to problems from image deblurring and channel modeling, which are known to have well-defined solutions. This example demonstrates that adjustable early stop methods can yield convergent sequences, which may be useful in developing new solution strategies. This research aims to expand the scope of early stop methods beyond standard gradient flow, which may lead to novel regularization techniques for recovering missing data. This study provides an in-depth review of its findings, which were confirmed through multiple numerical experiments. These examples emphasize the need for careful algorithmic design to ensure that these methods can effectively be used for recovering lost or missing information. Researchers have explored the temporal splitting strategy on discrete problems and continuous PDEs in separate sections of the study. These examples illustrate the potential of a spatial splitting strategy in balancing the effects of past and future information on problem solutions. Furthermore, a flexible stop algorithm for solving PDEs is formulated, which is an extension of earlier studies on discrete problems. This expanded approach is compared with a solution obtained through deep learning methods, which are considered due to their increasing popularity. These comparisons highlight the potential of flexible stop methods, which may be seen as an alternative to regularizing techniques for recovering lost or missing data.
